CM-EIP — Study Guide

CM-EIP — Study Guide

Capital Markets – Excluded Investment Products – Securities, Collective Investment Schemes (EIP) and Foreign Exchange

A guide to the CM-EIP examination: the securities, collective investment scheme and foreign exchange products an adviser may recommend to retail clients, and the analysis used to value them. It condenses the official study guide into what the examination tests, section by section.

  • Exam: 90 multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in 2 hours 30 minutes, including 3 case studies carrying 9 questions (3 per case study); 70% to pass.
  • Currency of the material: the official guide is version 1.1 (March 2025). Check the current MAS notices, SGX and SGX-DT rules, and each product's prospectus or Product Highlights Sheet before relying on a rule or specification.
  • This is a study aid, not a replacement for the prospectus, Product Highlights Sheet, trust deed, insurance policy or current law. If you will conduct regulated activity, you must also satisfy the MAS representative-notification and competency requirements under Notice SFA 04-N22.

How to use this guide

  1. Learn what the investor owns before learning how it is priced. Every product in this syllabus is one of four claims: a deposit, a debt claim, an equity claim, or a contract whose value derives from something else.
  2. For every product, ask: what is the underlying, what does the investor own, what drives the return, what can be lost, and who is the counterparty?
  3. Work the calculations in Chapter 2 and Chapter 7 by hand until the arithmetic is automatic. The examination supplies a formulae sheet but not the judgement about which formula applies.
  4. Practise the case studies in Chapter 12 last. They test the same method as the chapters, applied to a named investor with a stated objective.
  5. Use CMEIP_QUESTIONS.md only after reading the relevant section; its answers explain the reasoning rather than merely naming a letter.

Examination orientation

  • The examination tests knowledge, understanding and application of Excluded Investment Products.
  • Format: 90 multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in 2 hours 30 minutes, including 3 case studies of 9 questions; the passing mark is 70%.
  • Unless a question says otherwise, use a 365-day convention for Singapore Government Securities and a 360-day convention for all other products.
  • A non-programmable financial calculator may be used and a formulae sheet is provided.
  • Scope: financial markets and instruments, risk and return measurement, the drivers of market movements, foreign exchange, company and financial-statement analysis, equities, deposits and fixed income, portfolio management, ETFs, unit trusts, REITs, insurance, warrants, and technical and quantitative analysis.

Master mental model

Every product in this syllabus is a claim on someone else's cash flow, or a contract that transfers an exposure. Classify the product before analysing it.

Claim type Products in this syllabus What the investor owns Primary driver of return What can be lost
Deposit Savings and fixed deposits, currency deposits, structured deposits A debt claim on a bank Contracted interest rate Principal above the insured limit if the bank fails
Money market Treasury bills, commercial paper, CDs, banker's acceptances, repos A short-dated debt claim Discount to face value Issuer default; rollover risk
Bond Government, corporate, convertible, covered, high-yield, zero-coupon A contractual debt claim Coupon plus price change Principal on default; price on a rate rise
Equity Ordinary and preference shares, depositary receipts Residual ownership Earnings growth and dividends Entire investment, ranking last
Fund Unit trusts, ETFs, REITs, business trusts, hedge and private equity funds Units in a pooled vehicle The underlying portfolio, less fees Unit value; liquidity may be restricted
Insurance Whole life, endowment, annuities A contract with an insurer Insurer's crediting rate and bonuses Surrender value below premiums paid
Derivative-linked Warrants, structured warrants A contract, not ownership Movement in the underlying, less time decay Premium paid; gearing magnifies the loss

Conventions used throughout

  • Money is written as plain text (S$10,000, USD1,027,500), never as maths, so it renders literally.
  • Formulas are written as LaTeX and rendered by KaTeX. Every symbol is defined immediately after the formula.
  • Percentages are quoted to the precision the source uses; do not round intermediate steps in a calculation question.
  • Dates and thresholds are reproduced as printed. Where a rule has changed, the current figure is given and the change is noted once.

Chapter 1 — Introduction to Investing, Investments and Financial Markets

This chapter establishes the vocabulary the rest of the syllabus assumes: who the investor is, what a financial asset is, and how markets are organised. Every later chapter classifies a product against the four investor categories and the four asset classes introduced here.

Learning Objectives

The candidate should be able to:

  • Understand the definition and needs of different types of investors.
  • Describe what makes up the financial markets.
  • Define the term "financial assets".
  • Distinguish between financial assets and real assets.
  • Describe the types of money market securities.
  • Describe the types of capital market securities.
  • Explain the differences between the primary market and the secondary market.
  • Identify the characteristics of a good financial market.
  • Distinguish the money market from the capital market.
  • Discuss broadly the bond markets, the equity markets, and the options and futures markets.
  • Understand the inter-market relationships and how the economy is sustained by the financial markets.

1.1 Introduction

The investment environment is changing quickly. Regulatory infrastructure has developed, the mix of promoted products has shifted, and financial technology has widened access to investments while admitting new players who redefine how money, wealth and value are transferred and stored. A representative of a financial institution must keep expanding the breadth of investment knowledge to stay relevant.

Representatives must also be able to identify suitable products and services for the varying needs, expectations, risk profiles, preferences and limitations of their clients, subject to regulatory requirements and industry ethical considerations. Understanding client needs is the basis of every good recommendation, but client needs and return expectations must match what the markets can actually deliver.

1.1.1 Definition and Needs of Different Types of Investors

Whether the client is institutional or retail, the first step is to understand their needs before any advice or product recommendation is made. Section 4A of the Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA) defines Accredited Investors (AIs), Expert Investors (EIs) and Institutional Investors (IIs); anyone outside those definitions is a Retail Investor.

Category Statutory basis Why the classification matters
Institutional Investor (II) SFA s 4A: government, statutory boards, central banks, banks, insurers, CMS licensees, approved exchanges and clearing houses, pension funds, CIS, and similar prescribed entities Sophisticated, structured, and permitted the widest product access
Accredited Investor (AI) SFA s 4A: an individual meeting the wealth or income tests, or a corporation, trust, partnership or joint account meeting the prescribed tests Presumed able to bear more risk; may access unrated bonds and products needing neither a prospectus nor a reasonable basis for recommendation
Expert Investor (EI) SFA s 4A: a person whose business involves acquiring, disposing of or holding capital markets products Presumed to understand product risk through occupation, not wealth
Retail Investor Everyone not in the three categories above Receives the highest level of protective regulation

Accredited Investor thresholds. An individual qualifies as an AI on any one of three tests:

  • Net personal assets exceeding S2million**.Theprimaryresidenceiscountednetofanyoutstandingsecuredcreditfacilityandis**cappedatS2 million**. The primary residence is counted net of any outstanding secured credit facility and is **capped at S1 million.
  • Financial assets (bank deposits, investment products and other prescribed assets, net of liabilities) exceeding S$1 million.
  • Income in the preceding 12 months of not less than S$300,000.

A corporation or other entity qualifies with net assets exceeding S$10 million, as determined by its most recent audited balance sheet, or by a balance sheet it certifies as giving a true and fair view, dated within the preceding 12 months. A partnership (other than an LLP) qualifies when each partner is an AI; a corporation qualifies when its entire share capital is owned by one or more AIs; and a person holding a joint account with an AI qualifies in respect of dealings through that joint account.

The AI opt-in regime. MAS raised the qualifying benchmark for AIs and introduced an opt-in regime: a capital markets intermediary (CMI) can no longer automatically treat anyone who qualifies as an AI unless the investor opts to be treated as one. An AI may also elect to benefit from the full range of retail safeguards.

Institutional Investors. IIs are "super-investors" by size and market impact. Their capital and resources give them timely, wide access to market information and professional research. They generally have clearly defined investment goals with prescribed directives and explicit requirements covering costs, execution efficiency, research and reporting support, volatility and return ranges, and asset-allocation, concentration and exposure limits. Because they are sophisticated and act within an institutional structure, they are less likely to make uneducated investments and are typically permitted wider product access than other investor types.

IIs are commonly classified by the purpose for which the money is invested:

Type of II Purpose of the funds
Pension funds Providing retirement income
Insurance funds Meeting expected claims
Endowment funds Satisfying philanthropic spending commitments
Sovereign wealth funds Stabilising the national economy, or saving for future generations

Expert Investors. An EI trades capital markets products in the ordinary course of business. Like AIs, EIs receive less regulatory protection than retail investors, but for a different reason: not greater wealth, but occupational understanding of product risk. An EI is effectively a sub-set of retail investors meeting specific experience requirements in the SFA, so the same factors generally influence their decisions. Two differences matter: market rumours that move retail investors may not move EIs, and EIs tend to have a clearer idea of their objectives and constraints and may prefer greater involvement in the investment process.

Retail Investors. A retail investor buys securities for a personal account rather than for an organisation. Retail investors are the opposite of IIs: they trade in small amounts, trade less frequently, and have little influence over corporate decisions or the capital markets. Lacking access to boardrooms or timely market information, they are assumed to be less financially savvy and more risk-averse than AIs and IIs, and are therefore given more protective regulation.

Three regulatory developments shape how retail investors are treated in Singapore:

  • More stringent regulation of non-conventional products such as precious metal buy-back arrangements, and the regulation of collectively managed investment schemes as Collective Investment Schemes (CIS).
  • Refinement of investor classifications under the SFA and the Financial Advisers Act 2001 (FAA).
  • An option for AIs to benefit from the full range of retail safeguards.

Most factors influencing a retail investor's decision coincide with those of an individual AI, because an AI is a sub-set of retail investors meeting specific wealth and income requirements.

Factors influencing investment decisions. The factors differ between individual and corporate investors.

Individual Corporate
Demographics (age, gender, education level) Management outlook (growth vs decline)
Lifestyle (confidence level, number of dependants) Size of firm
Risk tolerance (volatility range, risk-return spectrum) Corporate governance — balancing vested interests against management control while safeguarding all stakeholders
Market trends and forecasts Market trends and forecasts
Tax (higher brackets prefer tax-exempt returns) Tax (fiscal incentives or barriers on asset classes)
Investment horizon Investment horizon
Liquidity Cash flow
Psychological influences (desires, prejudices, emotions) Corporate culture (aggressive vs passive)
Personal values (social or religious values shaping attitude to certain asset classes) Corporate values

Client profiling. A representative maps the client against a risk-and-return grid. The standard return expectations quoted in the guide are:

Objective Expected return
Preserve wealth and purchasing power 2–4%
Income with some growth 4–6%
Steady balanced growth 6–8%
Aggressive growth 8–12%

The profile also records investment knowledge (limited and low, average and occasional, experienced and regular, sophisticated and high), risk tolerance (low, medium, high), investment horizon (less than 1 year, 2–5 years, more than 5 years), the type of service sought (discretionary management, advisory, or transaction ideas and execution), product preferences (equities, fixed income, funds, derivatives), and the amount to invest (less than S2million,S2 million, S2–10 million, S10–50million,morethanS10–50 million, more than S50 million).

1.1.2 Investment Products and Services

Products range from those actively traded and aimed mainly at IIs to those designed for AIs, high net worth individuals (HNWIs) or retail investors. Most products built from traditional asset classes — deposits, foreign currency, fixed income and equity — seek to provide yield and/or capital gains. Financial innovation also lets investors take a bearish position using put options, futures and inverse exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to generate potentially higher yields.

Clients now have access to large amounts of online information, which raises their interest in the products available. Investment professionals must therefore widen their product knowledge to give the right information and timely advice.

Product or service Defined interest, yield or dividend Potential for higher yield Potential capital gains Regular payout stream Inverse or change in payout (hedge) Amplify gains/losses (leverage) Diversify

The wider range of securities and derivative structures lets investors:

  • Diversify their portfolios.
  • Optimise the risk-return profile of their portfolios.
  • Protect investments, or take advantage of downward market movement.
  • Selectively exploit opportunities through a leverage effect.

1.1.3 Financial Assets and Real Assets from the Individual Investor's Perspective

Beyond financial assets, individuals may own real physical assets and business assets whose values and cash flows can be significantly larger than their financial assets. For individuals the flow of funds between business, physical and financial assets is closely related.

Business owners have business financing needs and require corporate finance products and services as well as cash management. Business salaries and profits provide income that can be invested in financial assets or ploughed back into the business. Purchases of real physical assets such as real estate require financing and can be funded from financial assets. A representative must therefore be alert to business needs, changes and decisions about business assets and physical assets, because those can have a major impact on financial assets.

Financial assets Real, physical and business assets
Traditional asset classes: cash deposits, foreign currencies, short-term money market instruments, bonds and other fixed income instruments, equities, insurance Commodities: energy (crude oil, LNG, refined products, petrochemicals, coal, electricity), metals (precious, base, ferrous), agriculture (grain, softs, livestock, biofuel, dairy, forestry)
Derivatives: exchange-traded derivatives, financial futures, options, swaps, warrants, OTC structured products Real estate: commercial, residential, industrial, agricultural
Investment funds: ETFs, private funds sold OTC, pure asset class vs diversified funds, strategy funds, capital guaranteed funds Businesses: privately owned plant, property, equipment, rights, patents, technology, network, distribution
Alternative investments: hedge funds, commodity funds, REITs and real estate funds, private equity funds Precious stones and jewellery: diamonds, rubies, emeralds
Collectibles: art, antiques, wine, limited-edition memorabilia

1.2 Financial Assets

Financial assets are paper or electronic claims on an issuer. The issuer may be from the public sector — a government such as the Singapore Government, or an agency such as the Housing and Development Board — a supranational such as the World Bank, or the private sector, such as a corporation. Financial assets are broadly classified into debt, equity and derivative instruments or securities.

1.2.1 Local and Foreign Cash Deposits

The most basic asset class is cash: Singapore dollar deposits in current, savings or fixed (time) deposit accounts, plus foreign currency deposit accounts. In a low interest rate environment, holding investible funds in cash carries a high opportunity cost, because inflation erodes purchasing power. Foreign currency deposits carry currency exchange risk and have been relatively volatile since the global financial crisis.

1.2.2 Fixed Income Securities

Fixed income securities are primarily interest-bearing instruments providing a fixed return. They include treasury bills, fixed-rate bonds, certificates of deposit, commercial papers and debentures.

Short-term money market securities. Money market instruments are relatively low-risk, highly liquid, short-term debt instruments issued by governments, financial institutions and corporations. Minimum denominations are relatively large and transaction sizes can be substantial. Maturities range from 1 day to 1 year, and are often less than 90 days.

Instrument What it is Key examinable feature
Treasury bill Issued by a central bank on behalf of the government to raise short-term funds Obligation of the government, so treated as free of default; its return is the proxy for the risk-free rate. Issued on a discounted basis by tender, payable or redeemable at face value at maturity
Repurchase agreement (repo) Sale of a security at a specified price with a simultaneous commitment by the seller (borrower) to buy it back at a specified price and future date A form of borrowing for the seller. The effective interest is the difference between the purchase and sale prices
Reverse repo The converse: purchase of a security by the lending party combined with a forward sale back to the borrowing party A form of lending
Commercial paper Short-term unsecured promissory note issued by a corporation A discounted money market instrument, like a treasury bill
Banker's acceptance A time draft drawn on a bank by a customer, which the bank agrees to pay on a specified future date Created to facilitate commercial trade, particularly international trade; negotiable, so the holder can discount it in the money market
Certificate of deposit (CD) Certificate issued by a bank in exchange for a deposit placed with it Yields are quoted on an interest-bearing basis, not a discount basis

Debt securities. Debt securities are long-term fixed borrowings by issuers. The investor lends a principal to the issuer, which agrees to make periodic interest payments and repay the principal at maturity. Debt securities are also called bonds. Singapore has one of the most developed bond markets in Asia, offering Singapore Government securities, statutory board securities, supranational bonds and corporate bonds.

Bond label Definition
Eurobond An international bond denominated in a currency not native to the country where it is issued
Eurodollar bond Denominated in US dollars and sold outside the United States to non-US investors
Euroyen bond Denominated in yen and sold outside Japan — for example, a Japanese company issuing Euroyen bonds for sale in London
Yankee bond Sold in the United States, denominated in US dollars, but issued by a foreign corporation or government
Domestic bond Sold by an issuer within its own country in that country's currency

1.2.3 Equity Securities

Equity securities represent an ownership interest in a company. There are two forms:

  • Ordinary shares. Ordinary shareholders elect the directors and vote on company issues, usually with votes equal to the number of shares owned.
  • Preference shares. Technically equity, but also a hybrid security: voting rights are limited (they can vote only in limited circumstances) and the instrument resembles both equity and fixed income.

Priority of claim on the company's assets runs creditors first, then preference shareholders, then ordinary shareholders, who hold the residual claim.

1.2.4 Derivatives

Derivatives derive their value from the price of an underlying asset such as a stock, a bond or a market index. They include options, warrants, futures and convertible securities.

Instrument Definition Distinguishing feature
Structured product A note or deposit bundled with one or more derivatives Return is linked to the performance of one or more underlyings
Option Gives the buyer the right to buy (call) or sell (put) a specified amount of an underlying within a specified period at a specified price A right, not an obligation
Company-issued warrant Right to buy a given number of the company's shares at a specified price over a given period Usually runs for several years
Structured warrant Issued usually by banks; lets investors profit from upward (call warrant) or downward (put warrant) price performance of an underlying Costs a fraction of the underlying's price
Futures contract Agreement for future delivery of an asset between buyer and seller at a predetermined price Exchange-traded with standardised terms; may be cash settled or physically settled
Convertible security Holder may convert into a predetermined number of ordinary shares within a specified period Pays interest at a lower yield than the same issuer's plain corporate bond; the difference is the value of the embedded share option

1.2.5 Portfolio Management and Investment Funds

Clients may invest directly in single securities or entrust funds to portfolio managers. Professional management benefits clients who lack the time, information, expertise, discipline or emotional temperament to invest actively.

Different asset classes and securities are pooled and managed by professional fund managers, either as pure asset funds or diversified under asset allocation strategies matched to client risk profiles and objectives. Hedge fund managers offer alternative approaches that seek returns irrespective of market direction. Funds are offered on stock exchanges worldwide as ETFs, and over-the-counter (OTC) by financial institutions.

1.3 Financial Markets

Financial markets are where assets are bought or sold, borrowed or lent, or otherwise transacted among issuers, investors, speculators, hedgers and intermediaries. Investments may be made in equity securities (shares, equity unit trusts) and debt securities (short-term money market paper, long-term fixed income bonds); sophisticated investors may use derivatives such as equity options and futures. The resulting markets include the equities market, money market, fixed income market, commodities market, options and futures market, and foreign exchange market.

These markets have seen extensive liberalisation and global consolidation, the impact of information technology enabling alternative platforms such as Electronic Communications Networks (for example Instinet), and rapid adoption of online technology letting professional and retail investors use brokerage services through computer networks and personal devices.

Technology also enables algorithmic trading, which uses a computer program following a defined set of instructions to execute a trade and can slice large trades to minimise market impact. A form of algorithmic trading is high frequency trading, which relies on computer speed to analyse large amounts of market information and self-execute trades in fractions of a second.

Structure of the financial markets. Four asset-class pillars sit under the markets:

Debt securities Equity securities Derivatives Foreign exchange
Money market, fixed income Ordinary shares, preference shares Options, futures, swaps, structured products Spots, forwards

Participants in financial markets:

  • Investors — retail, private bank and institutional investors, including fund management companies.
  • Issuers — public and private sector companies.
  • Intermediaries — broker/dealer firms and market makers.
  • Regulators.
  • Electronic exchanges — for equities, debt, derivatives and commodities.
  • Infrastructure providers — clearing houses, central depositories, communications networks, trade repositories.
  • Financial institutions — distribution and underwriting of initial public offerings (IPOs), and participation in the secondary markets.

How markets sustain economic growth. Capital seekers (issuers of stocks and bonds) pay through arrangers and intermediaries (investment banks, underwriters, distributors, brokerages) to reach wholesale capital providers (banks, hedge and pension funds, insurance companies), who in turn serve retail capital providers (individuals, small firms).

Beyond regulated exchange-based capital markets there is growing activity in private equity and mezzanine financing, where capital seekers and providers negotiate funding for mergers, acquisitions or buy-outs. In these pre-primary market sectors, capital is raised from private investors rather than from the public. Some forms are referred to as "shadow banking".

1.3.1 Primary Market

The primary market is where new issues of securities are listed on the stock exchange and sold to the public. New sales of debt or equity take place through IPOs. The issuer receives the cash from subscribers, who receive financial claims that previously did not exist.

1.3.2 Secondary Market

Once new securities have been sold in the primary market they are listed and begin trading in the secondary market, which involves buying and selling securities initially sold in the primary market. Proceeds from a secondary-market sale go to the selling investor, not the original issuer. Secondary markets provide the liquidity essential to the proper functioning of capital markets.

1.3.3 Characteristics of a Good Financial Market

Characteristic What it requires
Availability of information Timely, accurate information on the volume and prices of past transactions and on all currently outstanding bids and offers, so participants can determine an appropriate price
Liquidity Ability to buy or sell quickly at prices not substantially different from previous transactions, absent new information. Marketability (likelihood of a quick sale) is necessary but not sufficient; price continuity (prices do not change much between transactions) is the other component. A continuous market requires depth — numerous buyers and sellers willing to trade at current prices
Transaction costs Low across all aspects: the cost of reaching the market, brokerage, and transferring the security. This attribute is internal efficiency
Bid-offer spread Narrow, reflecting wide and deep market-making where market makers readily quote two-way prices
Information efficiency Prices adjust quickly to new information on supply or demand, so prices reflect all available information
Price discovery The most important function of any financial market: with the other characteristics in place, prices become transparent and responsive to market forces

1.3.4 Bond Markets

The largest domestic bond market in the world is the US bond market. The US Treasury issues notes and bonds with maturities greater than 1 year, and is the largest single issuer of debt globally, making the treasury market the most active and liquid in the world. Treasury bills, notes and bonds are usually issued through an auction where dealers submit competitive bids.

The Eurobond market remains important for investors seeking foreign currency bonds, particularly while quantitative easing held interest rates very low and pushed investors into long-term issues. Because participation is worldwide, dealing and settlement procedures are governed by the rules of the Association of International Bond Dealers (AIBD).

Although many corporate bonds are listed on major exchanges such as the NYSE, bond trading is mostly OTC through bond dealers, which are mostly banks and large investment banking firms.

1.3.5 Equity Markets

Ordinary shares, preference shares, warrants and ETFs trade actively on equity markets. Equity markets differ across countries in size, liquidity, degree of regulation, trading and settlement systems, and restrictions on foreign ownership. Internet brokerage has made equity investment more international.

Size and structure facts to remember:

  • The NYSE and NASDAQ combined account for slightly more than half of world stock market capitalisation.
  • Singapore is not in the top twenty global exchanges by market capitalisation, but SGX is the world's most liquid offshore market for the benchmark equity indices of China, India, Japan and ASEAN, and offers commodity and currency derivative products.
  • Japan has 8 stock exchanges, with the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) dominating.
  • The US has regional exchanges alongside the NYSE and the American Stock Exchange (AMEX), listing small companies with geographic interest.

Settlement periods vary by market:

Market Settlement
China T+0 — settlement on the trade date, on the philosophy that the investor must have funds on hand
United States T+2
Singapore T+2 (SGX ST Rule 9.2.1: 2 exchange business days after the trade day)
Hong Kong T+2

Securities not listed on an organised exchange may trade in the OTC market. In the US this is a negotiated market of dealers or market makers standing ready to buy and sell at market prices. Unlike brokers, dealers have a vested interest in transactions and earn the spread between bid and offer.

1.3.6 Options and Futures Markets

A futures exchange is a marketplace for financial instruments and commodities where buying and selling of underlying products is contracted for future delivery.

Exchange Position
Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) Group Largest futures exchange; processes 3 billion contracts of diverse derivatives worth approximately USD1 quadrillion annually on average
Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Second largest, created through mergers and acquisitions among exchanges and clearing houses mainly in the US and Europe
SGX Operates the largest derivatives market in Asia, benefiting from Singapore's position as the largest foreign exchange centre in Asia; offers futures on all the major Asian equity indices
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited Owns the London Metal Exchange in addition to its stock and futures exchange

Futures trade on electronic exchanges, with trades cleared through the clearing house each business day. The clearing house lets participants reverse a position before maturity because it tracks each participant's outstanding contracts.

US options trade on an exchange floor such as the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) using a system of market makers who quote bid and ask prices, with floor brokers trading either with the market maker or with other floor brokers. The Options Clearing Corporation (OCC) acts as intermediary between the brokers representing buyers and sellers (writers): it becomes the buyer for every seller and the seller for every buyer, guaranteeing that all contract obligations are met.

1.4 Digital Disruption and Fintech

The financial industry has undergone significant technological change and digital disruption. With internet access, the roles of financial institutions and capital markets are being challenged by new entrants, and banks work with fintech companies to design equivalent internet platforms and solutions.

Digital development Impact on the financial sector
Internet banking Consumer and branch banking redefined; tasks split between what can be done online and what needs face-to-face interaction; fewer brick-and-mortar branches; roles and activities redefined
Rise in non-bank internet lending New non-bank entrants provide direct financing over the internet; big-data credit analysis, profiling and direct access let them compete with banks, finance companies and traditional moneylenders
Internet business transactions reducing cash float Transactions that took days to clear through the banking system now clear directly, reducing the daily float of cash
Non-bank digital wallets bypassing banks Excess cash moves from current and savings accounts into digital wallets (for example Tencent, Alibaba); platform providers now recommend investment funds, bypassing retail banks offering lower deposit rates
Digital currencies for transactions in cyberspace Cryptocurrencies are not backed by reserves or central banks, are authenticated through blockchain, bypass the banking system and provide some anonymity. They are not recognised as legal tender and make up only about 1% of currency transactions; Bitcoin futures trade on the CME and CBOE

1.5 Summary

  • Representatives must distinguish institutional, accredited, expert and retail investors in the local context and identify their investment needs.
  • Financial assets are broadly classified as debt securities, equity securities, collective investment schemes, funds or derivatives.
  • Money market instruments are highly liquid, short-term debt instruments with maturities of less than one year.
  • Fixed income debt securities are borrowings by issuers who agree to make periodic interest payments and return principal at maturity.
  • Equity securities represent ownership interest in a corporation; the two types are ordinary shares and preference shares.
  • Derivative securities derive their value from underlying assets; options, warrants, futures and convertible bonds are examples.
  • Investors may invest directly in single securities or entrust funds to portfolio managers.
  • The primary market is where new securities are distributed by the issuer to investors; the secondary market is where those securities then trade.
  • In evaluating the quality of a financial market, consider availability of information, liquidity, transaction cost, the bid-offer spread, and informational and price-discovery efficiency.
  • Bond trading is mostly over-the-counter through bond dealers rather than through organised exchanges.
  • Equity markets differ across countries in size, liquidity, degree of regulation, trading and settlement systems, and restrictions on foreign ownership.
  • The financial sector and capital markets are going through a digital revolution, upgrading traditional functions and admitting new entrants and joint ventures with financial institutions.

Exam cues

  • Four investor categories, one statutory source. SFA s 4A defines II, AI and EI; everyone else is retail. Retail gets the most protection; II gets the widest product access.
  • AI thresholds — memorise all three individual tests: net personal assets > S2m**(primaryresidencenetofsecuredcredit,**cappedatS2m** (primary residence net of secured credit, **capped at S1m), financial assets > S1m**netofliabilities,orincomeinthepreceding**12months≥S1m** net of liabilities, or income in the preceding **12 months ≥ S300k. Corporate AI: net assets > S$10m on the latest audited balance sheet, dated within the preceding 12 months.
  • AI opt-in. A CMI cannot automatically treat a qualifying investor as an AI; the investor must opt in, and may instead elect full retail safeguards.
  • EI is about occupation, not wealth. An EI trades capital markets products in the ordinary course of business — a sub-set of retail investors meeting experience requirements.
  • Money market vs capital market. Money market: maturity 1 day to 1 year, often < 90 days, large denominations, low risk, highly liquid. Capital market: > 1 year (bonds, equities).
  • Discount vs interest-bearing. Treasury bills, commercial paper and banker's acceptances are discounted instruments; certificates of deposit are quoted on an interest-bearing basis.
  • Repo vs reverse repo. A repo is borrowing by the seller of the security; a reverse repo is lending by the buyer. The effective interest is the difference between the purchase and sale prices.
  • Bond labels turn on two questions: which currency, and where sold. Eurobond = currency not native to the place of issue; Eurodollar = USD sold outside the US; Yankee = USD sold in the US by a foreign issuer; domestic = issuer's own country and currency.
  • Claim priority: creditors → preference shareholders → ordinary shareholders (residual).
  • Primary vs secondary. Primary: issuer receives the cash, new claims are created. Secondary: the selling investor receives the cash, and the market supplies liquidity.
  • Six characteristics of a good market: information availability, liquidity (marketability + price continuity + depth), low transaction costs (internal efficiency), narrow bid-offer spread, information efficiency, price discovery.
  • Settlement: China T+0; US, Singapore and Hong Kong T+2.
  • Clearing house roles: futures clearing house tracks outstanding contracts so positions can be reversed; the OCC becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer.
  • Trap: a dealer earns the bid-offer spread and has a vested interest in the transaction; a broker acts as agent for a commission. Do not use the terms interchangeably.
  • Trap: preference shares are equity in law but behave like debt in priority and payout — the examination tests the hybrid character, not a simple label.
  • Trap: the AI net-personal-assets test counts the primary residence net of the secured loan and capped at S$1m, not at market value.

Chapter 2 — Risk, Return and Time Value Calculations

This is the most calculation-heavy chapter in the syllabus, and the one every later valuation chapter depends on. It defines six measures of return, four measures of risk, the classification of investment risk, and the time-value formulas used in Chapters 6, 7, 8 and 12.

Learning Objectives

The candidate should be able to:

  • Explain the concepts of risk and return in the management of investments.
  • Explain the relationship between risk and return in the context of the risk-return trade-off.
  • Identify the components of the total return and compute expected return on an investment.
  • Explain the statistical measures of risk.
  • Compute standard deviation and coefficient of variation as risk measures.
  • Identify the various risks associated with investments.
  • Calculate the present and future value of a single cash flow.

2.1 Risk and Return

The risk-return (or risk-reward) principle holds that rational investors demand higher potential returns when they take on more risk, and do not demand as high a rate of return when risk is lower.

The choice of assets follows the investor's risk profile. An investor with a low appetite for risk fears losing any part of capital and considers relatively safe money market instruments offering a steady flow of interest income. An investor with a higher appetite is prepared to lose some — and in some cases all — of capital, and considers riskier securities such as equities in expectation of higher return.

Risk is a property of the instrument, not the asset class. Several examples make the point:

  • Cash is often considered least risky because it is a medium of exchange and is liquid, yet cash is volatile against other currencies. Currency volatility rises with political change, currency-management policy change, and fiscal and monetary policy change.
  • Government bonds, once unquestionably secure, now carry more counterparty risk, changing the traditional view of "riskless" sovereign debt (Portugal, Italy, Greece, Spain).
  • A CCC-rated (junk or speculative grade) bond is much riskier than a AAA-rated blue-chip corporate bond. The blue-chip company's stock may be safer than the CCC bond if its business and financial profile is conservative, even though equities are generally the riskier asset class.
  • Derivatives sit at the upper end of the risk-return continuum because most structured products embed long and/or short options. The range is diverse, however: some are capital guaranteed and therefore safer than some equities.

A representative must therefore examine the riskiness inherent in the security itself, review the product documents (Product Highlights Sheet and prospectus), and ask the relevant questions. Only after understanding the product structure, underlying strategy and payoff scenarios should a recommendation be made.

The VIX. The Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) Volatility Index — the "VIX" — is the bellwether risk indicator for the US stock market and, indirectly, for global equities because of the weight of the US economy. It measures the market's expectation of 30-day S&P 500 volatility and is called the "investor fear gauge".

VIX level Interpretation
Above 30 High volatility; usually spikes upward during periods of great market uncertainty
Below 20 Relative stability
89.5 The high reached at the height of the Global Financial Crisis in October 2008
48 The high reached during the European Debt Crisis

A higher VIX means more risk and volatility are expected. Market maturity also matters: financial assets in mature markets (the United States) are perceived as less risky than those in emerging markets (China) or frontier markets (Sri Lanka).

2.2 Calculating Returns

Six measures of return are examinable. Each answers a different question, and the examination tests whether you pick the right one.

Measure Question it answers Section
Total return What did I earn over the holding period? 2.2.1
Expected rate of return What do I expect, given probabilities? 2.2.2
Annualised rate of return What is the equivalent one-year rate? 2.2.3
Real rate of return What did I earn after inflation? 2.2.4
Currency-adjusted return What did I earn in my reference currency? 2.2.5
Internal rate of return What rate equates my actual cash flows? 2.2.6

2.2.1 Total Return

Total return on a pre-tax basis has two components:

  • Current income — income received during the holding period, such as dividends from shares and interest from fixed income securities or fixed deposits.
  • Capital gain or loss — the change in price of the security.

Total Return=Income+Capital Gain or LossPurchase Price\text{Total Return} = \frac{\text{Income} + \text{Capital Gain or Loss}}{\text{Purchase Price}}

Because the capital gain or loss is the ending price minus the beginning price, the same relationship is written:

Total Return=CFt+(PE−PB)PB\text{Total Return} = \frac{CF_t + (P_E - P_B)}{P_B}

where CFtCF_t is the sum of cash flows during measurement period tt, PEP_E is the price at the end of period tt (the sale price), and PBP_B is the price at the beginning of period tt (the purchase price).

Worked example. You buy 1,000 shares of XYZ at $5 each and receive a dividend per share of $0.20. You sell one year later at $6.

Total Return=0.20+(6−5)5=0.24=24%\text{Total Return} = \frac{0.20 + (6 - 5)}{5} = 0.24 = 24\%

2.2.2 Expected Rate of Return

The historical rate of return is known; the expected rate of return is the future rate, which may or may not be realised. A single figure such as "15%" is a point estimate. Because the future is uncertain, several returns are possible under different economic outlooks, and probabilities can be assigned to each.

E(R)=∑i=1nripiE(R) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i p_i

where E(R)E(R) is the expected return on the security, rir_i is the iith possible return, pip_i is the probability of that return, and nn is the number of possible returns. The expected return is therefore the probability-weighted average of possible returns.

Worked example.

Economic scenario Probability (pip_i) Return (rir_i)
Economic boom 0.20 25%
Recession 0.20 −30%
Stable 0.60 15%
1.00

E(R)=(0.20×0.25)+(0.20×−0.30)+(0.60×0.15)=0.05−0.06+0.09=0.08=8%E(R) = (0.20 \times 0.25) + (0.20 \times -0.30) + (0.60 \times 0.15) = 0.05 - 0.06 + 0.09 = 0.08 = 8\%

2.2.3 Annualised Rate of Return

Returns are often presented on an annualised basis. The annualised rate compounds the holding-period return to a one-year equivalent.

Annualised Rate of Return=(1+rperiod)12/m−1\text{Annualised Rate of Return} = (1 + r_{\text{period}})^{12/m} - 1

where mm is the number of months in the holding period.

Worked example. A product is expected to generate a maximum return of 2.5% over 3 months.

(1.025)12/3−1=1.10381−1=0.104≈10.4%(1.025)^{12/3} - 1 = 1.10381 - 1 = 0.104 \approx 10.4\%

The compounding logic, step by step, on $1:

Period end Value
3 months $1 × 1.025 = $1.025
6 months $1.025 × 1.025 = $1.0506
9 months $1.0506 × 1.025 = $1.0769
12 months $1.0769 × 1.025 = $1.1038

The annual return is therefore 10.38%, which is (1.025)4−1(1.025)^4 - 1, the same as (1.025)12/3−1(1.025)^{12/3} - 1. The assumption is that the investment plus interest is reinvested — the return is compounded, earning interest on interest.

Working backwards. To find the return achievable over 4 months from a product quoting an annualised target of 12%:

(1+r4)12/4−1=0.12(1 + r_4)^{12/4} - 1 = 0.12 (1+r4)=(1.12)4/12(1 + r_4) = (1.12)^{4/12} r4=(1.12)1/3−1=0.0385=3.85%r_4 = (1.12)^{1/3} - 1 = 0.0385 = 3.85\%

2.2.4 Real Rate of Return (Inflation-Adjusted Return)

The real rate removes the effect of inflation, because asset prices rise with general inflation independently of the investment's performance.

Real Return=1+rnominal1+inflation−1\text{Real Return} = \frac{1 + r_{\text{nominal}}}{1 + \text{inflation}} - 1

Worked example. With an annualised return of 10.4% and inflation of 2%:

1.1041.02−1=0.08235=8.24%\frac{1.104}{1.02} - 1 = 0.08235 = 8.24\%

With deflation of 1% (asset values fell 1%), the same formula gives:

1.1041−0.01−1=11.52%\frac{1.104}{1 - 0.01} - 1 = 11.52\%

Note the sign convention: inflation is added to 1 in the denominator, deflation is subtracted.

2.2.5 Currency-Adjusted Return

Assets and income generated in a foreign currency must be restated in the investor's base (reference) currency. A fund invested in foreign securities must have its performance restated in the desired reference currency, usually the local currency.

Worked example. A Singapore portfolio manager reviews a JPY portfolio pegged to the Nikkei 225 and a USD portfolio pegged to the S&P 500 over January 2013 to December 2017.

Jan 2013 Dec 2017 Change
Nikkei 225 10,688.11 23,714.53 +121.88%
SGD/JPY 71.4943 85.0038 +18.89%
S&P 500 1,466.47 2,743.15 +87.06%
USD/SGD 1.2272 1.3268 +8.12%

JPY portfolio, restated in SGD. The reference currency (SGD) is the first listed currency of SGD/JPY, so divide.

  • Beginning Nikkei in SGD: 10,688.11/71.4943=149.496010{,}688.11 / 71.4943 = 149.4960
  • Ending Nikkei in SGD: 23,714.53/85.0038=278.982023{,}714.53 / 85.0038 = 278.9820
  • Currency-adjusted return: (278.9820/149.4960)−1=0.8662=86.62%(278.9820 / 149.4960) - 1 = 0.8662 = 86.62\%

This is lower than the Nikkei's 121.88% because the SGD strengthened against the JPY, so the JPY gains are adjusted down.

USD portfolio, restated in SGD. The reference currency (SGD) is the second listed currency of USD/SGD, so multiply.

  • Beginning S&P 500 in SGD: 1,466.47×1.2272=1,799.65201{,}466.47 \times 1.2272 = 1{,}799.6520
  • Ending S&P 500 in SGD: 2,743.15×1.3268=3,639.61142{,}743.15 \times 1.3268 = 3{,}639.6114
  • Currency-adjusted return: (3,639.6114/1,799.6520)−1=1.0224=102.24%(3{,}639.6114 / 1{,}799.6520) - 1 = 1.0224 = 102.24\%

This is higher than the S&P 500's 87.06% because the SGD weakened against the USD, so the USD gains are adjusted up.

The shortcut rule. The same answers come from combining the portfolio return with the currency return directly:

  • JPY portfolio: (1+1.2188)/(1+0.1889)−1=0.8662=86.62%(1 + 1.2188) / (1 + 0.1889) - 1 = 0.8662 = 86.62\%
  • USD portfolio: (1+0.8706)×(1+0.0812)−1=1.0224=102.24%(1 + 0.8706) \times (1 + 0.0812) - 1 = 1.0224 = 102.24\%

The rule of thumb: divide (1+portfolio return)(1 + \text{portfolio return}) by (1+currency return)(1 + \text{currency return}) when the reference currency is the first listed currency of the pair, and multiply when it is the second listed currency.

In SGD terms the US portfolio outperformed the Japanese portfolio, because the SGD strengthened against the JPY but weakened against the USD.

Some corporate and high net worth (HNW) investors use a major world currency such as USD or EUR as their reference currency because they take an international view of their invested assets. The US remains the largest capital market and many instruments, including commodities, are still denominated in USD, so a USD reference is convenient. Some HNW individuals in Asia keep offshore investments separate from domestic ones and use USD as the reference; in some countries local currencies have proven more volatile than global currencies, so investors prefer not to use them as the reference.

2.2.6 Internal Rate of Return

The internal rate of return (IRR) equates all cash outflows (investments) against all cash inflows (proceeds) evaluated at the same point in time. It is used for projects and investments with uneven cash flows, such as private equity.

Worked example (1). An investment requires $1 million now and a further $2 million at the start of the next year. The client receives $3.5 million only at the end of year 3.

Year 1 Year 2 Year 3
−$1m −$2m +$3.5m

Evaluated at the end of year 3, with IRR denoted rr:

1(1+r)3+2(1+r)2+0(1+r)=3.51(1+r)^3 + 2(1+r)^2 + 0(1+r) = 3.5

The first $1m compounds for 3 years, the second $2m for 2 years, and the $0 for 1 year.

Choosing a starting guess. Total invested is $3m and total received is $3.5m, implying (3.5/3)−1=16.7%(3.5/3) - 1 = 16.7\%, which divided by 3 years gives 5.55%.

Trial rate Left-hand side Conclusion
5.55% $3.4041m Below $3.5m, so the rate must be higher
7.00% $3.5148m Marginally above $3.5m, so the rate must be slightly lower
6.80% $3.4999m Close; 6.81% improves accuracy

The IRR is approximately 6.8%. In a spreadsheet the calculation is =IRR(cell range, [guess]), solved iteratively.

IRR versus compounded annualised return. The IRR is the money-weighted return in a portfolio context: it is the actual return generated for the client given the movement of their cash flows, and it is sensitive to the size and timing of those flows. The compounded annualised rate is the time-weighted return and is unaffected by them.

Worked example (2). A client invests $5m in a fund at the end of 2016. The fund returns 2% in 2017, so the client withdraws $3m at the end of the year. The fund returns 10% in 2018, so the client adds $8m at the start of 2019, and the fund loses 4% in 2019.

(a) Fund value at the end of 2019:

Step Calculation Result
Value at end of 2017 $5m × 1.02 $5.1m
Withdrawal −$3.0m
Value at end of 2018 $2.10m × 1.10 $2.31m
Contribution +$8.00m
Value at end of 2019 $10.31m × 0.96 $9.898m

(b) The client's actual (money-weighted) return. Total outlay is $5m + $8m = $13m; total proceeds are $3m + $9.898m = $12.898m. A first estimate of the loss is 12.898/13−1=−0.7846%12.898/13 - 1 = -0.7846\%. No division by the number of years is needed because contributions and withdrawals are spread relatively evenly through the period.

Restating the cash flows:

5(1+r)3−3(1+r)2+8(1+r)=9.8985(1+r)^3 - 3(1+r)^2 + 8(1+r) = 9.898

Trial rate Left-hand side
−0.786% 9.867 — rate must be less negative
−0.700% 9.881 — rate must be less negative
−0.600% 9.898 — close

The IRR, and therefore the money-weighted return, is −0.6%.

(c) The annualised compounded (time-weighted) return. The cumulative return is (1.02×1.10×0.96)−1=0.0771=7.71%(1.02 \times 1.10 \times 0.96) - 1 = 0.0771 = 7.71\%. Annualising:

(1+R)3=1.0771⟹R=(1.0771)1/3−1=0.0251=2.51%(1 + R)^3 = 1.0771 \implies R = (1.0771)^{1/3} - 1 = 0.0251 = 2.51\%

The fund itself made 2.51% a year; the client lost 0.6% a year because of the timing of their own contributions and withdrawals. That gap is the whole point of the money-weighted versus time-weighted distinction.

2.3 Measures of Risk

Risk is the uncertainty of returns associated with an investment — in simple terms, the degree of fluctuation in the value of assets such as stocks. Return and risk are inextricably linked.

2.3.1 Variance and Standard Deviation

Variance and standard deviation are the most widely used statistical measures of risk. They measure the dispersion of returns from the average return: the smaller the dispersion, the lower the risk.

σ2=∑pi[ri−E(R)]2\sigma^2 = \sum p_i \left[ r_i - E(R) \right]^2

σ=∑pi[ri−E(R)]2=σ2\sigma = \sqrt{\sum p_i \left[ r_i - E(R) \right]^2} = \sqrt{\sigma^2}

where σ2\sigma^2 is the variance of returns and σ\sigma is the standard deviation, the positive square root of the variance.

Worked example, using the expected-return example from 2.2.2:

rir_i pip_i ripir_i p_i ri−E(R)r_i - E(R) [ri−E(R)]2[r_i - E(R)]^2 pi[ri−E(R)]2p_i [r_i - E(R)]^2
0.25 0.20 0.05 0.17 0.0289 0.00578
−0.30 0.20 −0.06 −0.38 0.1444 0.02888
0.15 0.60 0.09 0.07 0.0049 0.00294
1.00 E(R) = 0.08 0.03760

Variance σ2=0.03760\sigma^2 = 0.03760. Standard deviation σ=0.03760=0.1939=19.39%\sigma = \sqrt{0.03760} = 0.1939 = 19.39\%.

Volatility is the standard deviation of the security. A share with a standard deviation of 19.39% calculated on daily price changes has a daily volatility of 19.39%. This is historical volatility, which differs from implied volatility — the volatility implied by the price of a share option.

2.3.2 Coefficient of Variation

The coefficient of variation (CV) measures the risk per unit of expected return, which lets investments with different returns and different standard deviations be compared.

CV=Standard Deviation of ReturnsExpected Rate of ReturnCV = \frac{\text{Standard Deviation of Returns}}{\text{Expected Rate of Return}}

Worked example.

Investment A Investment B
Expected return 0.05 0.15
Standard deviation 0.08 0.20

On standard deviation alone, B looks less attractive because its risk is higher. But B also has a higher expected return:

CVA=0.080.05=1.60CVB=0.200.15=1.33CV_A = \frac{0.08}{0.05} = 1.60 \qquad CV_B = \frac{0.20}{0.15} = 1.33

On a risk-per-unit-of-return basis, B is more attractive — it has the lower coefficient of variation.

2.3.3 Shortfall Risk — Probability of Losses Using Normal Distribution

Assuming returns are normally distributed, the probability of observing a range of returns can be computed. Investors care most about the probability of a loss.

Worked example. A balanced diversified portfolio of stocks and bonds has, over the last 20 years, an average return of 6% with a standard deviation of 12%.

The return that deviates by exactly ±1 standard deviation from the expected return:

X−E(r)=±1σ⟹X=0.06±0.12=−0.06 or 0.18X - E(r) = \pm 1\sigma \implies X = 0.06 \pm 0.12 = -0.06 \text{ or } 0.18

The Z-score expresses how many standard deviations a return deviates from the expected return:

Z=X−E(r)σZ = \frac{X - E(r)}{\sigma}

For −6%: Z=(−0.06−0.06)/0.12=−1Z = (-0.06 - 0.06)/0.12 = -1. For +18%: Z=(0.18−0.06)/0.12=+1Z = (0.18 - 0.06)/0.12 = +1.

The standard normal table gives the cumulative probability — the area to the left of the specified return. For Z=1.00Z = 1.00 the probability is 0.8413, so there is an 84.13% probability of an annual return lower than 18%. Because the total area is 100%, the probability of a return above 18% is 1−0.84=0.161 - 0.84 = 0.16. Because the distribution is symmetrical, the probability of a return below −6% (Z=−1.00Z = -1.00) is also 0.16.

The table carries only cumulative probabilities for Z-scores at or above zero — the right tail. The left tail is inferred from symmetry: to find the probability of −6% or worse, look up Z=1.00Z = 1.00 (0.8413) and take 1−0.8413=0.161 - 0.8413 = 0.16.

The probability of a return between −6% and +18% is therefore 0.84−0.16=0.680.84 - 0.16 = 0.68.

Range Z-scores Probability inside
±1 standard deviation ±1.00 68%
±2 standard deviations ±2.00 95.4% (97.7% − 2.3%)

Probability of a loss. The question "what is the likelihood of making a loss?" means the likelihood that the return XX is less than 0:

Z=0−6%12%=−0.5Z = \frac{0 - 6\%}{12\%} = -0.5

For Z=−0.5Z = -0.5 the table gives a 69% probability of a positive return and therefore a 31% chance of a negative return.

2.3.4 Value at Risk

Value at risk (VaR) extends shortfall risk and is actively used to estimate portfolio risk. It asks: "What is the smallest proportion of our portfolio value that is at risk 2.5% or 0.5% of the time?"

Balanced portfolio — expected return 6%, standard deviation 12%.

Confidence Left-tail probability Z-score Calculation VaR
97.5% 0.025 −1.96 −1.96(0.12)+0.06=−0.1752-1.96(0.12) + 0.06 = -0.1752 ≈ −18%
99.5% 0.005 −2.58 −2.58(0.12)+0.06=−0.2496-2.58(0.12) + 0.06 = -0.2496 ≈ −25%

For the 0.025 tail, look up a probability of 0.975 (that is, 1 − 0.025). For the 0.005 tail, look up 0.995; the table shows 0.9949 and 0.9951 but not 0.995, so 0.9951 is used, corresponding to Z=−2.58Z = -2.58.

So there is a 2.5% chance of losing at least 18% and a 0.5% chance of losing at least 25% in a given year.

Defensive portfolio — expected return 4%, standard deviation 4%.

Confidence Z-score Calculation VaR
97.5% −1.96 −1.96(0.04)+0.04=−0.0384-1.96(0.04) + 0.04 = -0.0384 ≈ −4%
99.5% −2.58 −2.58(0.04)+0.04=−0.0632-2.58(0.04) + 0.04 = -0.0632 ≈ −7%

There is a 2.5% chance of losing at least 4% in a given year — about 1 year in 40 — and a 0.5% chance of losing at least 7%.

Probability of any loss. For a 0% return, Z=(0%−4%)/4%=−1Z = (0\% - 4\%)/4\% = -1, which implies a 16% probability of loss; 84% of the time the portfolio should yield positive returns.

The limitation. Using historical data to predict the probability of future returns assumes the factors and conditions influencing the next few years resemble those influencing the past. They may not. The financial community therefore also uses the Monte Carlo method, which computes VaR from randomly generated returns under distributional assumptions, and computer-based models.

2.4 Types of Risk and Risk Management

Section 2.3 defined risk as volatility — deviation from the expected return in either direction. The average investor is mainly concerned with negative deviation, the risk of loss. Risks are grouped into six categories.

Category What it covers Impact
Issuer and counterparty Business risk, credit risk, fraud risk Fall in value from business conditions affecting earnings growth or financial health; failure to meet financial obligations (interest, principal, financial ratios, pledge clauses)
Product-specific Leverage structure; term and maturity; product features (option triggers, strike levels, pricing, payoffs, obligations); currency Augmented downside risk from leverage; losses from unfavourable product terms; fall in value from a fall in the denominated currency
Market (systematic) Market shocks; country, political and currency risk; unexpected economic developments; natural and man-made disasters, wars, terrorism; liquidity risk Sudden unexpected market shocks; negative impact and volatility across the whole market from economic or policy factors; rising factor costs, inflationary pressures, tightened liquidity
Execution and operational Execution error; system failure; process errors and restrictions; computer viruses; data breaches Losses from execution errors; disruption to execution and sudden corrections from system failure; computer-driven trading augmenting downside risk
Management Risk profile mismatch; concentration risk (lack of diversification) Sub-optimal risk-adjusted returns; failure to diversify, leading to excessive risk exposure, higher volatility and larger losses
Liquidity Lack of market depth Trades at unfavourable prices that do not reflect fair value, especially when news is released to the market

2.4.1 Risks in Investments

a. Issuer and counterparty risks.

Issuer risk is the risk of loss when issuers of securities — shares, bonds, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, structured notes and deposits — default on their obligations.

The Lehman Brothers case is the standard illustration. In 2008 Lehman had close to USD680 billion of assets supported by only USD22.5 billion of the firm's capital. As the housing market weakened, mortgage loans began to default, and the value of Lehman's mortgage-backed securities plummeted once it became apparent the issuer could not support interest and principal payments. Investors in Singapore, Hong Kong and elsewhere who bought Lehman-issued minibonds (structured notes) suffered major losses.

Counterparty risk is the risk that one or more parties to a contract fails to fulfil its contractual obligation. Some instruments are not exchange-traded but are OTC contracts between counterparties, which creates this exposure.

The counterparty may also be the issuer. When a bank designs a structured product and sells it to its clients, the bank is both counterparty and issuer. An issuer may increase sales through other banks that distribute and market the product, paying a retrocession fee or commission for doing so. In the Lehman minibond case, affected investors tried to claim against the distributing banks, which saw themselves as distributors rather than counterparties — a distinction not fully evident to some clients. Some banks provided partial compensation to preserve reputation and client relationships. The lesson: "caveat emptor" and standard disclaimers may not always work, especially where it is unclear whether clients are novices or sophisticated investors.

Both issuer and counterparty risk can arise from business risk and, in some cases, outright fraud.

i. Business risk is uncertainty about a company's ability to meet its financial goals. For equity investors the downside risks are changes in earnings growth or potential:

  • Earnings failing to meet market expectations.
  • An unexpected slowdown in earnings growth, warranting a downward re-rating of the stock.
  • An unexpected loss, which may trigger a sell-off.
  • Events signalling deterioration in the potential growth of the business.

Bond traders and bond fund managers must also watch weakening business conditions for issuers — Singapore's offshore oil and gas engineering industry in 2015–2016 is the example. At a minimum, when bond prices fall, portfolios are marked to market and the fall must be reported. If conditions become dire, issuers may default and losses must be realised.

ii. Fraud is relatively uncommon because financial institutions conduct due diligence. But outsourcing and open-architecture concepts have led many institutions and HNW individuals to invest in boutique, hedge and private equity funds. Bernie Madoff ran a Ponzi scheme for several years affecting more than 4,800 clients, including institutions; it was exposed only during the 2008 financial crisis when redemptions could not be met.

b. Product-specific risk. Equity shareholders, as part owners, bear higher business risk; bondholders focus on the firm's ability to finance interest and principal. Beyond business and credit risk, the risk of a product depends on its specific features and contractual terms:

  • Leverage multiple.
  • Maturity period.
  • Payoff structure (timing, size, sequence, limits).
  • Sale of put or call options within the structure.
  • Currency.

Leveraged products — futures, warrants, daily leveraged certificates, contracts for difference — have significantly higher volatility, moving multiple times their underlying. Some structured products with attractive yields effectively require the investor to sell put options to the counterparty (equity-linked notes). Others require increased accumulation of securities as they fall in value (accumulators), creating more risk. Private equity requires long gestation periods and shows drawdowns in the initial years before potentially achieving high returns later.

Currency denomination matters too: payment flows in a foreign currency can significantly affect returns in the domestic currency, and bond yields can be wiped out by currency losses when flows are converted back.

c. Market risk. Market risk affects most assets in the market and therefore cannot be fully diversified. All asset classes are affected, though the impact differs across them, and market shocks can be short- or long-lived.

Shock type What happens Examples
Financial shocks Ripple effect across markets and asset classes. During the GFC of 2008–2009 almost all financial assets except cash and government bonds fell in tandem; correlations tend toward 1 during crises. Managers may be forced to sell performing assets to meet redemptions; investors facing margin calls sell less-affected securities to cover losses elsewhere; fear drives unwinding into cash Asian Currency Crisis (1997); Russian Financial Crisis (1998); LTCM collapse (1998); Dot.Com bubble (2000–2001); Global Financial Crisis (2008–2009); European Sovereign Debt Crisis (2012)
Political shocks Sudden change in government creates uncertainty about the direction of the economy and businesses UK Brexit Referendum (2016); US Presidential Election surprise (2016)
Unexpected contractionary policy or negative data Unexpected rate hikes, tax increases, inflation and unemployment figures, rising factor costs, tighter liquidity. Governments and central banks usually manage expectations carefully so the market is not caught off guard, unless a surprise is deliberate (cooling measures, capital controls, taxation, purchasing restrictions) —
Natural disasters, wars, terrorism Affect domestic and global market stability, but the impact is usually very short-lived, with a rebound in the days or weeks after; some disasters have no impact at all. Events threatening for more than a day tend to have more impact, and such events have proven to be buying opportunities World Trade Centre attack (Sep 2001); SARS in Hong Kong and Singapore (2002–03); Fukushima nuclear disaster (Mar 2011)

d. Execution and operational risks. These can arise from a counterparty, the exchange, or the systems and platforms handling internet trades initiated from an investor's own device.

Human error remains a live risk. In 2015 a typing error caused Mizuho Securities to lose at least 27 billion yen (about $225 million) on a single stock trade: a trader tried to sell 610,000 shares at 1 yen each when he intended to sell 1 share at 610,000 yen (about $5,041).

i. Execution risk within financial institutions. Wrong trades must be reversed. Most institutions pay for losses caused by their own error, but the loss of trust and reputation may drive clients away, which is often the greater concern. Staff involved in execution undergo regular training, and new systems and processes reduce error rates. During system upgrades, temporary glitches, or compliance restrictions imposed at an inopportune time, trading may freeze and a client may miss an opportunity — a cost of lost opportunity. A system might flag a breach of trading or funding limits while ignoring available funds from completed transactions.

The main conflict between clients and representatives arises in communicating and confirming trade orders; representatives are trained in best practice for receiving, confirming, recording and executing orders to minimise disputes. Execution risk is increasingly pushed to clients because trading platforms are made directly available to them; institutions do set limits on client trades, which caps the risk to the institution and the financial system.

ii. False orders and flash crashes. Some trading risk arises from market manipulation. In 2010 a software program was used to place and cancel large orders within fractions of a second; computer-based strategies reacted to the false selling orders with real selling orders, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 9% and recovered within 36 minutes of intraday trading — a flash crash. In February 2018 high frequency trading was blamed for a smaller flash crash when the DJIA fell almost 1,600 points (4%) in a few minutes. Regulators have not fully solved the problem. The representative's response is to be aware of conditions that may cause greater volatility, remind long-term investors not to panic, and recognise that such events may present opportunities to acquire quality investments for clients willing to hold.

iii. Market disruption is the effect of a large and rapid change in market prices that stops the market functioning normally. It is characterised by price declines, widespread panic, and a massive increase in trade execution and volatility. Regulators and exchanges mitigate it with circuit breakers, shock absorbers or price limits.

  • Circuit breakers vary across exchanges. On SGX, a circuit breaker triggers if a stock's price would move by more than 10% of the traded price 5 minutes prior (the reference price). A large move can still proceed if it is gradual over a longer timeframe; the breaker halts trading only when volatility is excessive within a very short time. Once triggered, a 5-minute cooling-off period follows during which trading can only take place ±10% from the reference price. Trading then resumes with new reference prices established during the cooling-off period.
  • Shock absorbers are similar and the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Some use "shock absorbers" for halting index futures trading when the futures price falls substantially; others use it for halting computer-based HFT in specific stocks.

iv. Technical disruptions. Market halts have occurred from hardware or software problems, communication data feed errors and system updates. They usually last from half an hour to half a day. Most exchanges maintain back-up systems tracking execution and trade data.

v. Computer and data protection breaches. Viruses, hacking and data corruption could seriously affect financial markets. Institutions and governments have built defences, and representatives are expected to follow best practice in handling messages and communications.

e. Management risk. This is the risk that investments are mismanaged, resulting in excessive risk-taking.

i. Risk profile mismatch. Clients expect professional management. Each client has a risk profile and return expectation determining which investment suits them; conservative clients take less risky investments and accept modest returns, aggressive clients pick higher expected returns with greater volatility. Allocating the right proportion of assets to each client type based on their risk-return expectation is strategic asset allocation. When profiling is done poorly, or only to fit the available sales offering, a risk profile mismatch can result, creating potential grounds for mis-selling, negligence or mismanagement.

ii. Concentration risk, or lack of diversification. Fund managers normally ensure proper diversification and minimal concentration. Clients managing their own money may end up highly concentrated in specific securities, industries or markets because there is no formal diversification strategy. Remaining concentrated can be a deliberate client choice, but representatives have a responsibility to advise diversification for the longer term, especially where clients lack the time, expertise or temperament to manage their own investments.

f. Liquidity risk. Liquidity risk has two aspects.

  • Funding liquidity — the availability of funding for investments. In a crisis a liquidity crunch can occur, driving interest rates abnormally high.
  • Market liquidity — the ability to liquidate a position quickly at a fair price, which depends on the availability of buyers and sellers. An instrument has more liquidity risk if its trading volume is low or its available float is small, with major blocks controlled by strategic investors. Poor market-price liquidity widens the bid-offer spread and makes trading more costly.

Major surprises can cause liquidity to drop. If negative news is released and sellers try to offload while buyers exist only at much lower prices — say 12% lower — the price can gap downwards, several times a day, as selling pressure mounts. The mirror case is a short squeeze: a short position in a derivative may face a sudden rise in the underlying on good news, and with an absence of sellers the trader may be forced to cover at substantially higher prices.

2.4.2 Risk Management

Risk management involves due diligence, timely research and risk processes, client profiling and product suitability, diversification, and process and system risk management.

a. Due diligence checks. Security selection typically uses both fundamental and technical analysis. Selecting fund managers — traditional or hedge — requires regular due diligence and audit checks that go beyond tracking performance. Personnel changes, structural changes, cost pressures and market pressures can cause lapses in management, so external service providers must have proper checks and balances. This matters most in segments or jurisdictions with weak regulatory oversight.

b. Research and risk management processes. Not every institution performs primary research; cost and efficiency considerations usually produce a mix of primary and secondary research (gathering, evaluating and summarising research from other institutions and providers). Whatever the approach, keeping research current and having timely review processes shortens reaction time to deterioration in an investment or market, and allows underweighting of markets, sectors and companies before conditions worsen.

c. Client profile and product suitability. The products recommended depend on the client's objectives, investment purpose, risk profile, return expectation, experience and sophistication, desired manager engagement and servicing, net worth, the size of the investment relative to net worth, financial obligations and limitations.

A client may have a different purpose for money placed at one bank than at another. The risk profile selected for core family investments to be kept safe may differ sharply from that for excess cash held for opportunistic investments. Products are therefore recommended against the client's desired risk profile for those particular investments. Some corporate clients have a dedicated purpose with a specific timeline — money set aside for a building project starting in 12 months — so the investments must fit the limits and parameters the client sets.

d. Process and system risk management. Most banks have upgraded processes and systems to handle a changing environment. The recent focus has been compliance with regulatory requirements (documentation, declarations, alerts, checks), which slowed execution and required re-tooling and re-training. Systems are also upgraded to protect information, to make execution "error-proof" with prompts and computer checks that limit human error, and to provide back-ups so transaction records can be retrieved after unexpected market disruption.

2.5 Time Value of Money

Money has time value: a dollar received in the future is worth less than a dollar received today, because a dollar today can be invested immediately. The time value of a sum depends on the date of receipt and prevailing interest rates. Discounted cash flow techniques are therefore necessary for correct investment analysis, because bond interest and dividends are paid at different points in time.

2.5.1 Simple and Compound Interest

A deposit of $10,000 for one year at 2.5% has principal $10,000, an interest period of 1 year, and a rate of 2.5%. For a Singapore dollar deposit the day basis is 365 days.

Simple Interest=Principal×Interest Rate (in %)×Interest Period (in days)36,500\text{Simple Interest} = \frac{\text{Principal} \times \text{Interest Rate (in \%)} \times \text{Interest Period (in days)}}{36{,}500}

The denominator depends on the currency's day basis: Singapore dollar interest uses a 365-day basis; US dollar interest uses a 360-day basis.

Worked example — simple interest. A SGD 1 million deposit earning 8% for 91 days:

1,000,000×8×9136,500=SGD 19,945.21\frac{1{,}000{,}000 \times 8 \times 91}{36{,}500} = \text{SGD } 19{,}945.21

Worked example — compound interest. The same deposit rolled over for another 91 days at 8%:

1,019,945.21×8×9136,500=SGD 20,343.02\frac{1{,}019{,}945.21 \times 8 \times 91}{36{,}500} = \text{SGD } 20{,}343.02

Total interest is 19,945.21+20,343.02=SGD 40,288.2319{,}945.21 + 20{,}343.02 = \text{SGD } 40{,}288.23. The annualised compounded rate is:

40,288.231,000,000×36,500182=8.08%\frac{40{,}288.23}{1{,}000{,}000} \times \frac{36{,}500}{182} = 8.08\%

The second period earns interest on the first period's interest, which is why the annualised rate exceeds the nominal 8%.

2.5.2 Future Value

FVn=PV(1+k)nFV_n = PV(1 + k)^n

where FVnFV_n is the future value at the end of nn years, PVPV is the present value or original amount invested at the beginning of the first year, nn is the number of years of compounding, and kk is the annual interest rate.

Worked example. $1,000 in an account paying 5% compounded annually for 10 years:

FV10=1,000(1.05)10=1,000(1.62889)=$1,628.89FV_{10} = 1{,}000(1.05)^{10} = 1{,}000(1.62889) = \$1{,}628.89

2.5.3 Time Value of Money in Negative Interest Rate Environment

Traditionally, interest rates represent the time value of money determined by the demand for and supply of funds: users of funds compensate suppliers for the loss of liquidity and opportunity cost, so rates are expected to be positive.

Recent years have seen negative rates imposed by central banks. In 2017, 10–20 European countries had negative yields on their 2-year sovereign debt, meaning commercial banks were required to pay for holding excess reserves with the central bank. The intent was to push banks to minimise excess balances and increase productive lending. Sovereign debt issued at a premium above par and redeemed at par produces an implicit interest cost to the bank.

Country Yield (%) Country Yield (%) Country Yield (%) Country Yield (%)
Switzerland −0.92 Denmark −0.69 Slovakia −0.57 Italy −0.17
Czech Rep −0.81 Finland −0.67 France −0.53 Japan −0.13
Germany −0.74 Austria −0.65 Slovenia −0.38 Portugal −0.09
Netherlands −0.71 Ireland −0.58 Spain −0.37 Cyprus −0.08
Sweden −0.70 Belgium −0.58 Bulgaria −0.33 Lithuania −0.08

Banks have generally not charged negative interest on depositor cash, because of the risk of political backlash and because depositors would move money abroad into foreign currency deposits, causing a capital outflow the central bank does not want. Even with positive nominal deposit rates, when inflation exceeded deposit rates, real interest rates were effectively negative.

Impact on the short end of the yield curve. Negative central bank rates drive short-term rates on other fixed income investments down.
