9.8.3 Risks of Investing in Hedge Funds

  • Risky investment strategies — speculative strategies combined with leverage can produce outsized losses. Leveraged positions are sometimes hedged with derivatives, bringing basis risk (the risk remaining from an imperfect hedge because a complete offsetting position may not exist) and counterparty risk (the other party failing to meet its contractual obligation).
  • Illiquidity — hedge funds can invest in highly illiquid assets and may not unwind at fair prices. An unanticipated downturn can produce margin calls on leveraged positions and unusually large redemptions, forcing liquidation at unfavourable prices. Many hedge funds impose lock-up periods during which investors cannot redeem, and some have gate provisions letting the manager limit withdrawals on a given date to a percentage of net assets.
  • Poorer investor protection — hedge funds are more lightly regulated and less transparent than conventional funds.

9.8.4 Hedge Funds — Relative Value Arbitrage Strategies

a. Long-short equity. A relative value approach: the manager goes long on a stock believed undervalued and short on a stock believed overvalued within the same sector. For example, going long TSMC and short Intel on the view that TSMC's premium over Intel will widen.

For such strategies it is useful to set a target for closing the positions. Positions can be rolled over, but there must be justification for further widening. If there is no additional news that would cause the premium to widen further, the spread position should be closed.

If the manager has strong conviction, they can take a net long position by investing more in the long leg than is short-sold — but then the strategy is no longer market-neutral and has partial exposure to a sector decline.

b. Convertible arbitrage. Also a relative value approach, but the analysis is between the convertible securities and the common stock of the same company. The strategy purchases convertibles while shorting the underlying stock. The rationale is that convertibles are usually slower to reprice to fair value than the underlying stock, creating arbitrage opportunities. The strategy is not riskless: the stock price can rise while the convertible falls.

Other, less widely used relative value strategies include fixed income arbitrage (exploiting yield differences between bond types), credit long-short and volatility arbitrage.

9.8.5 Hedge Funds — Event-Driven Strategies

Event-driven strategies emerge when specific events present themselves, and hedge funds opportunistically exploit them. Events include financial distress (bankruptcies, liquidation), acquisitions, capital restructuring and consolidation.

a. Distressed securities. Some hedge funds — sometimes called vulture funds — look selectively for opportunities in bonds priced at distressed levels. Depending on the severity of the company's crisis, distressed bonds can be priced at 10% to 99% of par. Hedge funds buy distressed debt and borrowings they believe undervalued.

When there was a global downturn in oil and gas, the bonds of many oil-related companies, including several in Singapore, were priced at distressed levels. Some investors and banks were willing to sell at a discount, and these were bought by investors and hedge funds willing to bear the risk for potential gains.

Hedge funds typically have three options:

  • Resell the debt at a much higher price when the credit situation improves.
  • Exchange debt for equity and sell the equity for a profit, or combine the stake with a private equity firm and other investors to make a takeover bid.
  • Allow time for the company to recover and pay off the full principal at maturity, yielding substantial gains above the discounted price.

Investing in distressed debt is very risky and should be managed by experts. A well-known Swiss bank was forced to sell its billion-dollar portfolio to a distressed-debt specialist at a huge loss in 2016 when it decided to exit the high-risk business.

b. Corporate events arbitrage. Event-driven funds also look for mergers, acquisitions, takeovers and liquidations. Depending on valuation and the deal process, they may:

  • Buy the target and sell the acquirer, when the acquirer is overvalued.
  • Buy both acquirer and target, when the acquisition is believed to create greater value for the merged entity through synergies.
  • Buy shares of the target in a hostile takeover with competing offers.

Not every corporate finance deal offers mispricing opportunities, so such funds may face dry periods.

9.8.6 Hedge Funds — Global Macro Strategies

Global macro strategies take directional views on financial products and derivatives in anticipation of market reactions to significant economic or political changes in one or more countries. The manager decides to go long or short based on how macroeconomic trends will affect interest rates, currencies, sovereign credit, commodities, equity indices, equities and bonds.

Approaches range from very qualitative fundamental to quantitative computer-based models, or a blend. Because of the size of their positions and risks, they need to invest in fairly liquid assets to unwind or hedge.

Examples. Shorting the pound sterling and British stocks on the London Exchange during the Brexit Referendum was an effective global macro strategy. Conversely, a strategy that shorted US equities expecting a decline after the Republican victory in the US elections would have had to reverse quickly to avoid losses when US equities rallied shortly after. Global macro funds must be nimble to unwind positions and cut losses.

9.8.7 Hedge Funds — Directional Computer-Based Quantitative Trading Strategies

Directional quantitative strategies combine technical analysis, market data and funds flow to make decisions, mainly following technical price trends and momentum. As long as the trend is intact, the fund maintains its position until a reversal is observed.

Momentum trading. A fund following momentum continues to buy options and futures on indices in line with upward trend momentum — the philosophy that "the trend is your friend". Once the model signals a slowdown or reversal, cumulative gains are realised at once and the model awaits confirmation of the next trend. If indicators signal further correction, shorting of futures and options begins until the next reversal point, at which shorts are closed with purchases.

Such strategies benefit from clear and persistent trends over weeks or months. With disruptive reversals or a high frequency of reversals over very short periods, transaction costs are likely too high to make profits.

9.8.8 Funds of Hedge Funds — Multi-Strategies

Funds of hedge funds adopt different strategies, allocating more to some over others in a given period, because in any period some strategies outperform others due to market conditions.

The fund of hedge funds approach attempts to provide the expertise and due diligence to ensure:

  • Adequate diversification between hedge funds, reducing concentration risk.
  • That monies can be actively reallocated to strategies that do well under certain market conditions.

The service comes with additional management cost, on top of the performance and incentive fees paid to hedge fund managers. With diversification, returns typically fall to the average hedge fund return, which may not fit some investors' expectations.

9.8.9 Overview of Private Equity Funds

Private equity funds are long-term investments sold OTC, mainly to accredited individuals, corporate clients, institutional clients and sovereign wealth funds to complement their overall portfolio. They invest in businesses at different stages of their growth cycles.

Private equity provides businesses with capital to grow to a particular size before being listed through an IPO or sold privately to major corporations. It therefore gives founders a viable exit option and investors the opportunity to realise gains.

9.8.10 Stages of Private Equity Investment

a. Venture capital. Venture capitalists co-invest with an entrepreneur to provide seed and/or start-up capital in the early stages. Many newly founded tech and biotech companies are at the conceptual or research stage where products are not yet developed, and may go through several years of R&D and losses before potential revenues and profits. In return for the higher risk, venture capitalists expect a higher-than-average return.

b. Growth capital. Funds for companies looking to scale up and take advantage of high growth or expansion. Growth capital tends to focus on later-stage investments — companies already established but still requiring funds or co-sharing of expansion risk when scaling product range, production volume, distribution and market reach.

c. Buyout funds. Invest in mature companies with stable cash flows, established products and developed personnel. The buyout may occur pre-IPO for owners wanting to exit before the IPO process, or as part of the IPO process with an agreement to transfer shares between major shareholders 1–2 years after the IPO to facilitate smooth running.

d. Special situations.

  • Going private — when major shareholders believe the market undervalues the company. Buying the company and taking it private lets them benefit from a larger share of profits. Private equity vehicles can act as intermediary, or major shareholders can raise private capital among friendly parties to make an offer to remaining shareholders. When the time is ripe the business can be re-listed or consolidated with other businesses for listing.
  • Distressed businesses — private equity firms work with private parties to take over companies facing financial distress. In downturns, good businesses may succumb to financing and liquidity issues and be forced to sell; private equity can work with creditor banks to take them over.

9.8.11 The Private Equity J-Curve

Private equity investments tend to have negative initial returns and cash flows for a relatively long period, so cash flows follow a J-curve.

The first 5–6 years are the investment period. If an investor commits $10 million, it is not all invested at the outset: the manager makes several cash calls and draws down the capital as good opportunities arise. If many good opportunities arise early, the drawdown is faster. The harvest period typically begins from the 6th year, when the fund starts making payouts.

The incentive is that the expected internal rate of return is typically in the double digits (10–15%). The downside is that funds are locked up for several years, and early redemption or withdrawal before the 6th year typically results in losses. To address suitability, it must be highlighted that private equity is long-term in nature: the investor must be willing to sacrifice liquidity to secure the targeted returns, the first few years involve only drawdowns, returns usually accrue only from the 6th year, and early redemptions result in losses.

9.8.12 Commodity Funds and Real Estate Funds

Commodity and real estate funds are largely similar to commodity ETFs and REITs. The main difference is that commodity and real estate funds are sold OTC, while commodity ETFs and REITs are exchange-traded. Some OTC funds distinguish themselves by being more transparent about their investment approach and types of investments.

a. Commodity funds. Offer indirect exposure to a portfolio of commodity-related stocks, bonds, futures and funds. They can focus on pure sectors (metals, agriculture, energy) or be a fund of funds diversified across commodity types, possibly overweighting one sector. The more diversified the fund, the less volatile it should be, though exposure to the futures market makes some volatility unavoidable.

  • Agriculture funds suffer the same problem as their underlying commodities: successful production often outstrips demand, causing long downward cycles of overhanging supply.
  • Energy, base metal and ferrous metal sectors are more cyclical: they do well when global economic activity picks up, driving underlying demand, and poorly when activity slows.
  • Precious metals funds typically do well in times of uncertainty and volatility in traditional asset classes, and can be heavily influenced by major currency movements and interest rates.
Agriculture funds Energy funds Metals funds
Grains Crude oil Precious metals
Soft commodities Natural gas Base metals
Livestock Refined products Ferrous metals
Dairy Petrochemicals
Biofuel Electricity

b. Real estate funds. Not too different from REITs. OTC real estate funds can cover agricultural, industrial, residential, commercial, medical and even undeveloped land banks. Although focused on generating stable, high rental income, OTC real estate funds sold through private banks can be less liquid.

As with REITs, the main concern is the mismatch between unit liquidity and the illiquidity of underlying assets. In a property bubble, asset prices can fall very sharply once the bubble bursts, leading to redemptions. When redemptions mount, funds without deep pockets that struggle to unwind property holdings may be caught in a liquidity crunch and be unable to meet redemptions. Selling underlying property at market lows forces managers to realise losses, so in such situations real estate funds typically seek to delay redemptions.

9.9 Insurance

Some events are unpredictable as to when they occur but have severe financial repercussions when they do. Risk management processes must mitigate the effects of such unforeseen events.

Some insurance products also serve as investment instruments, and representatives should understand them to advise clients well. The two main types of life insurance policies that can also serve as savings or investment instruments are whole life and endowment insurance.

9.9.1 Whole Life Insurance Policy

Premiums for a whole life policy provide a combination of life cover and investment, and therefore have cash or surrender values. The sum assured is payable on the death of the life insured, whenever that occurs. Policy owners pay fixed monthly or annual premiums and beneficiaries receive fixed death benefits. Meanwhile, reserves and assets backing future liabilities earn interest and grow, building cash values that can be withdrawn through surrender (cancellation) of the policy, subject to its terms.

Alternatively, if owners do not want to surrender, they have access to accumulated policy savings: they can normally obtain policy loans from the insurer up to a certain percentage of the policy's cash value, the limit being insurer- and policy-specific.

9.9.2 Endowment Insurance Policy

Premiums also provide a combination of life cover and investment, but endowment policies usually mature after a fixed period — for example 10, 15 or 20 years — and the sum assured is payable on the maturity date or on death, whichever is earlier. As with whole life, the sum assured is fixed.

Endowment policies carry higher premiums than conventional whole life and term insurance, but may be useful for special lump-sum needs such as college expenses or buying a retirement home. The guaranteed cash values received may be less than the sum of premiums paid, because part of the premium pays for insurance protection while the rest is invested and subject to investment risk.

9.9.3 Using Insurance Policies for Investments

Both whole life and endowment policies are effectively investments payable at a future date, either on death or earlier. Policies structured to provide a fixed death benefit only are non-profit (non-participating) policies, in contrast to with-profits policies.

The return of insurance policies can be linked to the insurer's investment performance either through a with-profits policy, where benefits are indirectly affected, or through an investment-linked policy, which has a direct link.

a. With-profits policies. Each year the insurer values the assets and liabilities of its life fund. This normally reveals a surplus, part of which can be allocated to the with-profits policy owner as an addition to the sum assured. This addition — a bonus or profit — is usually reversionary, meaning it is payable only at the same time as the sum assured.

Under a with-profits policy the link between benefits and the insurer's investment and operating performance (mortality experience, operating expenses) is not direct and depends on the annual valuation of fund assets and liabilities, where many other factors are considered.

Allocation of the surplus as a reversionary bonus ultimately depends on the board of directors, based in part on the appointed actuary's recommendations. Bonuses are therefore only loosely linked to investment and operating performance. Allowances must be made for guarantees on the basic sum assured, so the bonus system does not directly reflect the value of the underlying assets. Bonuses are also declared yearly, so they cannot match daily fluctuations in asset values.

b. Investment-linked life insurance policies. Offer policies whose values are directly linked to the investment performance of the underlying instruments, usually by formally linking policy values to units in a fund run by the insurer or by external fund managers. Such funds usually consist of a mixture of equity, fixed income, managed and other funds. The investment element varies with the underlying assets and fluctuates daily with their performance.

9.10 Annuities

An annuity is a series of payments guaranteed for a number of years or over the lifetime of the party receiving the payments (the annuitant).

9.10.1 Types of Annuities

  • Immediate annuity — payments begin as soon as it is purchased. Always purchased with a lump sum (single premium).
  • Deferred annuity — payments begin at some future date, specified in the contract or at the annuitant's option. The amount received depends on contributions, the interest earned, the annuitant's gender and the annuitant's age when payments begin. May be purchased with a single premium or periodic premiums.

Examples of non-insurance annuities include monthly payments on home mortgages and fixed-rate coupon payments on a bond.

9.10.2 Annuity Calculations

Present value of an annuity:

PVannuity=C×[1−(1+i)−ni]PV_{\text{annuity}} = C \times \left[ \frac{1 - (1+i)^{-n}}{i} \right]

where CC is the cash flow per period, ii the interest rate and nn the number of payments.

Worked example. $1,000 paid every year for 5 years, at an annual discount rate of 3%:

PV=1,000×[1−(1.03)−50.03]=$4,579.71PV = 1{,}000 \times \left[ \frac{1 - (1.03)^{-5}}{0.03} \right] = \$4{,}579.71

Calculator: PMT = −1,000, N = 5, I/Y = 3; compute PV.

Future value of an annuity:

FVannuity=C×[(1+i)n−1i]FV_{\text{annuity}} = C \times \left[ \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i} \right]

Worked example. $1,000 paid every year for 8 years, at 5%:

FV=1,000×[(1.05)8−10.05]=$9,549.11FV = 1{,}000 \times \left[ \frac{(1.05)^8 - 1}{0.05} \right] = \$9{,}549.11

Calculator: PMT = −1,000, N = 8, I/Y = 5; compute FV.

9.10.3 Uses of Annuities

a. Insurance against outliving one's income. In its pure form a life annuity is a contract whereby, for a cash consideration, the insurer agrees to pay the annuitant a stipulated sum periodically throughout life. The consideration is fully earned by the insurer immediately on the annuitant's death. The purpose is to protect against loss of income from excessive longevity — exactly the opposite of life insurance, which protects against loss of income from premature death.

b. Investment vehicle or savings instrument. Most annuities are savings instruments designed to accumulate funds and then systematically liquidate them, usually during retirement. The annuitant can pay a lump sum or regular premiums; at the annuity starting date they receive a guaranteed income for life, the amount depending on the cash value and the payment option selected.

Annuities are attractive for someone who has not yet accumulated an estate but wants financial independence in old age. Professional entertainers and athletes, who enjoy very large income for a limited period, find annuities particularly attractive as a savings medium, purchasable through flexible periodic premiums or a single premium when large sums arrive.

c. Hedge against adverse financial developments. Wealthy individuals who have accumulated an estate purchase annuities as a hedge against adverse financial developments. Large estates can be wrecked through unwise investments, and individuals once wealthy can depend on annuity payments purchased when they were more affluent.

d. Comparing life insurance and annuities. Life insurance guards against living too short a life; life annuities guard against living longer than expected, supporting post-retirement living expenses for as long as the annuitant lives. To provide sufficient retirement income, life annuity products are often structured as savings and investment products before payments begin. The savings and asset-building phase is crucial to retirement planning and an integral part of many life annuity products, where regular premiums are paid into the retirement savings fund for investment and growth.

9.11 Risk Management for Retirement Funds

For investment of CPF funds ultimately meant for retirement, the CPF Board has provided guidance aligned with risk management best practice:

  • Investors should be made aware that funds with higher equity proportions are generally riskier and more volatile.
  • Investment providers should highlight focused or concentration risk — geographical, sector or specific investment-related.
  • For a fund to be included under CPFIS and eligible to take CPF monies, it must meet the CPFIS funds admission criteria, including being in the top quartile of the global peer group and benchmarking total expense ratios to the median of CPFIS funds in the respective risk class.

Diversification and dollar-cost averaging are recommended to spread risk and potentially improve overall returns.

9.11.1 Dollar Cost Averaging Versus Market Timing

a. Market timing. The technique of shifting investments in and out of risky asset classes to:

  • Capture the upside for risky asset classes during bull markets.
  • Exit before downturns, avoiding the downside during bear markets.

Market timing is an active investment approach.

b. Dollar cost averaging. A practice for investors who do not want to undertake market-timing risk: invest steady, equal amounts over a period of time. Because equal dollar amounts are invested, fewer shares are accumulated when the price is high and more when the price is low. Executing it accurately will likely leave the investor with odd lots.

Worked example. An investor with 60,000**isconsideringasecuritycurrentlypricedat**60,000** is considering a security currently priced at **5.

  • Invest all $60,000 at the start: 60,000 / 5.00 = 12,000 units.
  • Buy $5,000 worth evenly over the next 12 months.
Month Price Quantity Cost
1 5.00 1,000 5,000.00
2 4.80 1,042 5,000.00
3 4.60 1,087 5,000.00
4 4.60 1,087 5,000.00
5 4.70 1,064 5,000.00
6 4.50 1,111 5,000.00
7 4.50 1,111 5,000.00
8 4.50 1,111 5,000.00
9 4.30 1,163 5,000.00
10 4.30 1,163 5,000.00
11 5.00 1,000 5,000.00
12 4.80 1,042 5,000.00
Total 4.622 12,980 60,000.00

Investing all at the start gives an average price of $60,000 / 12,000 = 5**.Dollarcostaveraginggives**5**. Dollar cost averaging gives **60,000 / 12,980 = 4.622**.Thisisalsoalwaysmathematicallylowerthanthesimpleaverageofthetwelvemonthlyprices(**4.622**. This is also always mathematically lower than the simple average of the twelve monthly prices (**4.633), but that does not mean much: what matters is whether the average cost is below the final price at the end of the 12 months, which depends on the price trend.

c. Missing the best days. Advocates of passive investing cite empirical evidence that most investors fail to use market timing to make a positive impact sustainably. Not only are the odds against them, the "punishments" are devastating if the best trading days are missed.

Consider the best 25 days of the S&P from 1970 to 2016 (47 years). An investor who started at 18 and retired 47 years later in 2016, but missed the best 25 days, would see the return fall from 1,910% to just 371% — from 6.7% to 3.0% annually. That is even lower than the return on a 1-month US T-bill rolled over regularly, which would generate an average yield of 4.9% over the period. Passive buy-and-hold would have done much better.

Two further considerations:

  • The best trading days usually occur immediately after some of the worst trading days, so the chance of missing the best days is high because many investors sell in panic.
  • Best trading days tend to occur in close proximity to each other, further increasing the risk of missing most of them.

It is almost impossible to predict the best and worst trading days, because daily movements are affected by many highly unpredictable events; they are usually identified only in hindsight. Rather than trying to identify good and bad days, a better strategy may be dollar cost averaging.

d. Missing the best and worst days. Market timers may miss some of the best days, but they may also miss some of the worst. Removing the worst 25 days of S&P 500 performance over the same period, the return rebounds to 2,750% (7.6% annualised) — better than the 1,910% (6.7% annualised) earned by the buy-and-hold investor.

These results do not necessarily show that market timing is superior to passive management. Because market timers are not always invested, their non-participation means they are likely to miss some of the best and some of the worst days. Direct evidence that market timers can beat a passive strategy is needed.

Unfortunately, most working adults lack the time, expertise or emotional temperament to be disciplined active managers of their own portfolios, and 70–80% of active fund managers have been found to underperform the market each year. Dollar cost averaging as a passive form of investing for retirement may therefore be a good approach.

9.12 Summary

  • In Singapore, pooled investments are CIS or unit trusts, governed by the Code on CIS. The VCC structure, introduced by the Variable Capital Companies Act in October 2018, allows free issuance and redemption of shares, dividends paid from capital, and an umbrella structure with sub-funds.
  • ETFs track indices or fixed baskets and involve no active management. They trade during exchange hours, unlike unit trusts which transact at the daily closing NAV.
  • Physical ETFs use full replication or representative sampling; synthetic ETFs use swaps and derivatives, reducing tracking error but adding counterparty risk.
  • ETF advantages: diversification, small capital outlay, low costs, liquidity, transparency. Risks: tracking error, counterparty, market and sector, FX, and taxation.
  • Smart beta ETFs select and weight securities on performance criteria rather than market capitalisation.
  • VIX ETFs are for very short-term trading; leveraged and inverse ETFs are generally unsuitable for retail investors.
  • A unit trust pools funds under an independent trustee. Open-end trusts issue units continuously at NAV; closed-end trusts have a fixed number of units priced by market demand and supply.
  • Unit trust advantages: diversification, small outlay, professional management, flexibility, liquidity, lower transaction costs, security. Disadvantages: sales charges and management fees.
  • Fees include front-end load (1.5–5%), back-end load, management fee (0.5–2.0% of NAV), operational costs (0.1–0.15% of NAV), switching fee (about 1%) and performance fee subject to a high watermark.
  • The offer price adds purchase expenses, cash and accrued income and the manager's initial charge; the bid price deducts sale expenses and adds cash and accrued income.
  • Retrocessions create conflicts of interest and reduce NAV.
  • A REIT must invest at least 75% in income-producing real estate, distributes at least 90% of taxable income, and is subject to a 45% leverage limit. Properties are valued only once a year.
  • Business trusts are governed by the Business Trusts Act 2004, are not separate legal entities, use a single trustee-manager, may distribute from operating cash flow, have no gearing limit and no investment restrictions.
  • Stapled securities combine two or more securities traded as one instrument, and cannot be marketed as REITs.
  • UCITS is an EU directive providing a passport for cross-border fund sales; MAS has allowed UCITS distribution in Singapore since 2006.
  • Alternative investments diversify because they are less correlated with equities and bonds, but do not necessarily buffer during crises.
  • Hedge fund strategies include relative value (long-short equity, convertible arbitrage), event-driven (distressed securities, corporate events), global macro, and directional quantitative trading.
  • Private equity stages: venture capital, growth capital, buyout, and special situations (going private, distressed). Cash flows follow a J-curve, with the investment period of 5–6 years and harvest from year 6.
  • Whole life insurance provides life cover plus cash value; endowment insurance matures after a fixed period. With-profits policies link benefits indirectly; investment-linked policies link directly.
  • Immediate annuities begin payments at purchase; deferred annuities begin later. Annuities protect against longevity risk, the opposite of life insurance.
  • CPFIS admission requires top-quartile performance and total expense ratios benchmarked to the CPFIS median.
  • Dollar cost averaging invests equal amounts over time, accumulating more units when prices are low.

9.13 Additional Reference Materials

9.13.1 Key Features of Variable Capital Companies

The Variable Capital Company (VCC) is a legal entity structure for investment funds introduced to offer asset managers greater flexibility and lower costs, encouraging fund managers to co-locate fund domiciliation with their substantive fund management activities in Singapore and deepen the asset servicing ecosystem.

Key features:

  • A VCC can be used for both traditional and alternative funds, and for both open- and closed-end funds.
  • A VCC can house a standalone fund or a collection of sub-funds under an umbrella structure, with segregation of assets and liabilities of the sub-fund. An umbrella structure lets asset managers achieve cost efficiencies by consolidating administrative functions at the umbrella level.
  • Shares of the VCC can be redeemed without shareholders' approval, and dividends are payable from capital, offering greater flexibility than existing investment companies. Shares are redeemed and issued at NAV.
  • A VCC must be managed by a fund manager that is registered, licensed or exempted by MAS.
  • For taxation, a VCC is a company and a single tax entity.
  • A VCC does not need to publicly disclose its shareholder register, offering investor privacy.

9.13.2 CPF Investment Risk Classification System

The CPF Board has classified unit trusts included under the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS) under different risk categories. The Risk Classification System splits the investment risk of a unit trust into two axes: equity risk and focus risk.

i. Equity risk relates to the proportion of "riskier" investments in the unit trust. The greater the proportion invested in stocks, the higher the equity risk; the greater the proportion in bonds and cash, the lower the equity risk. Four categories:

Category Fund type
Higher risk Equity funds
Medium to high risk Balanced funds
Low to medium risk Bond funds
Lower risk Cash funds

ii. Focus risk reflects how focused the investments are in one particular geographical region, country, industry or individual company. Two categories:

  • Broadly diversified — investments spread across relatively more regions, countries, industries and companies.
  • Narrowly focused — investments concentrated in particular regions, countries, industries or companies.

In general, a unit trust has a higher level of focus risk when it is relatively less diversified. A unit trust investing in shares of companies worldwide has lower focus risk than one investing only in Japanese corporations; the Japan-only trust has higher focus risk because it invests in one foreign country only.

Within the focus risk category, CPFIS-included unit trusts are further divided into sub-groups:

  • Regional — regional exposure, for example Europe, Asia or Emerging Markets.
  • Sector — specific industry exposure, for example healthcare and biotechnology.
  • Country — country-specific, for example Japan or China.

These sub-groups make it easier for CPF members to compare unit trusts that are roughly similar in geographic focus.

The system works alongside the CPFIS admission criteria: a fund must be in the top quartile of its global peer group and have its total expense ratio benchmarked to the median of CPFIS funds in the respective risk class before it can accept CPF monies.

Exam cues

  • VCC Act passed October 2018. Two features: free issue and redemption of shares with dividends from capital, and an umbrella structure with sub-funds.
  • SPDR STI ETF: priced at about 1/100th of the STI level; board lot 100 units; dividends twice a year; annual costs 0.3%; creation and redemption only through participating dealers in 100,000-unit blocks.
  • ETF arbitrage: traded price above NAV → sell ETF, buy the basket; below NAV → sell the basket, buy the ETF.
  • Physical vs synthetic: physical uses full replication or representative sampling; synthetic uses swaps and derivatives. Synthetic has lower tracking error but higher counterparty risk.
  • ETF advantages: diversification, small outlay, low cost (under 1% vs 1–2% for active unit trusts), liquidity, transparency.
  • ETF risks: tracking error (greater in physical), counterparty, market and sector, FX, and US withholding tax for non-US investors in US ETFs.
  • Securities lending creates counterparty risk; collateral is typically about 105% of the lent stock's value.
  • Smart beta weights on performance criteria rather than market capitalisation.
  • VIX ETFs are for trading, not investing. VXX returned −56.85% while SVXY (short VIX) returned +35.26% in the same period.
  • Leveraged ETFs are 2x or 3x, with normal daily moves of 2–4% and possible ±20–25% in a session. Not suitable for retail investors. Issuers use reverse splits to reset prices.
  • Unit trust terminology: US = mutual fund; UK = unit trust; Germany = investment fund; Luxembourg = Sicaf (closed-end) and Sicav (open-end). Most offshore funds are domiciled in Luxembourg.
  • Open-end vs closed-end: open-end issues units continuously at NAV; closed-end has a fixed number of units priced by market demand and supply.
  • Trustee holds the assets and issues or redeems units; the manager does neither.
  • Unit trust advantages: diversification and divisibility, small outlay (1,000–1,000–5,000), professional management, flexibility (switching within a family of funds), liquidity, lower transaction costs, security.
  • Unit trust disadvantages: sales charges and management fees paid regardless of performance.
  • Front-end load 1.5–5% of NAV; management fee 0.5–2.0% of NAV; operational costs 0.1–0.15% of NAV; switching fee about 1%; back-end load often waived after 60 days.
  • High watermark prevents a performance fee being paid twice on the same recovered value.
  • Offer price = NAV + purchase expenses + cash and accrued income + manager's initial charge. Bid price = NAV − sale expenses + cash and accrued income.
  • Concentration: many funds cap a single security at 5%; some allow 8–9%.
  • Fund size: a SGD10,000 expense is 0.125% of an SGD8m fund but 1% of an SGD1m fund. Very large funds lose nimbleness and stop accepting subscriptions at optimal capacity.
  • Retrocessions create conflicts of interest, reduce NAV, and are banned by the courts in Switzerland but still practised in Asia.
  • REIT: at least 75% in income-producing real estate; distributes at least 90% of taxable income; 45% leverage limit; properties valued once a year; listed on SGX Mainboard.
  • REIT advantages over direct property: affordability, diversification, liquidity, 90% distribution tax advantage, professional management.
  • REIT risks: market, income, concentration, liquidity, leverage, refinancing.
  • Business trust: Business Trusts Act 2004; not a separate legal entity; single trustee-manager; distributions from operating cash flow; no gearing limit; no investment restrictions; single-tier taxation.
  • REIT vs BT: REIT has separate trustee and manager, passive investments, mandatory 90% distribution, 45% gearing cap, 90% rental income requirement, tax-exempt for individuals. BT has a single trustee-manager, active business, no minimum distribution, no gearing cap, no investment restriction, single-tier tax.
  • Stapled securities combine a passive and an active income security; the issuer must still meet the REIT's 90% distribution on the REIT component; cannot be marketed as a REIT.
  • UCITS: EU directive, in the UK since 2002; UCITS III allows derivatives and index tracking; MAS permitted distribution in Singapore since 2006.
  • Hedge funds vs conventional: alpha vs alpha+beta, absolute vs index targets, leverage permitted vs limited, less transparent and slower to unwind, performance fees.
  • Hedge fund risks: risky strategies (basis and counterparty risk), illiquidity (lock-ups and gates), poorer investor protection.
  • Hedge fund strategies: long-short equity, convertible arbitrage, fixed income arbitrage, credit long-short, volatility arbitrage; event-driven (distressed, corporate events); global macro; directional quantitative (momentum).
  • Distressed debt can be priced at 10–99% of par. A Swiss bank sold a billion-dollar portfolio at a huge loss in 2016.
  • Private equity J-curve: investment period 5–6 years, harvest from year 6, expected IRR 10–15%, early redemption typically results in losses.
  • Private equity stages: venture capital, growth capital, buyout, special situations (going private, distressed).
  • Commodity funds: agriculture suffers overhanging supply; energy and metals are cyclical; precious metals do well in uncertainty.
  • Whole life pays on death whenever it occurs and builds cash value; endowment matures after a fixed period (10, 15 or 20 years) and pays on maturity or death, whichever is earlier. Endowment premiums are higher, and guaranteed cash values may be less than premiums paid.
  • With-profits links benefits indirectly through annual valuation and a reversionary bonus decided by the board; investment-linked links directly to unit values and fluctuates daily.
  • Immediate annuity begins payments at purchase with a single premium; deferred annuity begins later and depends on contributions, interest, gender and age.
  • Annuity formulas: PV=C[1−(1+i)−n]/iPV = C[1 - (1+i)^{-n}]/i; FV=C[(1+i)n−1]/iFV = C[(1+i)^n - 1]/i. Worked: 1,000for5yearsat31,000 for 5 years at 3% → **4,579.71**; 1,000for8yearsat51,000 for 8 years at 5% → **9,549.11**.
  • Annuities protect against longevity risk; life insurance protects against premature death — exact opposites.
  • CPFIS admission: top quartile of the global peer group, total expense ratio benchmarked to the CPFIS median in the risk class.
  • Dollar cost averaging worked example: $60,000 over 12 months at prices averaging 4.633givesanaveragecostof**4.633 gives an average cost of **4.622** and 12,980 units, against 12,000 units at $5 if invested at the start.
  • Trap: a REIT must distribute 90% of income, which is why it cannot easily build cash reserves — the source of its refinancing risk.
  • Trap: a business trust has no gearing limit, but that is not a licence for indiscriminate borrowing.
  • Trap: capital guaranteed funds guarantee only if held to maturity; capital preservation funds have no guarantor and use less onerous language.
  • Trap: a hedge fund is not necessarily hedged — it may be net long or short.
  • Trap: retrocessions are paid by the fund house to the distributor and reduce the fund's NAV, so they harm existing investors as well as creating a conflict.

Chapter 10 — Warrants

Warrants are the smallest chapter in the syllabus but one of the most calculation-heavy per page. This chapter covers what a warrant is, how company warrants differ from structured warrants, and the four valuation measures the examination tests: intrinsic value, conversion price, warrant premium and gearing ratio.

Learning Objectives

The candidate should be able to:

  • Describe the features of stock warrants.
  • Explain the valuation of warrants using intrinsic value, conversion price and warrant premium.
  • Describe the gearing ratio in the context of warrant pricing.
  • Understand the determinants of the minimum and maximum values of warrants.
  • Illustrate how the warrant premium is influenced by the underlying stock price, the life of the warrant, exercise price, price volatility of the underlying stock, dividend on the underlying stock, leverage, interest rates and size of the warrant issue.

10.1 Definition and Terminology

10.1.1 Definition of Warrants

A warrant is a derivative instrument giving the holder (buyer) the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a specified number of securities — usually the issuer's common share — at a fixed price (the exercise or strike price) within a specified time period.

Warrants issued by companies trade on the Singapore Exchange Securities Trading Ltd (SGX-ST) platform and are known as company warrants. They may be considered long-dated equity call options: while call options expire within a few months, warrants typically have maturities of a few years.

Warrants are generally issued by corporations as a sweetener, attached to an offering of bonds or rights issues. This lets the issuer obtain financing at a lower interest rate, reducing its financing cost. Warrants can be detached from the host security and traded separately. Because they are issued as an incentive, there is no price paid per se for the warrant by the buyer of the host security.

When warrants are exercised, new shares are issued, increasing shares outstanding and diluting the issuer's earnings among shareholders. This differs from equity call options, which cause no dilution because no new shares are issued on exercise.

10.1.2 Company Warrants versus Structured Warrants

Two types of warrant are available on SGX.

Company warrant. Issued by companies to their shareholders. Maturity is usually measured in years from the issue date. If exercised, the company issues new shares, so the number of shares in the market increases.

Structured warrant. Issued by a bank, financial institution or other investment entity — usually a third-party issuer, not the underlying company. The issuer is effectively selling the holder an option to buy or sell the underlying company's shares at a predetermined price at a later date. The underlying company does not endorse or guarantee such warrants.

The terminology for structured warrants is more complex. The example CapitalaMBeCW181009 (COWW), issued by Macquarie Bank, decomposes as:

Term or code Attribute Detail
Capitala Underlying asset (security) CapitaLand Limited shares
MB Issuer Macquarie Bank Limited
e Exercise style European style warrant
CW Type of warrant Call Warrant (PW represents a Put Warrant)
181009 Expiry date (YYMMDD) Expires 9 October 2018
COWW Warrant code or symbol A unique 4-digit identification code ending with the letter "W", assigned by SGX
Company-issued warrants Structured warrants
Issued by the company on its own shares Issued by a third party such as a financial institution
Less liquidity More liquidity
One direction only — call warrant Both call and put warrants can be issued
Usually one exercise price Can have warrants on the same underlying with different exercise prices
Maturity typically measured in years Shorter-term maturity, usually 6–12 months
New shares issued upon exercise No new shares issued upon exercise

10.1.3 Basic Features of Warrants

  • Underlying security — the security that can be purchased on conversion of the warrant.
  • Exercise price — the price at which the holder can buy the underlying security. Typically, when warrants are issued, the exercise price is set above the prevailing share price.
  • Conversion ratio — the number of warrants required for conversion to one share.
  • Expiration date — the last date a warrant can be exercised.

When warrants are not converted into the underlying shares, holders do not receive dividends.

10.2 Warrant Valuation

The worked example throughout is Duty Free International Limited (DF Int'l). One DF Int'l warrant converts into one DF Int'l share by paying an exercise price of 0.430**.Onthedatethewarrantswerelisted(**18May2017**),thestocktradedat**0.430**. On the date the warrants were listed (**18 May 2017**), the stock traded at **0.38. By 17 January 2018, the share price had fallen to 0.26**andthewarrantstradedat**0.26** and the warrants traded at **0.030.

10.2.1 Intrinsic Value

When the share price is greater than the exercise price, the warrant is in-the-money and intrinsic value is the difference between the current share price and the exercise price:

Intrinsic Value=SP−EPn\text{Intrinsic Value} = \frac{SP - EP}{n}

where SPSP is the share price, EPEP the exercise price, and nn the conversion ratio.

When the share price is below the exercise price, the warrant is out-of-the-money and intrinsic value is zero.

Since issuance, DF Int'l's share price has remained below the $0.430 exercise price, so intrinsic value is zero because the difference is negative.

Worked example. If the share price rises to $0.48, the warrant is in-the-money and intrinsic value is:

0.480−0.4301=$0.05\frac{0.480 - 0.430}{1} = \$0.05

10.2.2 Conversion Price

The total price the investor must pay to convert warrants into one underlying share:

Conversion price=n×WP+EP\text{Conversion price} = n \times WP + EP

where WPWP is the warrant price. With a warrant price of $0.03:

Conversion price=0.030+0.430=$0.46\text{Conversion price} = 0.030 + 0.430 = \$0.46

10.2.3 Warrant Price and Warrant Premium

The warrant premium is the additional amount spent by purchasing warrants and paying the exercise price to convert to one share, as opposed to buying the share outright in the market. The term "premium" here does not carry the same meaning as in conventional options, where the premium is the option price.

Warrant premium ($)=n×WP+EP−SP\text{Warrant premium (\$)} = n \times WP + EP - SP

In percentage terms:

Warrant Premium (%)=n×WP+EP−SPSP×100\text{Warrant Premium (\%)} = \frac{n \times WP + EP - SP}{SP} \times 100

Worked example — two scenarios.

Scenario 1 (17 January 2018) Scenario 2 (today)
Underlying stock price $0.26 $0.480
Intrinsic value Zero per warrant (0.480 − 0.430)/1 = $0.05 per warrant
Warrant price $0.03 per warrant $0.08 per warrant (assumed price rise)
Warrant premium ($) 0.030 + 0.430 − 0.26 = $0.20 0.080 + 0.430 − 0.480 = $0.030
Warrant premium (%) 0.20 / 0.26 × 100 = 76.92% 0.030 / 0.480 × 100 = 6.25%

Leverage. Investors are interested in warrants mainly because of the leverage effect: the potential for greater percentage gains and losses than the underlying share for a given change in the underlying's price. Comparing the two scenarios, the DF Int'l share price rose 85% from $0.26 to $0.480, but the warrant price rose 167% from $0.03 to $0.08.

10.2.4 Gearing Ratio

The gearing ratio compares the price of warrants needed to convert to one share relative to the share price at a point in time. Gearing gives investors the ability to participate in the underlying share's performance at a lower price.

Gearing ratio=SPn×WP=0.2650.030=8.8x (approximately)\text{Gearing ratio} = \frac{SP}{n \times WP} = \frac{0.265}{0.030} = 8.8x \text{ (approximately)}

10.2.5 Minimum Value and Maximum Value

Warrants should trade within well-specified price bounds in an arbitrage-free market.

For a warrant with a conversion ratio of 1:

  • The maximum value is the underlying share price. Most warrant prices do not trade at their maximum, and prices fall as warrants approach expiration.
  • The minimum value is the intrinsic value:

Minimum value=SP−EP if SP>EP;=0 if SP≤EP\text{Minimum value} = SP - EP \text{ if } SP > EP; \qquad = 0 \text{ if } SP \le EP

In the DF Int'l example, with a share price of 0.26**andexercisepriceof**0.26** and exercise price of **0.43, the share price is below the exercise price and the warrant is out-of-the-money. If the share price rises to $0.48, the warrant is in-the-money. If the share price equals the exercise price, the warrant trades at-the-money.

Reading the price bounds. When the share price is below the exercise price, the minimum value is zero, represented by the horizontal line. As the share price rises above the exercise price, the minimum price becomes positive and rises.

As the underlying share price increases beyond a point, the premium of the warrant price over intrinsic value decreases, because the leverage potential declines — a given share price increase becomes an increasingly smaller percentage of the share price.

The line representing the maximum price is at a 45-degree angle to the x-axis, meaning the maximum price of a warrant equals its underlying share price.

10.3 Factors Affecting the Price of a Company Warrant

Company warrants are typically attached to bonds or rights issues as a sweetener but can be detached and traded independently. Once detached, the price is directly influenced by eight factors.

a. Underlying share price. Warrants are affected by the underlying share price. Unlike structured warrants, which may be call or put, company warrants are all call warrants, so they are worth more if the underlying share price rises.

b. Life of the warrant. Other things equal, the longer before expiry, the greater the warrant price. An out-of-the-money warrant may become attractive later as the share price appreciates. As the life shortens, the warrant loses its speculative value. On the day of expiration, warrants are worth their intrinsic value, after which they are worthless.

c. Exercise price. The lower the exercise price, the greater the warrant price. The ability to convert by paying a lower exercise price increases intrinsic value and hence the warrant's price.

d. Price volatility of the underlying share. The more volatile the underlying share, the higher the warrant price, because warrants benefit from price upside but limit price downside. Volatility can change over time.

e. Dividend on the underlying share. Because warrant holders are not entitled to dividends, the declaration of dividends reduces the call warrant's price slightly, since call warrants "lose out".

f. Leverage. Warrants with greater leverage opportunities command higher prices.

g. Interest rates. The higher the interest rate, the higher the call warrant price, because of interest savings from the lower capital needed to buy warrants compared with an equivalent long stock position. For completeness, the higher the interest rate, the lower the put warrant price, because more interest must be paid to buy warrants whereas an equivalent short stock position gains more interest on the short-sale proceeds.

h. Size of warrant issue. The more warrants outstanding, the larger the potential earnings dilution of existing shares. If the warrants were deep in-the-money, conversion would increase shares outstanding and reduce the value of each share. There is therefore a negative relation between the size of the warrant issue and the warrant price.

Factor Effect on warrant price
Remaining life of warrant ↑ ↑
Exercise price ↑ ↓
Underlying share price ↑ ↑
Volatility ↑ ↑
Dividend expectations ↑ ↓
Leverage opportunities ↑ ↑
Interest rates ↑ ↑
Issue size of warrant ↑ ↓

10.4 Summary

  • Company warrants are call warrants issued only by the company. Both call and put structured warrants are issued by a third party, usually a bank. Company warrants are settled by delivery of shares; structured warrants are cash-settled, with no delivery of shares.
  • A company warrant gives the investor an option to buy a stated number of common shares at a specified price within a specified period. Unlike common shares, warrants expire, and warrant holders are not entitled to dividends.
  • Beyond the fundamental value of the underlying share, the warrant investor must consider intrinsic value, warrant premium, gearing ratio and expiration date.
  • The maximum value of a warrant is the underlying share price. The minimum value is the intrinsic value — zero or the difference between the share price and exercise price, whichever is larger.
  • The price investors will pay depends on the underlying share price, the life of the warrant, the exercise price, the price volatility of the underlying share, dividend expectations, leverage opportunity, the interest rate level, and the size of the warrant issue.

Exam cues

  • A warrant is a right, not an obligation, to buy or sell at a fixed price within a specified period. Company warrants are long-dated equity call options — maturities of years, not months.
  • Warrants are issued as a sweetener on bonds or rights issues, letting the issuer finance at a lower interest rate. There is no price paid per se by the buyer of the host security.
  • Exercise dilutes earnings because new shares are issued — unlike equity call options, which cause no dilution.
  • Company vs structured warrants: company = own shares, less liquid, call only, one exercise price, years, new shares issued. Structured = third party, more liquid, call and put, multiple exercise prices on the same underlying, 6–12 months, no new shares.
  • Structured warrant code decomposition: CapitalaMBeCW181009 = underlying CapitaLand, issuer Macquarie Bank, e = European style, CW = call warrant (PW = put), 181009 = expiry 9 October 2018, COWW = SGX code ending in W.
  • Four basic features: underlying security, exercise price (set above the prevailing share price at issue), conversion ratio (warrants per one share), expiration date.
  • Warrant holders receive no dividends.
  • Intrinsic value =(SP−EP)/n= (SP - EP)/n when in-the-money; zero when out-of-the-money. DF Int'l at $0.48 with EP 0.43andn=1→**0.43 and n = 1 → **0.05**.
  • Conversion price =n×WP+EP= n \times WP + EP. DF Int'l: 0.030 + 0.430 = $0.46.
  • Warrant premium ($) =n×WP+EP−SP= n \times WP + EP - SP; premium (%) divides by SPSP. Scenario 1: 0.20/76.920.20 / 76.92%**. Scenario 2: **0.030 / 6.25%.
  • Gearing ratio =SP/(n×WP)= SP/(n \times WP). DF Int'l: 0.265/0.030 = 8.8x.
  • Leverage worked example: share price rose 85% ($0.26 → 0.480)whilethewarrantrose**1670.480) while the warrant rose **167%** (0.03 → $0.08).
  • Maximum value = underlying share price (the 45-degree line). Minimum value = intrinsic value (zero or SP − EP).
  • Premium over intrinsic value falls as the share price rises well above the exercise price, because leverage potential declines.
  • Eight price factors: underlying share price ↑ → price ↑; life ↑ → ↑; exercise price ↑ → ↓; volatility ↑ → ↑; dividends ↑ → ↓; leverage ↑ → ↑; interest rates ↑ → ↑; issue size ↑ → ↓.
  • Interest rates raise call warrant prices (interest saved on the smaller capital outlay) but lower put warrant prices.
  • Issue size has a negative relation to warrant price because of potential dilution.
  • On expiry day a warrant is worth its intrinsic value; afterwards it is worthless.
  • Trap: the "premium" in warrant premium is not the option price — it is the extra cost of the warrant route versus buying the share outright.
  • Trap: company warrants are call only. Only structured warrants can be puts.
  • Trap: a warrant's maximum value is the share price, not the intrinsic value — the intrinsic value is the minimum.

Chapter 11 — Technical Analysis and Quantitative Analysis

Technical analysis is the alternative to fundamental analysis: it studies past price and volume to predict future direction, and it is not concerned with fair value. This chapter covers its philosophy and assumptions, the challenges to it, the indicators, the chart patterns, Elliott Wave Theory, and the role of quantitative analysis.

Learning Objectives

The candidate should be able to:

  • Explain the philosophy and assumptions in the application of technical analysis to investment decisions.
  • Discuss the challenges to technical analysis.
  • Describe the various technical indicators.
  • Distinguish between support and resistance levels.
  • Describe share price and volume analysis techniques.
  • Explain chart patterns such as head and shoulders, double tops and bottoms, consolidation rectangles, triangles, flags and pennants, wedges and gaps in identifying price trends.
  • Explain Elliott Wave Theory as a technical analysis approach.
  • Describe the essentials of quantitative analysis.

11.1 Overview

11.1.1 What is Technical Analysis?

Besides fundamental analysis, another approach to security evaluation is technical analysis. Though controversial, many traders employ technical trading rules or indicators to make investment decisions.

11.1.2 Basic Philosophy and Assumptions

Technical analysis is the methodology of forecasting fluctuations in securities prices through an examination of historical market data. It can be applied to individual securities, the entire market, and any asset class — foreign exchange, gold or bonds.

Technical analysis uses charts, technical trading rules and indicators. It is sometimes called market or internal analysis because it studies demand and supply conditions based on market data such as price changes and trading volume. It differs from fundamental analysis, which focuses on factors affecting a company's business profitability — economic, industry and company-specific factors.

Technical analysis holds that prices are determined by demand and supply, which are affected by both fundamental factors (macroeconomic forces) and non-fundamental factors (market sentiment and speculative forces). Technical analysts study past price and volume behaviour to identify shifts in supply and demand so as to predict future price behaviour. They are not concerned about a security's fair value.

The five underlying assumptions:

  • A security's market value is determined only by its supply and demand.
  • Supply and demand are affected by both rational and irrational factors — not only economic variables but also hopes, fears, opinions, moods and guesses of potential buyers and sellers. The market constantly assesses all these factors.
  • Prices of individual securities and the overall market exhibit trends, which tend to persist over an appreciable length of time.
  • Trends develop in reaction to changes in the supply-demand balance, and such changes can be detected by studying market actions.
  • Chart patterns tend to repeat themselves.

Where analysts agree and disagree. Generally, technical and non-technical analysts accept the first two assumptions: at any point in time price is determined by supply and demand, and supply and demand is governed by many variables. The key difference concerns irrational factors — technical analysts expect them to persist, while fundamental analysts expect only a temporary effect, with rational beliefs prevailing in the long run.

Opinions differ on the third assumption, about the speed of adjustment. Technical analysts believe new information is priced by the market over a period of time rather than at one point, because there are different sources of information and some investors have earlier access. Prices therefore adjust gradually to the gradual flow of information, and because the adjustment is gradual, prices exhibit trends that persist over long periods.

The fourth assumption implies that as prices move from one equilibrium to a new one, the change can be detected sooner or later in charts. Technical analysts hope to benefit by being among the first to detect a shift in trend.

11.1.3 Challenges to Technical Analysis

The Efficient Market Hypothesis presents the greatest challenge. Studies testing weak-form market efficiency generally support the notion that prices adjust rapidly to new information, leaving little opportunity for technical analysts to exploit market data.

According to the random walk theory, share prices follow a random walk, meaning price movements are independent over time. Whether past price data can predict future prices is therefore questionable.

Another criticism: many technical analysts are familiar with chart patterns and act on them at the same time. If a popular rule is followed by many participants, some act first, causing prices to change quicker than expected, so only those who act earliest benefit. The popularity and resulting competition eventually negate the value of the rule. That said, chart reading is a very subjective exercise, and several interpretations of the same pattern are not unusual, so there is always an element of doubt and disagreement.

11.2 Price-based Technical Indicators

Price-based technical indicators attempt to mine information from current and historical market prices to "beat" the market. They typically measure market momentum and the relative state of the market — whether it is overbought or oversold.

11.2.1 Moving Average

A moving average is the average of a security's closing price over a given period. Typically each day is given the same weight: in a 100-day moving average, each day has a weight of 1/100. A more sophisticated moving average gives higher weights to more recent prices. The moving average is more stable than the daily price because it includes past prices, making it more useful for detecting trends. If the current market price starts to diverge directionally from the moving average, this may indicate a trend reversal.

11.2.2 Advance-Decline Line (Breadth Index)

Daily index movements can be misleading because an index is based on selected shares that may not represent the overall market. The advance-decline (A/D) line, an index covering all securities traded, overcomes this by capturing the breadth of the market.

The A/D line measures, on a cumulative daily basis, the net difference between the number of shares with price advances and those with price declines in a period (usually a day or a week). The net advance or decline is the number of advances minus the number of declines, and the line plots a running total over time.

The A/D line is compared with an index such as the Straits Times Index (STI) and normally rises and falls in line with it. If both are rising (declining), the market is technically strong (weak).

  • In a rising market, any divergence between the index and the A/D line is of concern, because it means most shares are not participating — indicating a market peak.
  • If the A/D line is rising while the index is declining, it signals a reversal of the falling trend.

11.2.3 Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)

MACD is a trend-following momentum indicator showing the relationship between two moving averages of a security's price. It reveals changes in the strength, direction, momentum and duration of a trend.

The MACD indicator is a collection of three time series calculated from historical price data, most often the closing price:

  • The MACD series is the difference between a "fast" (short-period) exponential moving average (EMA) and a "slow" (longer-period) EMA of the price series.
  • The signal or average series is an EMA of the MACD series itself.

An exponentially weighted moving average reacts more significantly to recent price changes than a simple moving average (SMA), which applies equal weight to all observations.

The indicator therefore depends on three time parameters — the time constants of the three EMAs. The notation MACD (a,b,c) denotes the indicator where the MACD series is the difference of EMAs with characteristic times aa and bb, and the average series is an EMA of the MACD series with characteristic time cc. Parameters are usually measured in days, and the most common values are 12, 26 and 9 — MACD (12,26,9).

A fast EMA responds more quickly than a slow EMA to recent price changes. By comparing EMAs of different periods, the MACD series indicates changes in trend:

  • When the MACD crosses and falls below the signal line, it is a bearish signal — possibly time to sell.
  • When the MACD crosses and rises above the signal line, it is a bullish signal, suggesting upward momentum.

11.2.5 Bollinger Bands

Bollinger Bands are a type of price envelope developed by John Bollinger. Price envelopes define upper and lower price range levels. Bollinger Bands are plotted at a standard deviation level above and below a simple moving average. Because the distance is based on standard deviation, the bands adjust to volatility swings in the underlying price.

Calculation:

  • Compute the simple moving average, typically a 20-day SMA. The first data point averages the first 20 closing prices; the next drops the earliest price, adds day 21 and averages, keeping the data set at 20.
  • Obtain the standard deviation of the price over that data set.
  • Multiply the standard deviation by two (a commonly used multiplier) and both add and subtract that amount from each point along the SMA, producing the upper and lower bands.

The purpose is to provide a relative definition of high and low prices. By definition prices are high at the upper band and low at the lower band. Many traders believe the closer prices move to the upper band, the more overbought the market; the closer to the lower band, the more oversold. An overbought or oversold market may be primed for a trend reversal or price correction.

Individual indicators are typically not used in isolation but in conjunction with others. Moving averages and the relative strength index are also common.

11.3 Trends, Support and Resistance Levels

Technical analysts rely on trend lines and trend channels to identify trends.

  • An uptrend is a rising trend line connecting a series of ascending lows.
  • A downtrend is a falling trend line connecting a series of descending highs.

An uptrend is in place when current highs are above previous highs and current lows are also above previous lows. When current highs are no longer above previous highs and, more importantly, current lows fall below previous lows, a trend reversal may be occurring.

A downtrend occurs when current lows are lower than previous lows and current peaks are lower than previous peaks. A potential change may occur when this pattern is no longer intact.

The trading range between the top and bottom trend lines is the trend channel, which may be rising, flat or declining. If share prices stay within a rising channel, the technician would hold the share and ride the trend.

Support and resistance.

  • A support level is a price range where a substantial increase in demand is expected. At this level prices are relatively attractive to buyers who missed the opportunity earlier.
  • As prices increase, a resistance level develops where buyers refuse to pay higher prices, while sellers may be attracted by higher prices to take profits. This supply is the market "overhang".

A movement through and beyond either level is a breakout, signalling strong confirmation and continuation of the primary trend. A breakout above resistance is bullish; a breakout below support is bearish.

Technical analysts are also alert to reversals. A penetration below a support line is a sell signal, indicating a reversal of the uptrend. In the standard illustration, the move to point C creates a new low past the previous low at A, and the move to D is lower than the previous high at B — confirming the trend has reversed downwards.

11.4 Significance of Volume

Volume — the number of securities transacted — shows the intensity of excess demand or supply at a point in time and reflects changes in investor attitudes.

  • If prices advance on low volume, the enthusiasm implied is not as strong as when a rise is accompanied by very high volume.
  • A price increase with heavy volume relative to normal is an indication of bullish activity.
  • A price decline with heavy volume is very bearish, reflecting a strong and widespread desire to sell.
  • In a sustained bull market, if prices correct downward on declining volume, this may indicate a lull followed by continuation of the rally.
  • A rally that develops on contracting volume could signal a possible trend reversal.

11.5 Share Price and Volume Techniques

Three techniques: the Dow Theory, the Moving Average Line, and the Relative Strength Index.

11.5.1 The Dow Theory

Named after Charles Dow, the oldest and most popular method for identifying long-term trends in the equity market. It is based on the movements of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) and the Dow Jones Transportation Average (DJTA).

Three movements:

Movement Duration Character
Primary Several months to several years The market trend, either bullish or bearish. Historically, bear markets last for a shorter period than bull markets
Secondary Several weeks to months Shorter than the primary and opposite in direction. Usually retraces one-third to two-thirds of the previous advance (decline) in a bull (bear) market
Daily fluctuations Day to day Considered random, with no forecasting value for long-term investors and no impact on long-term trends

Dow Theory forecasts are based on the primary and secondary movements. Its purpose is to determine where the market is and where it is going, but not the magnitude of the movements.

In practice: if the swings of the market index are successively higher and the successive lows are also higher, the trend is up and investors are in a bull market. If successive highs and successive lows are lower, the direction is down and investors are in a bear market.

Confirmation. A new primary trend is confirmed only when both the DJIA and DJTA give the same signals. When the two averages diverge, the Dow Theory assumes the prior trend is maintained.

Five weaknesses:

  • It relies too heavily on the DJIA, which contains a limited selection of shares — old, large "blue chip" companies, with aggressive high-tech companies under-represented.
  • It is slow in identifying a major trend and may miss an important price move or be "whiplashed" — caught by a short-term reversal even though the long-term trend is intact but not yet visible.
  • It uses the Transportation Average, comprising mainly railway shares that no longer have a major impact on the economy.
  • It is designed to identify the major trend and is therefore not useful for trading the short trend.
  • It does not help identify which shares to buy or sell.

11.5.2 Moving Average Line

Moving averages smooth out erratic price changes so the underlying trend can be clearly observed, and are used to confirm the direction of price trends. Popular averages are the 200-day and 50-day; the 200-day identifies long-term trends while a 20- to 30-day average identifies short- and intermediate-term trends.

Trend changes are identified not by a change in the direction of the moving average, but by a crossover between the moving average and the index itself.

  • If the overall trend has been negative, the moving-average line lies above current prices. If the price reverses and breaks upwards through the moving-average line from below, accompanied by heavy volume, most technical analysts consider this a very positive change and expect a reversal of the downtrend.
  • In an uptrend the moving-average line is rising but below current prices. If prices break downwards through the line from above with heavy volume, this is a bearish pattern signalling a reversal of the long-run uptrend.

Because the moving average is an average of past prices, if prices keep rising the line also rises but at a slower rate than current prices. If current prices (which lead the averages) fall, the line follows the downtrend. The price line therefore naturally cuts the moving average when a trend reversal occurs.

The signal is stronger if:

  • The price cuts both short- and long-term moving averages, and
  • The short-term average cuts the long-term average in the same direction.

11.5.3 Relative Strength Index (RSI)

The RSI is a momentum indicator measuring the degree of buying or selling interest in a security. Developed by J. Welles Wilder, it measures the speed of change of price movements.

RSI=100−[1001+Average of upward price changeAverage of downward price change]RSI = 100 - \left[ \frac{100}{1 + \dfrac{\text{Average of upward price change}}{\text{Average of downward price change}}} \right]

The index ranges from zero to 100. An RSI above 70 is considered overbought; below 30 signals an oversold condition.

A better way to use the RSI is to track the past peaks and troughs of the underlying and examine the typical RSI levels for that market and security, to calibrate the overbought and oversold levels.

The RSI is useful in situations of surprises and shocks:

  • Emotional selling under unwarranted conditions produces oversold conditions. For the contrarian, a low RSI of 20–30 or lower could signal a buying opportunity.
  • In situations of overly optimistic demand, a strong RSI of 70–80 or higher could signal a profit-taking opportunity.

The RSI is less useful when trends are steady and consistent. Where constant demand for a growth stock keeps its RSI persistently high, the level should not be read as a sell signal; instead look for an opportunity to accumulate when the RSI is not as high.

In practice, periods of overselling and overbuying can last one to two weeks, during which prices can continue to rise or fall. Technical analysts therefore usually wait for a few days of overbuying before recommending profit-taking, and of overselling before recommending accumulation.

11.6 Charts and Chart Patterns

Charts are the technical analyst's main tool. Types include:

  • Line charts.
  • Bar charts.
  • Candlestick charts.
  • Point and figure charts.

Most show the high, low, opening and closing prices for each trading day.

There are two types of price pattern:

  • Reversal patterns indicate that an important reversal in trend is occurring.
  • Continuation patterns suggest the market is only taking a pause, possibly to correct a short-term overbought or oversold condition, after which the existing trend is expected to resume.

11.6.1 Head and Shoulders

The head-and-shoulders pattern is a reversal pattern and probably one of the more reliable indicators of major reversals. The upright formation occurs at market peaks and consists of a left shoulder, a head and a right shoulder.

Component Description
Left shoulder First strong price rally, normally accompanied by heavy volume, followed by a decline on considerably less volume
Head Prices advance again on high volume to a level higher than the top of the left shoulder, then fall on lower volume. Prices fall below the top of the left shoulder but stay above or near the low of the left shoulder
Right shoulder A third rally on less volume than during either the left shoulder or the head. Prices fail to reach the height of the head and fall through the neckline

A breakout is confirmed if the price closes below the neckline by 3% of the share price. Once penetrated, the potential magnitude of decline is measured by the distance between the head and the neckline, projected downward from the neckline.

Formation time varies: with rapid price reactions it can take a few weeks; otherwise a few months or years. Formation tends to be quicker for currencies and slower for commodities.

Inverse head and shoulders indicates a market bottom.

Component Description
Left shoulder Begins with a significant selloff on high volume, followed by a brief rally, sometimes supported by short covering, usually on lower volume
Head A second wave of selling as participants in the initial rally give up their positions. Heavy volume drives the price to bottom out and form the head. The head may be extended and consolidated while selling is absorbed by bargain hunters. The RSI would typically indicate an oversold position at this point. Prices are driven up slightly by demand from parties seeing value
Right shoulder Profit-taking by shorter-term traders and those who did not sell earlier. This sell-off is lighter and shorter-lived, met with demand, so the right shoulder becomes a low higher than the previous low. The resistance at the right shoulder creates the neckline

When demand picks up and price breaks past the neckline, volume typically rises. Once fully formed, the pattern implies the prior downtrend is over and an uptrend reversal is likely.

11.6.2 Double and Triple Tops and Bottoms

A double top is a reversal pattern indicating a market top. It consists of two tops separated by a valley. The main feature is that the second top forms with distinctly lower volume than the first. A double top is confirmed when the neckline is broken on the way down.

There can be more tops rising to a resistance level, resulting in a selloff. Once resistance is reached, the volume of each subsequent rise falls and the number of buyers pushing prices toward the peak dwindles, forcing a correction as buying interest is overwhelmed by selling.

A double bottom occurs in a bear market and signals a potential reversal. The first bottom is normally accompanied by heavy volume, while the second bottom is usually dull with little volume. Volume increases significantly on the breakout. Some patterns extend to triple tops or bottoms. As with the double top, a double bottom is confirmed if the neckline is broken on the way up.

11.6.3 Consolidation Rectangles

A consolidation rectangle forms when prices move sideways within a narrow range for an extended period, usually as a continuation pattern. A breakout is technically significant: upwards indicates a bullish trend, downwards signals further weakness.

During formation it is difficult to predict which way price will break, so it is assumed the prevailing trend continues until proven otherwise.

11.6.4 Triangles

Triangles form with four points of contact — two support and two resistance points. Three types:

Type Boundaries Signal
Symmetrical Upward-sloping support line and downward-sloping resistance line A breakout may occur on either side and indicates a major move in the same direction
Ascending Upward-sloping support line and an almost horizontal resistance line Bullish. Buyers are more aggressive than sellers. Once the limited supply is absorbed, prices are expected to advance rapidly
Descending Almost horizontal support line and a downward-sloping resistance line Bearish. Sellers are more aggressive, lowering rally peaks while buyers buy at a set price. Once limited demand is filled at the floor, prices fall sharply if selling continues

11.6.5 Flags and Pennants

A flag looks like a flag on the chart — a parallelogram of price fluctuations. It usually occurs after a sharp, almost vertical rise or fall, followed by declining volume. As the flag completes, prices break out in the same direction they were moving before.

  • In a rising market the flag usually forms with a slight downtrend. Volume is very heavy just before formation, then dries up as the pattern develops, only to explode as price works out of the formation. Flags can take as few as 5 days to as many as 3–5 weeks. They represent a period of controlled profit taking in a rising market.
