  • In a falling market the flag usually forms with a slight upward bias, also on declining volume. Rising prices with declining volume is essentially bearish. When price breaks out downwards, the almost vertical slide resumes. Volume tends to pick up but does not have to be explosive, unlike the breakout from a flag in an upward move.

A pennant forms after a sharp rise or fall with lower volume during formation. The difference from a flag is that a pennant is formed by a set of converging, instead of parallel, lines.

11.6.6 Wedges

A wedge is formed by a series of converging peaks and troughs, with both converging lines moving in the same direction.

  • A rising wedge has both boundary lines slanting upwards. It usually develops on a falling price trend. After completion, prices usually fall very sharply, especially if volume is high. Rising wedges are characteristic of bear market rallies.
  • A falling wedge is bounded by converging lines slanting downwards. It represents a temporary interruption of a rising trend. When prices move out of a falling wedge they are likely to drift sideways before beginning to rise.

11.6.7 Gaps

A gap is a price range where no transactions occur. Gaps occur when the lowest (highest) traded price for a period is higher (lower) than the highest (lowest) traded price in the previous period. On a chart it appears as an empty vertical space between adjacent trading periods. Daily gaps are more common than weekly or monthly gaps.

A gap is closed or covered when price retraces the entire range of the gap. A gap may be covered in a few days, weeks or months, if at all. Although the general principle is that gaps will eventually be covered, this is not always the case, so trading strategies should not be implemented solely on the assumption that a gap will be filled in the immediate future.

Gap type Where it appears Character
Breakaway When price breaks out of a price pattern Emphasises the bullishness or bearishness of the breakout. An upside breakout should be accompanied by relatively heavy volume to confirm a change to bullish sentiment
Runaway (continuation) During rapid, straight-line rises or falls when trends accelerate and emotions run high Occurs in the middle of a move
Exhaustion The last in a series of runaway gaps Represents the end of a rapid rise or fall. It is not easy to tell whether a gap is another runaway gap or the exhaustion gap

Generally: breakaway gaps develop at the beginning of a move, runaway gaps in the middle, and exhaustion gaps at the end.

11.7 Elliot Wave Theory

In his study of equity prices in 1938, R.N. Elliott proposed the Elliott Wave Theory: prices move in cycles of waves and sub-sets of waves and exhibit the Golden Ratio, 1.618. Each cycle comprises a 5-wave advance and a 3-wave retreat.

In Elliott Wave charts, markets move in 5-wave and 3-wave patterns, and the turning points creating these patterns are often at Fibonacci support and resistance levels (61.8, 161.8, and so on).

The Fibonacci series is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …, where each number is the sum of the two preceding numbers. As the series progresses, the ratio of consecutive numbers (for example 21 ÷ 13) approaches the Golden Ratio of 1.618.

11.8 Quantitative Analysis

Quantitative analysis involves the abstraction of market reality — the economy, financial markets and their environment — into relations incorporated into a financial model. The objectives are to identify price anomalies and arbitrage possibilities and, lately, to increase the speed of access to market information that gives an advantage.

Its significance is evidenced by the rapid growth in the use and development of quantitative techniques. Quantitative analysis uses statistics and calculus for pricing, algorithmic trading, asset allocation, risk management, trading strategy modelling, portfolio optimisation, and identifying trading and investment opportunities.

Quantitative analysts are typically called "quants" or "rocket scientists". Within an organisation they may work in the front office developing trading strategies with complex mathematical tools, or in risk management measuring the risks bundled into a transaction or product.

Quant funds extensively use quantitative analysis in fund management decisions. This can be seen as an outcome of markets becoming more sophisticated in understanding and measuring risk. While less sophisticated traders look only at price changes, quants decompose those changes so specific risk profiles can be created to benefit from them: instead of looking only at the first order of price change (delta), quants look at second and third order derivatives.

There is controversy about the usefulness and fairness of such models. Long Term Capital Management was a hedge fund relying extensively on quantitative analysis; despite the elegance and apparent mathematical robustness of its strategies, it incurred huge losses.

High frequency trading, which relies on physical transmission speeds and complex price discovery algorithms, is under intense scrutiny from regulators.

Given rapid advances in computing and increasing global competition, quantitative analysis will continue to develop as a tool necessary to enhance industry standards in fund and risk management.

11.9 Summary

  • Technical analysis, also called market or internal analysis, studies past prices and volume to predict future price direction for individual securities or the aggregate market.
  • It assumes market prices discount everything and prices move in trends, and that shifts in trends can be detected by studying charts.
  • The greatest challenge is the Efficient Market Hypothesis, which argues prices adjust rapidly to new information, leaving little opportunity. Popular technical rules are followed by many participants, and the resulting competition eventually negates their effectiveness.
  • Indicators include the A/D line (breadth index), which measures the aggregate movement of all securities traded, and moving averages, which smooth erratic price changes so the trend is clearer.
  • MACD is a trend-following momentum indicator showing the relationship between two moving averages. Bollinger Bands are envelopes plotted at a standard deviation level above and below a simple moving average; closer to the upper band is more overbought, closer to the lower band more oversold.
  • Under the Dow Theory there are three movements: primary, secondary and daily fluctuations. Its objective is to identify the primary trend.
  • The moving average line smooths erratic movements, and crossovers between the moving average and the index identify trend reversals.
  • The RSI identifies overbought or oversold securities.
  • Chart types include line, bar, candlestick, and point and figure.
  • There are two types of chart pattern: reversal (head and shoulders, double tops and bottoms) and continuation (consolidation rectangles, triangles, flags, pennants, wedges).

Exam cues

  • Technical analysis is not concerned with fair value. It studies supply and demand through price and volume.
  • Five assumptions: price determined only by supply and demand; supply and demand affected by rational and irrational factors; prices exhibit persistent trends; trends develop from changes in the supply-demand balance and can be detected; chart patterns repeat.
  • The key disagreement with fundamental analysts is the persistence of irrational factors and the speed of adjustment — technical analysts believe information is priced gradually, producing trends.
  • Greatest challenge: the EMH. Weak-form efficiency and the random walk theory both undermine technical analysis. Popular rules are self-defeating because many act at once.
  • Moving average: equal weights by default; more stable than daily price; divergence from price may signal a reversal.
  • A/D line (breadth index): cumulative advances minus declines across all securities. Index rising with A/D falling = market peak warning; A/D rising with index falling = reversal of the downtrend.
  • MACD: three EMAs; MACD (12,26,9); MACD crossing below the signal line is bearish, above is bullish.
  • Bollinger Bands: 20-day SMA ± 2 standard deviations. Near the upper band = overbought; near the lower band = oversold.
  • Uptrend: current highs above previous highs and current lows above previous lows. Downtrend: the reverse.
  • Support = substantial increase in demand expected. Resistance = buyers refuse higher prices while sellers take profits — the overhang. Breakout above resistance is bullish; below support is bearish.
  • Volume: price rise on heavy volume = bullish; price decline on heavy volume = very bearish; a correction on declining volume in a bull market may be a lull; a rally on contracting volume may signal reversal.
  • Dow Theory: three movements — primary (months to years), secondary (weeks to months, opposite direction, retraces one-third to two-thirds), daily (random). Bear markets last a shorter period than bull markets. Confirmation requires both DJIA and DJTA to agree; divergence means the prior trend is maintained.
  • Dow Theory weaknesses: over-reliance on the DJIA (blue chips, high-tech under-represented), slow and prone to whiplash, the Transportation Average is railway-dominated, useless for short-term trading, and it does not say which shares to trade.
  • Moving average crossovers: price breaking up through the line from below on heavy volume = bullish reversal; price breaking down through the line from above on heavy volume = bearish reversal. Stronger if the price cuts both short- and long-term averages and the short-term average crosses the long-term in the same direction.
  • RSI: ranges 0–100; above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold. Contrarians buy at 20–30 and take profit at 70–80. Less useful in steady trends.
  • Head and shoulders: reversal at a peak. Left shoulder on heavy volume, head on high volume to a higher level, right shoulder on less volume failing to reach the head. Breakout confirmed by a close 3% below the neckline; the target decline equals the head-to-neckline distance projected down.
  • Inverse head and shoulders: reversal at a bottom; the RSI typically shows oversold at the head; the right shoulder is a higher low.
  • Double top: second top on lower volume; confirmed when the neckline breaks downwards. Double bottom: first bottom on heavy volume, second dull, volume increases on the breakout; confirmed when the neckline breaks upwards.
  • Consolidation rectangle: sideways range, continuation; assume the prevailing trend continues until proven otherwise.
  • Triangles: symmetrical (breakout either way), ascending (bullish), descending (bearish). Four points of contact.
  • Flags and pennants: continuation after a sharp move. Flag = parallel lines, 5 days to 3–5 weeks; pennant = converging lines. In a rising market the flag slopes down; in a falling market it slopes up.
  • Wedges: converging lines both moving the same direction. Rising wedge appears in a falling trend and is followed by a sharp fall — characteristic of bear market rallies. Falling wedge interrupts a rising trend.
  • Gaps: breakaway at the beginning, runaway in the middle, exhaustion at the end. Gaps are not always filled, so do not trade on that assumption alone.
  • Elliott Wave: R.N. Elliott, 1938; 5-wave advance and 3-wave retreat; Golden Ratio 1.618; turning points at Fibonacci levels (61.8, 161.8).
  • Quantitative analysis: abstracts market reality into models to find price anomalies and arbitrage; uses statistics and calculus; quants look at second and third order derivatives, not just delta.
  • LTCM is the cautionary example of quantitative models failing despite mathematical elegance.
  • Trap: the Dow Theory identifies direction, not magnitude.
  • Trap: a rising wedge is bearish and a falling wedge is a continuation of an uptrend — the names describe the shape, not the implication.
  • Trap: an ascending triangle is bullish and a descending triangle is bearish, but a symmetrical triangle can break either way.
  • Trap: the RSI being persistently high in a steady uptrend is not a sell signal.

Chapter 12 — Case Studies

The examination includes 3 case studies carrying 9 questions — 3 questions per case study, about a tenth of the paper. The ten case studies in the official guide are the model for those questions: each sets a named client or scenario, then tests one chapter's method applied to it. This chapter works through all ten, with the arithmetic shown.

Learning Objectives

The candidate should be able to:

  • Apply the investor-classification framework to a named client.
  • Compute expected return, standard deviation, coefficient of variation and real future value.
  • Read economic indicators and business-cycle phases to select asset classes.
  • Attribute a price fall to the correct behavioural driver.
  • Compute a carry trade's gain under three exchange-rate scenarios.
  • Compute prospective P/E, EPS growth and PEG, and act on the result.
  • Explain the DCF steps and compute enterprise value.
  • Read bond prices, yields and duration to judge interest-rate sensitivity.
  • Match a strategic asset allocation to a client's objectives and constraints.
  • Compute warrant intrinsic value, minimum gain and read an FX quote.
  • Distinguish unit trusts, business trusts and REITs, and select the vehicle that fits an income objective.

12.1 Individual versus Institutional Investor

Scenario. John Lim is moving from stockbroking to a private bank managing accredited investors. In his current job he works mostly with institutional investors, so he must adjust to the differences in client type. He asks you, as his soon-to-be colleague, to explain the key differences.

Question 1 — Which of the following is an accredited investor? (Select all that apply)

  • a. An entity with S$5 million worth of net assets.
  • b. A university lecturer with $500,000 in net personal assets.
  • c. An accountant that earns S$400,000 a year.
  • d. A university endowment trust that has S$6 billion in investible funds.

Answer: c and d.

Options (a) and (b) are incorrect because neither the individual nor the entity qualifies. Option (c) is an accredited investor because the individual earns more than S300,000**ayear.Option(d)isanaccreditedinvestorbecausethetrusthasfunds**exceedingS300,000** a year. Option (d) is an accredited investor because the trust has funds **exceeding S10 million in value.

Question 2 — Which of the following is not likely to be a return objective of an institutional investor?

  • a. Current income to meet recurring liquidity needs.
  • b. Long-term capital gain to beat inflation.
  • c. Potential for higher yields.
  • d. Regular savings to fund children's education.

Answer: d.

Options (a) to (c) can be return objectives of both individual and institutional investors. Option (d) is likely to be unique to an individual investor.

Question 3 — Which of the following shows the key differences between an accredited investor and a retail investor? (Select all that apply)

  • a. A retail investor is likely to be more risk averse than an accredited investor.
  • b. The accredited investor can withstand a higher level of monetary risk than the retail investor.
  • c. A retail investor has a longer investment time horizon than an accredited investor.
  • d. An accredited investor is able to access a wider range of investment products than a retail investor.

Answer: a, b and d.

Option (a) is correct: retail investors usually trade in small amounts and less frequently, and have little influence over corporate decisions or the capital markets. Option (b) is correct: given their wealth, accredited investors are considered financially savvy and better able to understand financial instruments, so they can withstand more monetary risk. Option (c) is incorrect because the investment time horizon depends on the needs of the investor, not the type. Option (d) is correct: accredited investors may access more complex and riskier products such as unrated bonds and products requiring neither a prospectus nor a reasonable basis for recommendation by a CMI representative.

12.2 Risk, Return and Time Value Calculations

Scenario. Edna Wong has just turned 35 and wants to set aside $200,000 for 30 years in an investment with the following annual returns under different economic scenarios. The average long-term inflation rate is expected to be 2%.

State of economy Probability Return
Boom 0.3 12%
Normal 0.5 8%
Recession 0.2 −6%

Question 1 — The expected rate of return is:

  • a. 5.30%
  • b. 6.40%
  • c. 8.45%
  • d. 9.28%

Answer: b.

The expected return is the probability-weighted average of the returns across economic states:

E(R)=0.3(0.12)+0.5(0.08)+0.2(−0.06)=0.0640=6.40%E(R) = 0.3(0.12) + 0.5(0.08) + 0.2(-0.06) = 0.0640 = 6.40\%

Question 2 — The coefficient of variation associated with this investment is:

  • a. 0.47
  • b. 0.68
  • c. 1.01
  • d. 1.33

Answer: c.

Variance is the probability-weighted average of the squared deviations from the mean:

σ2=0.3(0.12−0.064)2+0.5(0.08−0.064)2+0.2(−0.06−0.064)2=0.004144\sigma^2 = 0.3(0.12 - 0.064)^2 + 0.5(0.08 - 0.064)^2 + 0.2(-0.06 - 0.064)^2 = 0.004144

σ=0.004144=0.064374=6.4374%\sigma = \sqrt{0.004144} = 0.064374 = 6.4374\%

CV=0.0643740.064=1.01CV = \frac{0.064374}{0.064} = 1.01

Question 3 — Assuming the expected return is the average return for the next thirty years, the size of Edna's nest egg when she turns 65, in today's dollars, is:

  • a. $709,264.72
  • b. $1,610,176.77
  • c. $2,279,904.66
  • d. $2,865,831.06

Answer: a.

With expected inflation of 2%, the real rate of return is:

1+0.0641+0.02−1=0.0431=4.31%\frac{1 + 0.064}{1 + 0.02} - 1 = 0.0431 = 4.31\%

Future value in real terms:

200,000×(1.0431)30=$709,264.72200{,}000 \times (1.0431)^{30} = \$709{,}264.72

12.3 Key Drivers of Market Movement and Assets

Scenario. You are part of a team producing the market outlook for the US, China and Southeast Asia over the next 12 months. Your boss asks for a standard list of items to cover, forming an outline of the key topics the research team should provide for the sales force and clients.

Question 1 — One key concern of your US clients is the timing of a future economic downturn. Which of the following suggests a potential downturn?

  • a. Average duration of unemployment is increasing.
  • b. The 10-year T-bond spread over the Fed Funds rate is increasing.
  • c. Disposable personal incomes reported by the Bureau of Economic Analysis start to rise.
  • d. New orders by suppliers start to decline.

Answer: d.

Option (a) is a lagging indicator, so it is incorrect. Option (c) is a coincident indicator and its direction is inconsistent with a downturn. Option (b) is a leading indicator, but an increase in the spread generally bodes well for economic health. Option (d) is correct because suppliers normally cut orders when they expect demand to drop.

Question 2 — Strategists postulate a slowdown in the Chinese economy occurring with rising interest rates. Which asset classes are likely to do well?

  • a. Cash, real estate
  • b. Defensive stocks, investment grade bonds
  • c. Cyclical stocks, high-yield bonds
  • d. Growth stocks, precious metals

Answer: b.

A slowdown with rising interest rates is characteristic of the late bull to early bear phase. Defensive stocks and investment grade bonds are likely to do well.

Option (a) is incorrect: although raising cash may be wise, holding real estate is risky because it is typically leveraged and rates are rising. Option (c) is possibly the worst: cyclical stocks perform worse than the market when things turn down, and high-yield issuers may default. Option (d) is incorrect: some precious metals allocation may help in uncertainty, but growth stocks are less likely to meet growth expectations and may see P/E multiple contraction.

Question 3 — Uninformed fund managers reduced positions out of fear because news spread that many were doing likewise. Even though the scenario was unlikely, massive selling triggered computer-driven strategies. What is the root cause of the price fall?

  • a. Herd instinct
  • b. Loss aversion
  • c. Cognitive bias
  • d. Algorithmic trading

Answer: a.

The managers simply followed the crowd without exercising independent decision-making or due diligence — herd instinct. Loss aversion may have influenced them and algorithmic trading may have exacerbated the fall, but neither provided the original impetus. There is insufficient information about how the original discussants formed their conclusions to attribute the fall to cognitive bias.

12.4 Foreign Exchange Carry Trade

Scenario. An investor is tempted by IDR 100 billion of Indonesian government bonds. IDR-denominated 1-year government bonds pay 6%, while Singapore banks charge 1.5% for investment-related loans. SGD/IDR stands at 10,076.68. Assess three exchange-rate scenarios.

Question 1 — Ignoring bond price changes, what is the annual gain in SGD if the exchange rate stays flat?

  • a. SGD 148,858.55
  • b. SGD 446,575.66
  • c. SGD 595,434.21
  • d. SGD 9,923,903.51

Answer: b.

With a flat rate there is no currency gain or loss, so work in SGD. The IDR 100bn purchase is funded by an SGD-equivalent loan:

100,000,000,00010,076.68=SGD 9,923,903.51\frac{100{,}000{,}000{,}000}{10{,}076.68} = \text{SGD } 9{,}923{,}903.51

The investor earns 6% on the bonds and pays 1.5% on the loan, so the annual gain is:

(0.06−0.015)×9,923,903.51=SGD 446,575.66(0.06 - 0.015) \times 9{,}923{,}903.51 = \text{SGD } 446{,}575.66

Question 2 — What is the total gain if the IDR weakens against the SGD by 10% over the year?

  • a. −SGD 605,357.18
  • b. −SGD 942,771.98
  • c. SGD 605,357.18
  • d. SGD 942,771.98

Answer: a.

The loan is SGD 9,923,903.51, so annual interest expense is:

0.015×9,923,903.51=SGD 148,858.550.015 \times 9{,}923{,}903.51 = \text{SGD } 148{,}858.55

Interest income is IDR 6 billion (6% of IDR 100bn). With the IDR weakening 10%, the conversion rate is:

10,076.680.9=11,196.31\frac{10{,}076.68}{0.9} = 11{,}196.31

SGD-equivalent interest income:

6,000,000,00011,196.31=SGD 535,890.84\frac{6{,}000{,}000{,}000}{11{,}196.31} = \text{SGD } 535{,}890.84

The face value of the bonds converts back at 11,196.31:

100,000,000,00011,196.31=SGD 8,931,514.04\frac{100{,}000{,}000{,}000}{11{,}196.31} = \text{SGD } 8{,}931{,}514.04

Total gain:

(8,931,514.04−9,923,903.51)+(535,890.84−148,858.55)=−SGD 605,357.18(8{,}931{,}514.04 - 9{,}923{,}903.51) + (535{,}890.84 - 148{,}858.55) = -\text{SGD } 605{,}357.18

The interest income exceeds the borrowing expense, but the unfavourable FX movement has depreciated both the investment and the income. The carry trade is not profitable.

Question 3 — If in a year SGD/USD is 0.7 and USD/IDR is 13,086.60, how does the gain compare with Question 1?

  • a. Lower gain
  • b. Same gain
  • c. Higher gain
  • d. Insufficient information

Answer: c.

The SGD/IDR cross rate is:

0.7×13,086.60=9,160.620.7 \times 13{,}086.60 = 9{,}160.62

Since 9,160.62 is lower than 10,076.68, the IDR has appreciated against the SGD. The IDR-denominated investment and income appreciate in value, so the gain is higher than the SGD 446,575.66 in Question 1.

12.5 Equities Analysis

Scenario. Mr Quek has been recommended Mvidia, a semiconductor company with strong earnings growth. Demand for semiconductors in the PC industry remains sluggish, but companies focused on high-performance computing (HPC) — cloud computing, big data, artificial intelligence — are better positioned for strong growth. He has also heard that Mvidia's P/E is too high. Mvidia's stock price is USD 40.

Year EPS EPS change %
FY18A 1.12 −5.0
FY19E 1.08 −3.6
FY20F 2.57 +138.0
FY21F 4.19 +63.0
FY22F 4.67 +11.4
FY23F 5.81 +24.4

Question 1 — What is the prospective P/E for Mvidia and why?

  • a. The high ratio of 35.71 is likely because the market has overvalued Mvidia.
  • b. The high ratio of 35.71 is likely because the market is factoring in Mvidia's growth potential.
  • c. The high ratio of 37.04 is likely because the market has overvalued Mvidia.
  • d. The high ratio of 37.04 is likely because the market is factoring in Mvidia's growth potential.

Answer: d.

Prospective P/E=401.08=37.04x\text{Prospective P/E} = \frac{40}{1.08} = 37.04x

P/E ratios can be high because of strong expected future growth, so the high prospective P/E is likely because investors are factoring in Mvidia's high double-digit long-term growth potential.

Question 2 — What is the 5-year compounded annualised EPS growth rate?

  • a. 31.57%
  • b. 38.99%
  • c. 40.01%
  • d. 52.30%

Answer: b.

5-year EPS growth=[(5.811.12)1/5−1]×100%=38.99%\text{5-year EPS growth} = \left[ \left( \frac{5.81}{1.12} \right)^{1/5} - 1 \right] \times 100\% = 38.99\%

Question 3 — What recommendation would you give using Mvidia's prospective PEG ratio?

  • a. Buy Mvidia given the PEG ratio of 0.92.
  • b. Sell Mvidia given the PEG ratio of 0.92.
  • c. Buy Mvidia given the PEG ratio of 0.95.
  • d. Sell Mvidia given the PEG ratio of 0.95.

Answer: c.

Prospective PEG=37.0438.99=0.95\text{Prospective PEG} = \frac{37.04}{38.99} = 0.95

Because the PEG is less than 1, Mvidia is slightly undervalued even after accounting for its strong expected growth, so Mr Quek can consider buying the stock.

12.6 Estimating the Fair Value of a Stock

Scenario. A new client wants a brief explanation of the steps your firm's research team undertakes when estimating a company's fair value.

Question 1 — Free cash flows to a levered firm should be discounted using the firm's:

  • a. Cost of ordinary equity only.
  • b. Cost of preferred equity only.
  • c. Cost of debt only.
  • d. Weighted average cost of capital.

Answer: d.

The appropriate discount rate must account for capital from all sources for which a return is required. Option (a) would be correct only if the firm were all-equity funded, which it is not because it is levered. Options (b) and (c) are incorrect under any circumstance, since a firm must have ordinary equity.

Question 2 — Which of the following is NOT part of estimating free cash flows to the firm (FCFF)?

  • a. Interviewing company management on its revenue growth potential.
  • b. Consulting industry specialists on expected profitability margins.
  • c. Estimating the amounts of future fixed asset investments.
  • d. Analysing historical ratios to make interest expense projections.

Answer: d.

Revenue growth potential and profitability margins are needed to derive EBIT, a key FCFF input, so (a) and (b) are part of the estimate. Capital expenditure is another key input, so (c) is part of it. Interest expense is excluded from the FCFF computation, so (d) is not part of it.

Question 3 — Enterprise value can be calculated using ________. (Select all that apply)

  • a. Sum of the present values of the FCFFs for the projection period plus the terminal value.
  • b. Sum of the present values of the FCFFs for the projection period plus the present value of the terminal value.
  • c. Sum of the FCFFs for the projection period plus the present value of the terminal value.
  • d. Sum of the estimated market values of debt, common stock and preferred stock.

Answer: b and d.

Enterprise value can be calculated in two equivalent ways: the worth today of the cash flows the firm generates, or the value today of the claims on those cash flows. Option (a) fails to discount the terminal value; option (c) fails to discount the FCFFs in the projection period.

12.7 Fixed-Income Investments

Scenario. David is offered three USD fixed income instruments. The market expects interest rates to rise over the next year as the commodities, offshore oil, coal mining and energy industries come out of a slump.

Bond Maturity Yield to maturity Rating
New Offshore Oil Corp: 10-year 6% callable bond 5 years left 4.5% A−
Diversified Commodities Company: 10-year 4% bond 6 years left 6.0% BBB
Indonesian Coal Mining & Energy Company: 8% bond 4 years left 7.0% unrated

Question 1 — Why can some bonds be bought below face value?

  • a. The Indonesian Coal Mining & Energy Company bonds are unrated.
  • b. The New Offshore Oil Corp bonds are callable.
  • c. The YTM of the Diversified Commodities Company bonds is higher than the coupon rate.
  • d. The YTMs of the New Offshore Oil Corp and Indonesian Coal Mining & Energy Company bonds are lower than their respective coupon rates.

Answer: c.

A bond must be priced at a discount for its YTM to be higher than its coupon rate. Option (d) is wrong because those bonds will be priced at a premium (4.5% < 6%, and 7.0% < 8%). While investors may require higher yields for unrated and for callable bonds, that does not necessarily mean the yields exceed the respective coupon rates, so (a) and (b) are incorrect.

Question 2 — If David holds his bond to maturity, what should he be most concerned with?

  • a. A bond is callable.
  • b. Interest rates are increasing.
  • c. Interest rates are decreasing.
  • d. The coupon rate of a bond.

Answer: a.

A callable bond can be redeemed before maturity, and if that happens the investor faces reinvestment risk from having to reinvest the proceeds at lower yields.

Holding to maturity means the YTM, not the coupon rate, is the relevant measure — though to realise the YTM, coupons must be reinvested at the same yield. Option (a) is a much bigger concern than (d). Changes in interest rates affect price, but that is of little concern to a hold-to-maturity investor because the price converges to par on maturity, so (b) and (c) are incorrect.

Question 3 — Which scenario is likely in the coming year?

  • a. Diversified Commodities Company bond price is likely to decrease the most in percentage terms.
  • b. New Offshore Oil Corp bonds are likely to be called.
  • c. Indonesian Coal Mining & Energy Company bonds are likely to default.
  • d. Indonesian Coal Mining & Energy Company bonds are likely to increase the least in percentage terms.

Answer: a.

With rates expected to rise, bond prices are likely to fall. The Diversified Commodities Company bonds have the longest maturity (6 years) and lowest coupon (4%), so their prices are most sensitive to rate changes.

Option (d) is incorrect: although the Indonesian bonds are least sensitive because of the shortest maturity and highest coupon, a rate rise is likely to decrease the price, not increase it. Option (b) is incorrect because rising rates make a call unlikely. Option (c) is incorrect: being unrated does not necessarily mean poor credit — the company may simply have chosen not to seek ratings — and with the industries expected to recover, concluding default is a stretch.

12.8 Portfolio Management

Scenario. Mr Walter Koh is a retiree with 2million**ofinvestableassets,allcurrentlypassivelymanaged.Heiswillingtohave**2 million** of investable assets, all currently passively managed. He is willing to have **500,000 managed more actively and is prepared to risk 100,000**ofitinfull.Heplanstogiftabout**100,000** of it in full. He plans to gift about **100,000 from this actively managed fund three months from now to an art endowment fund. He is not a big spender but hopes to fund at least part of his annual expenses, which are highly predictable, from his active portfolio for the next twenty years. He is otherwise not concerned about liquidity.

Asset class Portfolio A Portfolio B Portfolio C Portfolio D
Money market funds 20% 10% 20% 20%
Treasury bills 10% 0% 10% 10%
Long-term government bonds 10% 80% 10% 50%
High yield bonds 10% 0% 40% 0%
Developed-market equities 50% 10% 20% 20%

Castor & Pollux shares have a beta of 1.2 and a past return of 9.5%, and have been recommended on their alpha potential after thorough fundamental analysis. The risk-free rate is 3% and the market risk premium is 6%.

Question 1 — Mr Koh does not believe one can achieve superior returns through fundamental analysis. Which form(s) of market efficiency must he necessarily believe in? (Select all that apply)

  • a. Weak form
  • b. Semi-weak form
  • c. Semi-strong form
  • d. Strong form

Answer: a and c.

Conducting fundamental analysis to identify a mispriced stock assumes all publicly available information is not already reflected in the price. So Mr Koh must believe the market is semi-strong form efficient. Because all publicly available information includes historical price and volume information, he must also believe it is weak form efficient. There is insufficient information about his views on private information to conclude he believes in strong-form efficiency. "Semi-weak form" is not a standard classification.

Question 2 — Jensen's alpha for Castor & Pollux is:

  • a. −2.9%
  • b. −0.7%
  • c. 0.7%
  • d. 2.9%

Answer: b.

Using CAPM, the required return is:

0.03+1.2(0.06)=10.2%0.03 + 1.2(0.06) = 10.2\%

With an actual return of 9.5%:

α=9.5%−10.2%=−0.7%\alpha = 9.5\% - 10.2\% = -0.7\%

Question 3 — Which portfolio best aligns with Mr Koh's objectives?

  • a. Portfolio A
  • b. Portfolio B
  • c. Portfolio C
  • d. Portfolio D

Answer: d.

Mr Koh needs $100,000, which is 20% of his $500,000 portfolio, as a gift shortly, so he should allocate that to money market investments, the most liquid asset class. Portfolio B is incorrect because of its low allocation to money market funds.

Portfolio C is incorrect because its combined 60% allocation to high-yield bonds and equities is likely too risky given he is only willing to risk up to $100,000. Portfolio A is incorrect for the same reason, and its allocation to long-term government bonds is likely too low to fund his annual expenses.

Portfolio D is correct: sufficient money market funds for the gift, an equity allocation that respects his risk aversion, and a sufficiently high allocation to long-term government bonds so the coupons can fund his annual expenses.

12.9 Warrants and Foreign Exchange

Scenario. Ms JL Tan has two questions. First, she is looking at the structured warrants of Poseidon Lines, a shipping company. Poseidon shares trade at 2.50**anditswarrantsat**2.50** and its warrants at **1.30. The warrants have a conversion ratio of 1:1 and an exercise price of $1.50. Second, she has sold some USD-denominated ADRs and will receive USD 50,000 in 2 business days, which she wants to convert to SGD.

Question 1 — What is the intrinsic value of Poseidon's structured warrant?

  • a. $0
  • b. $1
  • c. $1.50
  • d. $2.50

Answer: b.

The warrant is in-the-money, so:

Intrinsic value=2.50−1.501=$1\text{Intrinsic value} = \frac{2.50 - 1.50}{1} = \$1

Question 2 — You expect Poseidon's share price to rise to $4.00. What is Ms Tan's minimum gain on the warrants in percentage terms if she buys today?

  • a. 92.31%
  • b. 207.69%
  • c. 307.69%
  • d. Impossible to determine because the future price of the structured warrant is not known with certainty.

Answer: a.

If the share price rises to $4.00, the warrant's intrinsic value is:

4.00−1.501=$2.50\frac{4.00 - 1.50}{1} = \$2.50

Because the conversion ratio is 1, the minimum value of the warrant is its intrinsic value of $2.50. The minimum percentage gain is:

2.501.30−1=92.31%\frac{2.50}{1.30} - 1 = 92.31\%

Option (d) is incorrect: although the future warrant price is unknown, only the future minimum price is needed to compute the minimum percentage gain.

Question 3 — Ms Tan has two quotes. The best quote at which she can sell her ADR proceeds for SGD is:

Quote A: USD/SGD 1.2500 – 1.2550 Quote B: USD/SGD 1.2475 – 1.2515

  • a. USD/SGD 1.2500
  • b. USD/SGD 1.2550
  • c. USD/SGD 1.2475
  • d. USD/SGD 1.2515

Answer: a.

All quotations give the number of SGD (the counter currency) per one USD (the base currency). For each quote, the first rate is the price at which the market maker will buy USD and the second is the price at which it will sell USD. Since Ms Tan wants to sell USD, the first rate of each quote applies, and the highest of those is best: 1.2500.

12.10 Unit Trusts, REITs and Business Trusts

Scenario. Mr James Lim finds the jargon of collective investment schemes confusing. He asks you to demystify the differences between unit trusts, business trusts and REITs. He has investable funds and is deciding whether to invest in a property or one of these schemes. He is more interested in a steady stream of income than in large trading gains.

Question 1 — The common features among unit trusts, business trusts and REITs is/are that: (Select all that apply)

  • a. They are established under a trust deed.
  • b. They are exchange-traded.
  • c. They allow for diversification.
  • d. They are professionally managed.

Answer: a, c and d.

All three are established under a trust deed. By pooling and investing funds, all three allow diversification, albeit to different extents. The assets under all three are professionally managed. Option (b) is incorrect: while all REITs are listed, unit trusts are typically not listed and some business trusts are unlisted too.

Question 2 — The main difference(s) between business trusts and REITs is/are that: (Select all that apply)

  • a. The trustee and manager are separate in a REIT but not in a business trust.
  • b. Business trusts do not face investment restrictions, unlike REITs.
  • c. Business trusts are unlisted whereas REITs are listed.
  • d. There is a 75% gearing limit applicable on REITs but only a 45% gearing limit on business trusts.

Answer: a and b.

Unlike a REIT, a business trust is a single responsible entity organisation with a trustee-manager, so (a) is correct. Business trusts can actively engage in any business area, whereas REITs must invest only in real estate for rental income, so (b) is correct. Option (c) is incorrect because although some business trusts are unlisted, most are listed. Option (d) is incorrect: there is no gearing limit for business trusts and a 45% limit for REITs.

Question 3 — Given Mr Lim's objectives, the scheme most likely to suit his need is:

  • a. A unit trust described as an aggressive fund.
  • b. A business trust comprising investments in golf course assets.
  • c. A REIT that focuses on heartland retail malls.
  • d. All of the above.

Answer: c.

An aggressive unit trust generates returns from capital gains and is unlikely to provide a steady income stream, so (a) is incorrect. Cash flows from golf course assets are highly sensitive to economic fluctuations, and there is no mandatory minimum distribution for business trusts, so (b) will not provide steady income either. A REIT is often seen as an alternative to physical real estate and typically distributes at least 90% of annual income, which is likely to be more stable for heartland retail malls. Option (c) is therefore the best answer, which also makes (d) incorrect.

Exam cues

  • Case studies carry 3 questions each, 9 in total — about a tenth of the 90-question paper. Each tests one chapter's method applied to a named client.
  • Accredited investor tests: individual — net personal assets **> S2m**(residencecappedatS2m** (residence capped at S1m), financial assets > S1m**,orincome**≥S1m**, or income **≥ S300k in the preceding 12 months; entity — net assets > S$10m.
  • Time horizon depends on the investor's needs, not the investor type. This is the standard distractor.
  • Expected return =∑ripi= \sum r_i p_i. Worked: 0.3(12%) + 0.5(8%) + 0.2(−6%) = 6.40%.
  • Variance and CV: variance 0.004144, σ 6.4374%, CV 1.01.
  • Real future value: real rate = (1.064/1.02) − 1 = 4.31%; 200,000×1.0431³⁰=**200,000 × 1.0431³⁰ = **709,264.72**.
  • Leading indicators predict; coincident confirm the present; lagging confirm the past. New orders declining signals a downturn; average duration of unemployment is lagging; disposable personal income is coincident.
  • Slowdown with rising rates = late bull to early bear → defensive stocks and investment grade bonds.
  • Herd instinct is the root cause when managers follow the crowd without independent analysis; loss aversion and algorithmic trading may exacerbate but do not originate.
  • Carry trade worked example: IDR 100bn at 10,076.68 = SGD 9,923,903.51 loan. Flat rate → +SGD 446,575.66. IDR weakens 10% (rate 11,196.31) → −SGD 605,357.18. Cross rate 0.7 × 13,086.60 = 9,160.62 (IDR appreciated) → higher gain.
  • Prospective P/E = price / next-year EPS. Mvidia: 40/1.08 = 37.04x. A high P/E usually reflects growth expectations, not overvaluation.
  • 5-year EPS growth = (5.81/1.12)^(1/5) − 1 = 38.99%.
  • PEG = prospective P/E / EPS growth = 37.04/38.99 = 0.95. Below 1 → undervalued → buy.
  • FCFF is discounted at WACC, because capital comes from all sources. Interest expense is excluded from FCFF.
  • Enterprise value = PV of FCFFs + PV of terminal value = market value of debt + common stock + preferred stock.
  • Bond at a discount means YTM > coupon. New Offshore Oil: 4.5% < 6% → premium. Indonesian Coal: 7.0% < 8% → premium. Diversified Commodities: 6.0% > 4% → discount.
  • Hold-to-maturity investor's main concern is a call feature (reinvestment risk), not price volatility, because price converges to par.
  • Longest maturity and lowest coupon = most rate-sensitive. Diversified Commodities (6 years, 4%) falls most when rates rise.
  • Unrated ≠ poor credit. A company may simply choose not to seek a rating.
  • Fundamental analysis failing implies semi-strong efficiency, which necessarily implies weak-form efficiency too. "Semi-weak" is not a classification.
  • Jensen's alpha = actual − [Rf+β(Rm−Rf)R_f + \beta(R_m - R_f)]. Castor & Pollux: 9.5% − [3% + 1.2(6%)] = −0.7%.
  • Portfolio selection: match the liquidity need (20% for the gift), the risk budget ($100,000 of $500,000), and the income need (long-term government bond coupons).
  • Warrant intrinsic value = (SP − EP)/n. Poseidon: (2.50 − 1.50)/1 = $1.
  • Minimum gain uses the minimum value (intrinsic value), not the unknown future warrant price: 2.50/1.30 − 1 = 92.31%.
  • Selling USD: use the bid (first rate) and pick the highest — 1.2500.
  • Common to unit trusts, business trusts and REITs: trust deed, diversification, professional management. Not exchange-trading — unit trusts are typically unlisted.
  • REIT vs business trust: separate trustee and manager vs single trustee-manager; investment restrictions vs none; 45% gearing cap vs no cap; 90% mandatory distribution vs no minimum.
  • Income objective → REIT, because of the 90% distribution requirement and stable heartland retail cash flows.
  • Trap: a high P/E is not automatically overvaluation — check the growth rate with PEG before concluding.
  • Trap: an unrated bond is not automatically a default risk.
  • Trap: for a hold-to-maturity investor, interest rate risk is largely irrelevant; the call feature is the real risk.

Appendix A — Review Questions

Candidates should note that the sole purpose of the Review Questions is to familiarise candidates with the scope and general nature of the examinations, and the format of the examination questions. They are not intended as preparatory study material, and do not cover all the material tested. The correct answer for each question is in bold in the source booklet and is reproduced as Answer below.

All 50 review questions appear here, in the booklet's own order and chapter grouping, so the appendix can be worked as a single timed set. The booklet prints the correct option in bold; that convention is preserved.

Chapter 2 — Risk, Return and Time Value Calculations

1. As an investment manager, you are assessing a project with an immediate cash outflow followed by a series of cash inflows over the next 10 years. You calculate the project's net present value (NPV) — the sum of the present values of the cash inflows minus the initial cash outflow — and also its internal rate of return (IRR). You then discover you have underestimated the discount rate. What happens when you correct for the underestimation?

  • a. There will be a reduction to NPV with no change to IRR.
  • b. There will be no change to both NPV and IRR.
  • c. There will be an increase to NPV and a reduction to IRR.
  • d. Both NPV and IRR will increase.

Answer: a. NPV discounts the cash flows at the given rate, so raising the rate lowers NPV. IRR is the rate at which NPV equals zero and is a property of the cash flows alone, so it does not change.

2. A diversified portfolio has an expected return of 6% and a standard deviation of 12%. There is a 68% probability of a return between −6% and +18% (plus or minus one standard deviation). Returns are normally distributed, so the probability of a loss exceeding 6% is 16%. We can expect the portfolio's loss to exceed 6% once every ________.

  • a. 5–6 years.
  • b. 6–7 years.
  • c. 7–8 years.
  • d. 8–9 years.

Answer: b. A 16% probability is about 1 in 6.25, so roughly once every 6–7 years.

3. Which statements about value at risk (VaR) are TRUE?

  • a. It is not an applicable measure for loss probability on assets such as bonds, shares and currencies.
  • b. It measures and quantifies the minimum possible loss of an investment over a specific time and within a confidence level.
  • c. It can be calculated by applying Monte Carlo simulation or the historical method.
  • d. It can be used when determinants of future returns differ from those of past returns.

Options: (a) and (d) · (c) and (d) · (a) and (c) · (b) and (c)

Answer: (b) and (c). VaR quantifies the loss at a stated confidence level and can be computed historically or by Monte Carlo. It applies to bonds, shares and currencies, and its historical form assumes past determinants persist.

4. Which of the following are forms of operational risk?

  • a. A flash crash caused by a massive erroneous sell order.
  • b. Poor system infrastructure leading to technical disruptions.
  • c. Human errors resulting in erroneous trades.
  • d. Inability to access funding due to a credit downgrade of the borrower.

Options: (a), (b) and (c) · (b) and (c) · (b), (c) and (d) · (a) and (b)

Answer: (a), (b) and (c). Option (d) is funding liquidity risk, not operational risk.

Chapter 3 — Key Drivers of Market Movements and Asset Values

5. Which of the following is a leading indicator?

  • a. Average duration of unemployment.
  • b. The 10-year T-bond spread over the Fed Funds rate.
  • c. Nonfarm payroll employment.
  • d. The average prime rate charged by banks.

Answer: b. The 10-year spread is one of the ten CLEI components. Average duration of unemployment and the average prime rate are lagging; nonfarm payrolls are coincident.

6. A central bank lowers the reserve requirement ratio. What is the most direct effect?

  • a. The money supply contracts.
  • b. The money supply expands through credit creation.
  • c. Bond prices fall.
  • d. The exchange rate appreciates immediately.

Answer: b. Lowering required reserves expands the money supply and multiplies lending through the banking system.

7. Which of the following best describes the liquidity preference theory of the yield curve?

  • a. The curve's shape reflects investors' interest rate expectations.
  • b. The curve should always be upward sloping, because investors require a premium to hold longer maturities.
  • c. Each maturity's yield is set solely by supply and demand in that segment.
  • d. The curve is flat when the market is ambivalent.

Answer: b. Liquidity preference holds that the curve is upward sloping because long-maturity securities are more price-volatile and require a higher return.

Chapter 4 — Foreign Exchange

8. Spot USD/SGD is 1.2520 and the 30-day forward points are −10. The 30-day forward rate is:

  • a. 1.2510
  • b. 1.2530
  • c. 1.2520
  • d. 1.2500

Answer: a. Negative points are subtracted: 1.2520 − 0.0010 = 1.2510, a forward discount.

9. A Singapore investor holds a JPY portfolio that returned 121.88% while SGD/JPY rose 18.89%. The currency-adjusted return in SGD is approximately:

  • a. 140.77%
  • b. 86.62%
  • c. 102.99%
  • d. 121.88%

Answer: b. The reference currency (SGD) is the first currency of the pair, so divide: (1 + 1.2188)/(1 + 0.1889) − 1 = 86.62%.

10. Which of the following is a non-deliverable forward characteristic?

  • a. Physical delivery of the domestic currency at maturity.
  • b. Exchange of the full notional amount at settlement.
  • c. Cash settlement of the difference between the contracted rate and the spot rate, with no exchange of notional.
  • d. A tenor of five years or more.

Answer: c. An NDF is cash-settled with no delivery of the domestic currency and no exchange of notional; the normal tenor is 1 month to 1 year.

Chapter 5 — Company Analysis and Understanding Financial Statements

11. A company has current assets of 500,000**andcurrentliabilitiesof**500,000** and current liabilities of **250,000. Its current ratio is:

  • a. 0.5
  • b. 2.0
  • c. 1.5
  • d. 2.5

Answer: b. 500,000 / 250,000 = 2.0.

12. Which of the following would improve a company's reported ROE without any operational improvement?

  • a. Increasing the dividend payout ratio.
  • b. Writing down goodwill against equity reserves.
  • c. Increasing inventory levels.
  • d. Lengthening the depreciation period.

Answer: b. A goodwill write-down reduces equity (the denominator), raising ROE in later periods without any operational change.

13. Which of the following is a non-cash expense?

  • a. Staff costs.
  • b. Interest expense.
  • c. Depreciation.
  • d. Tax paid.

Answer: c. Depreciation is an accounting allocation, not a cash outflow, which is why it is added back in the cash flow statement.

13a. Derrick has prepared his company's financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2019, which reflect an operating profit of 280,000**,currentassetsof**280,000**, current assets of **510,000 and total assets of 833,000**.Hehassincediscoveredthatthedepreciationfigureheusedwasoverstated,ashedoublecountedthedepreciationcostof**833,000**. He has since discovered that the depreciation figure he used was overstated, as he double counted the depreciation cost of **55,000. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  • a. The revised operating profit for the year will be $335,000.
  • b. The revised depreciation expense figure will be $110,000.
  • c. The revised current assets figure will be $565,000.
  • d. The revised total assets figure will be $778,000.

Answer: a. Overstating depreciation by 55,000understatedoperatingprofitbythesameamount,sothecorrectionaddsitback:280,000+55,000=**55,000 understated operating profit by the same amount, so the correction adds it back: 280,000 + 55,000 = **335,000**. Depreciation is a non-current asset adjustment, so current assets are unaffected — option (c) is wrong. Total assets rise by $55,000 to $888,000, not fall to $778,000.

13b. The purposes of the statement of cash flows are to:

  • a. Evaluate liquidity.
  • b. Facilitate banking relationships.
  • c. Analyse cash position.
  • d. Compare investment performance.

Options: (a) and (b) · (a), (b) and (c) · (a) and (c) · (a) and (d)

Answer: (a), (b) and (c). The statement of cash flows evaluates liquidity, facilitates banking relationships and analyses the cash position. Comparing investment performance is the job of return measurement, not the cash flow statement.

Chapter 6 — Equity Securities

14. A company has 300 million shares at 2.00**andannouncesa**1−for−3**rightsissueat**2.00** and announces a **1-for-3** rights issue at **1.90. The theoretical ex-rights price is:

  • a. $1.50
  • b. $1.975
  • c. $2.00
  • d. $1.90

Answer: b. New shares 100m at $1.90 = $190m; total market value $600m + $190m = 790mover400mshares=**790m over 400m shares = **1.975**.

15. A stock trades at 34.68**withaconsensusnext−yearEPSof**34.68** with a consensus next-year EPS of **2.86. Its prospective P/E is:

  • a. 12.8x
  • b. 12.1x
  • c. 11.7x
  • d. 13.5x

Answer: b. 34.68 / 2.86 = 12.1x.

16. Which index weighting scheme automatically adjusts for bonus and rights issues?

  • a. Value-weighted
  • b. Price-weighted
  • c. Equal-weighted
  • d. Geometric average

Answer: a. Capital changes do not affect market capitalisation, so a value-weighted index adjusts automatically. A price-weighted index needs a divisor adjustment.

16a. Which of the following statements are TRUE about preference shares?

  • a. The preference rate of dividend is usually fixed and specified.
  • b. The issuer is not obliged to pay the preference dividend if there are poor earnings.
  • c. Preference shares can be issued as redeemable shares.
  • d. The preference dividend must be paid after the ordinary dividend has been paid.

Options: (a), (b) and (c) · (b), (c) and (d) · (a), (c) and (d) · (a), (b), (c) and (d)

Answer: (a), (b) and (c). The preference dividend is usually a fixed, specified rate; the issuer is not obliged to pay it when earnings are poor, and a missed preference dividend is not a default; and preference shares may be issued as redeemable. Statement (d) reverses the priority — preference dividends rank before ordinary dividends.

16b. A price-weighted index consists of four stocks. One of the stocks is subject to a 3-for-1 stock split. What is most likely to happen to the divisor for the index?

  • a. Decrease.
  • b. Increase.
  • c. Nullify.
  • d. Remain unchanged.

Answer: a. A 3-for-1 split cuts that stock's price to a third. Because the index is the sum of prices divided by the divisor and the numerator has fallen, the divisor must be reduced to keep the index level unchanged.

16c. MaMa Rich is a listed food and beverage firm. Its stock is slightly more volatile than the market, with a beta of 1.3, and the market's expected rate of return is 9.33%. The US 5-year Treasury bill rate is currently 5.8%. What is the firm's cost of equity capital?

  • a. 9.515%
  • b. 10.123%
  • c. 10.389%
  • d. 11.761%

Answer: c. CAPM: R = Rf + β(Rm − Rf) = 5.8 + 1.3(9.33 − 5.8) = 5.8 + 1.3(3.53) = 5.8 + 4.589 = 10.389%.

16d. The price-to-sales ratio (P/Sales) is a helpful valuation technique when examining firms ______________.

  • a. That have negative earnings.
  • b. In the technology sector only.
  • c. That are highly leveraged.
  • d. In the start-up or early stage of their life cycle.

Answer: d. P/Sales is useful where earnings are negative or unstable, which is typical of start-ups and early-stage firms. It is not confined to technology, and it does not correct for leverage — the ratio is conceptually flawed because the numerator relates to shareholders while sales are generated from funds supplied by both shareholders and debtholders.

16e. Which of the following are not advantages of American Depositary Receipts (ADRs)?

  • a. They allow US investors to invest in foreign companies.
  • b. They are denominated in US dollars and pay dividends in US dollars.
  • c. They are traded on US exchanges.
  • d. They eliminate currency risk.

Options: (a) and (b) · (b) and (c) · (d) only · (a), (b) and (c)

Answer: (d) only. ADRs give US investors access to foreign companies, are USD-denominated and pay USD dividends, and trade on US exchanges. They do not eliminate currency risk: the underlying shares remain denominated in the issuer's home currency, so the ADR price moves with the exchange rate.

Chapter 7 — Deposits and Fixed-Income Securities

17. A T-bill with 90 days to maturity, face value 100,000**,sellsfor**100,000**, sells for **98,000. The bank discount yield is:

  • a. 2.04%
  • b. 8.0%
  • c. 8.16%
  • d. 7.35%

Answer: b. (2,000/100,000) × (360/90) = 8.0%.

18. A 10-year bond with par $1,000 and an 8% coupon, with a required yield of 6% and annual coupons, is priced at approximately:

  • a. $1,000.00
  • b. $1,147.20
  • c. $1,148.77
  • d. $920.00

Answer: b. Discounting eight $80 coupons and the 1,000principalat61,000 principal at 6% gives **1,147.20**. The semi-annual equivalent is $1,148.77.

19. Which bond has the highest convexity?

  • a. A 5-year 8% coupon bond.
  • b. A 10-year 8% coupon bond.
  • c. A 10-year 4% coupon bond.
  • d. A 10-year zero-coupon bond.

Answer: d. The lower the coupon, the higher the convexity; a zero-coupon bond has the highest convexity of all.

20. A convertible bond has a conversion ratio of 40, a market price of 1,100**andanunderlyingsharepriceof**1,100** and an underlying share price of **24. The conversion premium in percentage terms is:

  • a. 4.2%
  • b. 14.6%
  • c. 27.5%
  • d. 51.0%

Answer: b. Conversion value = 40 × $24 = 960.Premium=(960. Premium = (1,100 − 960)/960)/960 = 14.6%.

20a. As compared with bonds selling at par, deep discount bonds such as zero-coupon bonds will have:

  • a. Greater reinvestment risk.
  • b. Greater price volatility.
  • c. Less call protection.
  • d. None of the above.

Answer: b. A zero-coupon bond has no reinvestment risk if held to maturity, because there is no coupon to reinvest — so (a) is the opposite of the truth. Its price is the most sensitive to interest rate changes, because all of its cash flow arrives at maturity.

20b. What is the main feature of a callable bond?

  • a. It gives the issuer the option to redeem the bond before maturity.
  • b. It gives the buyer the option to redeem the bond before maturity.
  • c. It gives the issuer the option to redeem the bond after maturity.
  • d. It gives the buyer the option to redeem the bond after maturity.

Answer: a. The call option belongs to the issuer, not the buyer, and it is exercisable before maturity. The buyer's equivalent right is the put provision.

20c. Which of the following are potential risks that may arise when investing in foreign government bonds?

  • a. Corporate sector downgrade risk.
  • b. Sovereign credit risk.
  • c. Currency risk.
  • d. Political risk.

Options: (a), (b) and (c) · (b), (c) and (d) · (c) and (d) · (a) and (c)

Answer: (b), (c) and (d). A foreign government bond carries sovereign credit risk, currency risk and political risk. Corporate sector downgrade risk is not a feature of a sovereign issue.

20d. What is the value of a bond that matures in 3 years, has an annual coupon of 110**,andaparvalueof**110**, and a par value of **1,000? Assume a required rate of return of 11%.

  • a. $330
  • b. $1,000
  • c. $970
  • d. $1,330

Answer: b. The coupon rate is 110/1,000 = 11%, exactly equal to the required return, so the bond prices at par. No discounting is needed once the coupon rate and the yield are seen to match.

20e. What happens to a bond's yield-to-maturity (YTM) if there is an increase in the bond price?

  • a. The bond's YTM rises.
  • b. The bond's YTM falls.
  • c. The bond's YTM remains unchanged.
  • d. The bond's YTM could fluctuate, depending on market conditions.

Answer: b. Price and yield are inversely related. A higher price means a lower yield to maturity.

Chapter 8 — Portfolio Management

21. A portfolio has an expected return of 18% and a standard deviation of 20%; a second has 9% and 10%. With weights of 40% and 60% and a correlation of 0.8, portfolio risk is:

  • a. 14.00%
  • b. 10.00%
  • c. 13.30%
  • d. 2.00%

Answer: c. √(0.4²×0.2² + 0.6²×0.1² + 2×0.4×0.6×0.8×0.2×0.1) = √0.01768 = 13.30%.

22. A portfolio returned 16% with a standard deviation of 20%; the risk-free rate is 6%. Its Sharpe ratio is:

  • a. 0.27
  • b. 0.50
  • c. 0.39
  • d. 0.80

Answer: b. (0.16 − 0.06)/0.20 = 0.50.

23. Which measure is most appropriate for evaluating a portfolio manager?

  • a. Dollar-weighted rate of return.
  • b. Time-weighted rate of return.
  • c. Current yield.
  • d. Total return.

Answer: b. The TWR is unaffected by the size and timing of client cash flows, which the manager does not control.

24. A portfolio has a beta of 1.2, the risk-free rate is 3% and the market risk premium is 6%. Its CAPM required return is:

  • a. 7.2%
  • b. 9.0%
  • c. 10.2%
  • d. 12.0%

Answer: c. 3% + 1.2(6%) = 10.2%.

24a. If you wish to eliminate the risk of your single-security portfolio, you will select a security that is ______________ to your portfolio.

  • a. Perfectly positively correlated.
  • b. Perfectly negatively correlated.
  • c. Not correlated.
  • d. Highly correlated.

Answer: b. Combining two securities with perfect negative correlation can eliminate portfolio risk altogether. This is the principle behind hedging strategies. Zero correlation reduces risk but does not eliminate it.

24b. Which of the following will affect the expected return of a portfolio under the Capital Asset Pricing Model?

  • a. Risk-free rate.
  • b. Idiosyncratic risk of an individual security.
  • c. Systematic risk of the portfolio.
  • d. Market risk premium.

Options: (a), (b) and (c) · (b), (c) and (d) · (a), (c) and (d) · (a), (b), (c) and (d)

Answer: (a), (c) and (d). CAPM prices only systematic risk, so idiosyncratic risk is not compensated — it can be diversified away. The risk-free rate, the portfolio's beta and the market risk premium are the three inputs.

24c. John recently bought a financial product with an initial investment capital of 500,000**.Attheendoftheproduct′stenurehisinvestmentvalueis**500,000**. At the end of the product's tenure his investment value is **550,000, and he received distributions worth $10,000 in the interim. What was the return on John's investment?

  • a. 2%
  • b. 8%
  • c. 12%
  • d. 10%

Answer: c. Total return includes distributions: (550,000 − 500,000 + 10,000)/500,000 = 60,000/500,000 = 12%. Ignoring the distribution gives 10%, which is the trap.

24d. When analysing a portfolio with frequent injections of capital, what would be the best measure for evaluating the investment manager's performance?

  • a. Simple return.
  • b. Expected return.
  • c. Time-weighted return.
  • d. Dollar-weighted return.

Answer: c. The TWR removes the effect of the size and timing of client cash flows, which the manager does not control. The DWR is the IRR and is dominated by those flows.

24e. The Sharpe performance measure is defined as:

  • a. The difference between the actual return on the portfolio and the return that would be expected from the capital asset pricing model.
  • b. The portfolio's excess return divided by the portfolio's beta.
  • c. The difference between the actual return on the portfolio and the return that would be expected from the capital asset pricing model, divided by the portfolio's total risk.
  • d. The portfolio's excess return divided by the portfolio's total risk.

Answer: d. Sharpe = (Rp − Rf)/σp. Option (a) describes Jensen's alpha, and option (b) describes the Treynor ratio.

Chapter 9 — ETFs, Unit Trusts, REITs and Insurance

25. Which of the following is not covered by the Singapore Deposit Insurance Scheme?

  • a. A Singapore dollar savings account.
  • b. A Singapore dollar fixed deposit.
  • c. A foreign currency deposit.
  • d. Monies under the CPF Investment Scheme.

Answer: c. The scheme covers Singapore dollar-denominated deposits only. Foreign currency deposits, structured deposits and investment products are excluded.

26. A REIT must invest at least what proportion of its fund in income-producing real estate?

  • a. 45%
  • b. 90%
  • c. 75%
  • d. 50%

Answer: c. The Code on CIS requires a minimum of 75% in income-producing real estate. The 90% figure is the distribution requirement.

27. Which of the following is a feature of a business trust but not a REIT?

  • a. A 45% gearing limit.
  • b. A mandatory 90% distribution.
  • c. No gearing limit and no investment restrictions.
  • d. A separate trustee and manager.

Answer: c. Business trusts have no gearing limit and no investment restrictions, and use a single trustee-manager.

28. An investor pays $1,000 a year for 5 years at a 3% discount rate. The present value is:

  • a. $5,000.00
  • b. $4,579.71
  • c. $4,212.36
  • d. $5,309.14

Answer: b. 1,000 × [1 − (1.03)⁻⁵]/0.03 = $4,579.71.

28a. Which of the following are advantages of investing in ETFs?

  • a. Access to a superior hedge fund manager.
  • b. Small capital outlay.
  • c. Low costs.
  • d. Transparency.

Options: (a), (b) and (d) · (b) and (c) · (a), (c) and (d) · (b), (c) and (d)

Answer: (b), (c) and (d). ETFs offer a small capital outlay, low costs and transparency. They give no access to a hedge fund manager, which is a feature of a fund of hedge funds.

28b. Which of the following is not a feature of real estate investment?

  • a. Provides security of income.
  • b. Provides a hedge against inflation.
  • c. Requires a high capital outlay.
  • d. Requires annual injection of capital.

Answer: c. A high capital outlay is a genuine feature of direct real estate investment, so it cannot be the exception. The statement that does not hold is that real estate requires an annual injection of capital: the asset is held, not topped up each year.

28c. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

  • a. Apart from REITs, trusts that invest in real estate can be structured as business trusts.
  • b. A business trust has a single responsible entity that serves as both the trustee and the manager.
  • c. A business trust has no gearing limit.
  • d. Both REITs and business trusts are required to distribute a minimum of 90% of annual income.

Options: (a), (c) and (d) · (a), (b) and (c) · (b), (c) and (d) · (a), (b), (c) and (d)

Answer: (a), (b) and (c). Statement (d) is wrong: only a REIT carries the 90% distribution requirement. A business trust has no mandatory minimum.

28d. Which of the following are main characteristics of hedge funds?

  • a. Use of leverage to increase potential returns.
  • b. Measured against absolute returns rather than relative returns.
  • c. Lower fees than other financial products.
  • d. Relatively unrestricted investment style.

Options: (a), (b) and (d) · (b), (c) and (d) · (a), (b) and (c) · (a), (c) and (d)

Answer: (a), (b) and (d). Hedge funds use leverage, target absolute returns and are relatively unrestricted. Their fees are higher, not lower, than those of conventional funds — typically a management fee plus a performance fee.

28e. Which statement best describes private equity investments?

  • a. Investments that are exclusive to private banking clients.
  • b. Investments in companies that are not publicly listed.
  • c. Investments in companies that operate in the private sector.
  • d. Investments that are not publicly disclosed to outsiders and non-clients.

Answer: b. Private equity is investment in companies that are not publicly listed. The private sector is not the defining test — a listed company is in the private sector too — and private equity is not restricted to private banking clients.

Chapter 10 — Warrants

29. A warrant has a share price of 2.50**,anexercisepriceof**2.50**, an exercise price of **1.50 and a conversion ratio of 1. Its intrinsic value is:

  • a. $0
  • b. $1.00
  • c. $1.50
  • d. $2.50

Answer: b. (2.50 − 1.50)/1 = $1.00.

30. A warrant trades at 1.30**withasharepriceof**1.30** with a share price of **2.50 and an exercise price of $1.50, conversion ratio 1. Its gearing ratio is approximately:

  • a. 1.9x
  • b. 1.9x to 2.0x depending on the share price used
  • c. 8.8x
  • d. 0.5x

Answer: b. Gearing = SP/(n × WP) = 2.50/1.30 = 1.92x.

31. Which factor reduces a company warrant's price?

  • a. An increase in the underlying share price.
  • b. An increase in volatility.
  • c. An increase in dividend expectations.
  • d. An increase in the remaining life of the warrant.

Answer: c. Warrant holders do not receive dividends, so higher dividend expectations reduce the call warrant's price.

31a. Company A's warrant is trading at 0.35**;itsexercisepriceis**0.35**; its exercise price is **0.50 while the share price is $0.65. What is its intrinsic value?

  • a. $0.85
  • b. $0.15
  • c. $0.30
  • d. $1.00

Answer: b. Intrinsic value = (SP − EP)/n = (0.65 − 0.50)/1 = $0.15.

31b. A warrant with an exercise price of 1.00**istradingat**1.00** is trading at **1.20. One warrant converts to one share. What is its conversion price?

  • a. $1.00
  • b. $1.20
  • c. $2.20
  • d. $0.20

Answer: c. Conversion price = n × WP + EP = 1 × 1.20 + 1.00 = $2.20. This is the total the investor pays to convert warrants into one share.

31c. The market price of Company B's common share is 5**andtheexercisepriceofthewarrantis**5** and the exercise price of the warrant is **3.50. Two warrants convert into one common share. The warrant price is $2. What is the warrant premium?

  • a. 10%
  • b. 50%
  • c. 57%
  • d. 100%

Answer: b. Premium ()=nWP+EP−SP=2(2.00)+3.50−5.00=**) = nWP + EP − SP = 2(2.00) + 3.50 − 5.00 = **2.50**. Premium (%) = 2.50/5.00 × 100 = 50%. The conversion ratio of 2 is the trap: using n = 1 gives (2.00 + 3.50 − 5.00)/5.00 = 10%, which is option (a).

31d. A warrant is trading at 0.40**.Theexercisepriceis**0.40**. The exercise price is **0.80. The share price is $2.40. What is its gearing? Assume the warrant is company-issued, so the conversion ratio is 1.

  • a. 2x
  • b. 6x
  • c. 3x
  • d. 5x

Answer: b. Gearing = SP/(nWP) = 2.40/0.40 = 6x.

31e. Which of the following will directly affect the price of a company warrant?

  • a. The length of time before the expiration date.
  • b. The coupon rate of bonds issued by the company.
  • c. The underlying share price.
  • d. The number of warrants issued by the company.

Options: (a), (b) and (c) · (a), (c) and (d) · (b) and (d) · (a) and (c)

Answer: (a), (c) and (d). Time to expiry, the underlying share price and the size of the warrant issue all affect the warrant price directly. The coupon rate on the company's bonds is not a direct determinant.

Chapter 11 — Technical Analysis and Quantitative Analysis

32. An RSI reading of 75 most likely indicates:

  • a. An oversold condition.
  • b. An overbought condition.
  • c. A neutral market.
  • d. A trend reversal has already occurred.

Answer: b. An RSI above 70 is considered overbought; below 30 is oversold.

33. Which chart pattern is a reversal pattern?

  • a. Ascending triangle.
  • b. Flag.
  • c. Head and shoulders.
  • d. Consolidation rectangle.

Answer: c. Head and shoulders is a reversal pattern. Triangles, flags and rectangles are continuation patterns.

34. Under the Dow Theory, the secondary movement typically retraces what proportion of the previous advance?

  • a. One-tenth to one-quarter.
  • b. One-third to two-thirds.
  • c. Three-quarters to nine-tenths.
  • d. The full amount.

Answer: b. The secondary movement usually retraces one-third to two-thirds of the previous advance or decline.

34a. The technical analyst is one who:

  • a. Buys shares whose intrinsic value is higher than the market price.
  • b. Tends to be long-term oriented.
  • c. Studies the prospects of earnings growth in forecasting future price trends.
  • d. Studies price and volume patterns of stocks.

Answer: d. Technical analysis studies historical market data — price changes and trading volume. Options (a) and (c) describe fundamental analysis, and technical analysts are typically shorter-term oriented than fundamental analysts.

34b. Which of the following indicates a buy signal to technical analysts?

  • a. The stock breaks through the moving average line from below.
  • b. A head and shoulders pattern is formed with a breakout below the neckline by 3% of the share price.
  • c. Both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Dow Jones Transportation Average are moving down.
  • d. The advance-decline line is falling in a rising market.

Answer: a. A break upward through the moving average is a bullish crossover. A head and shoulders breakout below the neckline is a sell signal, both averages moving down confirms a downtrend, and a falling advance-decline line in a rising market signals a market peak.

34c. Which of the following are bullish indicators?

  • a. Ascending triangles.
  • b. Descending triangles.
  • c. Double bottoms.
  • d. Reverse head and shoulders.

Options: (a), (c) and (d) · (b), (c) and (d) · (b) and (c) · (c) and (d)

Answer: (a), (c) and (d). Ascending triangles, double bottoms and inverse (reverse) head and shoulders are all bullish. A descending triangle is a bearish indicator.

34d. According to the Dow Theory, daily fluctuations are considered:

  • a. The secondary trend.
  • b. A moving average.
  • c. The primary trend.
  • d. Random and have no long-term forecasting value.

Answer: d. The Dow Theory holds that daily fluctuations are random noise with no forecasting value. Only the primary and secondary movements carry information.

34e. A low relative strength indicator (RSI) reading, below 20, could indicate that the stock is:

  • a. At a market peak and likely to head down.
  • b. Overbought.
  • c. Oversold.
  • d. Performing well compared with other stocks in the same risk category.

Answer: c. An RSI below 30 signals an oversold condition; below 20 is deeply oversold. Above 70 is overbought.

Chapter 12 — Case Studies

35. An individual earns S$400,000 a year. Under the SFA, is the individual an accredited investor?

  • a. Yes, because income in the preceding 12 months is at least S$300,000.
  • b. No, because net personal assets are not stated.
  • c. No, because only net personal assets qualify.
  • d. Yes, but only if the individual opts in.

Answer: a. Any one of the three individual tests suffices; income of at least S$300,000 in the preceding 12 months qualifies.

36. A carry trade borrows in a 1.5% currency and invests in a 6% currency, with the exchange rate unchanged. On an SGD-equivalent exposure of SGD 9,923,903.51, the annual gain is:

  • a. SGD 148,858.55
  • b. SGD 446,575.66
  • c. SGD 595,434.21
  • d. SGD 9,923,903.51

Answer: b. (0.06 − 0.015) × 9,923,903.51 = SGD 446,575.66.

37. A stock trades at 40**withnext−yearEPSof**40** with next-year EPS of **1.08 and a 5-year EPS growth rate of 38.99%. Its PEG ratio is approximately:

  • a. 0.92
  • b. 0.95
  • c. 1.05
  • d. 1.37

Answer: b. Prospective P/E = 40/1.08 = 37.04; PEG = 37.04/38.99 = 0.95.
