What these questions test

  • Q1–Q4 test the distinction between NPV and IRR, the normal distribution landmarks, VaR's construction, and the boundary between operational and funding-liquidity risk.
  • Q5–Q7 test the three indicator classes, credit creation, and the three yield-curve theories.
  • Q8–Q10 test forward points, the currency-adjustment divide-or-multiply rule, and NDF mechanics.
  • Q11–Q13 test the current ratio, the ROE manipulation route through goodwill, and the non-cash nature of depreciation.
  • Q13a–Q13b test the effect of a depreciation error on operating profit and total assets, and the stated purposes of the cash flow statement.
  • Q14–Q16 test rights-issue arithmetic, prospective P/E, and index weighting.
  • Q15a–Q15e test preference share characteristics, the price-weighted divisor after a split, CAPM with a beta of 1.3, the P/Sales use case, and the limits of ADRs.
  • Q16a–Q16e repeat the preference share, divisor, CAPM, P/Sales and ADR tests under the booklet's own numbering, so the appendix can be worked against it.
  • Q17–Q20 test the bank discount yield, bond pricing, convexity ordering, and the conversion premium.
  • Q20a–Q20e test zero-coupon price volatility, the direction of the call option, foreign government bond risks, par pricing when coupon equals yield, and the price-yield inverse relation.
  • Q21–Q24 test the two-asset risk formula, the Sharpe ratio, the TWR-versus-DWR choice, and CAPM.
  • Q24a–Q24e test perfect negative correlation, the CAPM inputs, total return including distributions, the TWR for frequent injections, and the Sharpe definition.
  • Q25–Q28 test deposit insurance exclusions, the REIT 75% investment test, business trust features, and annuity present value.
  • Q28a–Q28e test ETF advantages, real estate features, business trust versus REIT characteristics, hedge fund characteristics, and the definition of private equity.
  • Q29–Q31 test warrant intrinsic value, gearing, and the dividend effect.
  • Q31a–Q31e test warrant intrinsic value, conversion price, the premium with a conversion ratio of 2, gearing, and the determinants of a warrant's price.
  • Q32–Q34 test RSI thresholds, reversal versus continuation patterns, and Dow Theory retracement.
  • Q34a–Q34e test the technical analyst's remit, buy signals, bullish patterns, Dow Theory on daily fluctuations, and a deeply oversold RSI.
  • Q35–Q37 test the accredited investor income test, carry trade arithmetic, and PEG.

Exam cues

  • NPV falls when the discount rate rises; IRR does not change — IRR is a property of the cash flows alone.
  • ±1 standard deviation = 68%; ±2 = 95.4%. A 16% tail probability is about 1 in 6.25.
  • VaR can be computed historically or by Monte Carlo; it applies to bonds, shares and currencies.
  • Funding liquidity risk is not operational risk.
  • Leading: 10-year T-bond spread over Fed Funds. Coincident: nonfarm payrolls. Lagging: average duration of unemployment, average prime rate.
  • Lower reserve requirements expand the money supply through credit creation.
  • Liquidity preference: the curve is always upward sloping because long maturities need a premium.
  • Forward points: negative → subtract; positive → add. 1.2520 with −10 points = 1.2510.
  • Currency adjustment: reference currency first in the pair → divide; second → multiply.
  • NDF: cash-settled, no delivery, no notional exchange, tenor 1 month to 1 year.
  • Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities.
  • Goodwill write-downs raise ROE by shrinking the equity denominator.
  • Depreciation is non-cash and is added back in the cash flow statement.
  • Rights issue: theoretical ex-rights price = (old market value + new capital) / new share count.
  • Prospective P/E = price / next-year EPS.
  • Value-weighted indices adjust automatically for capital changes.
  • Bank discount yield = (D/F) × (360/t).
  • Bond price falls as the required yield rises above the coupon.
  • Zero-coupon bonds have the highest convexity.
  • Conversion premium (%) = (market value of CB − conversion value) / conversion value.
  • Portfolio risk is not a weighted average of constituent risks.
  • Sharpe = excess return / standard deviation.
  • TWR is the correct measure for judging a manager.
  • CAPM = Rf+β(Rm−Rf)R_f + \beta(R_m - R_f).
  • Deposit insurance covers S$ deposits only.
  • REIT: 75% investment test, 90% distribution test, 45% gearing cap.
  • Business trust: no gearing cap, no investment restrictions, single trustee-manager.
  • Annuity PV = C[1−(1+i)−n]/iC[1 - (1+i)^{-n}]/i.
  • Warrant intrinsic value = (SP − EP)/n; gearing = SP/(n × WP).
  • Dividends reduce a call warrant's price.
  • RSI above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold.
  • Head and shoulders is a reversal pattern.
  • Dow Theory secondary movement retraces one-third to two-thirds.
  • Accredited investor: any one of the three individual tests suffices.
  • Carry trade gain = interest differential × SGD-equivalent exposure when the rate is flat.
  • PEG below 1 suggests undervaluation.

Appendix B — Formulae Sheet

This formulae sheet is provided during the examination. The examination might not cover all formulas provided. Every symbol is defined where it first appears.

Risk, Return and Time Value Calculations

Measures of return

Total Return on a Security=Income+Capital Gain or LossPurchase Price\text{Total Return on a Security} = \frac{\text{Income} + \text{Capital Gain or Loss}}{\text{Purchase Price}}

Expected Rate of Return=E(R)=∑i=1nripi\text{Expected Rate of Return} = E(R) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i p_i

where E(R)E(R) is the expected return on a security, rir_i the iith possible return, pip_i the probability of that return, and nn the number of possible returns.

Measures of risk

Variance of Returns=σ2=∑pi[ri−E(R)]2\text{Variance of Returns} = \sigma^2 = \sum p_i \left[ r_i - E(R) \right]^2

Standard Deviation of Returns=σ=σ2\text{Standard Deviation of Returns} = \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}

Coefficient of Variation=CV=Standard Deviation of ReturnsExpected Rate of Return\text{Coefficient of Variation} = CV = \frac{\text{Standard Deviation of Returns}}{\text{Expected Rate of Return}}

Time value of money

Simple Interest=Principal×Interest Rate (in %)×Interest Period (in days)36,500\text{Simple Interest} = \frac{\text{Principal} \times \text{Interest Rate (in \%)} \times \text{Interest Period (in days)}}{36{,}500}

FVn=PV(1+k)nFV_n = PV(1 + k)^n

where FVnFV_n is the future value at the end of nn years, PVPV the present value or original amount invested at the beginning of the first year, nn the number of years of compounding, and kk the annual interest rate.

CAGR=[FVPV]1/n−1CAGR = \left[ \frac{FV}{PV} \right]^{1/n} - 1

where CAGRCAGR is the compounded annual growth rate, FVFV the future value, PVPV the present value, and nn the number of years.

FVn=PV(1+km)mnFV_n = PV\left(1 + \frac{k}{m}\right)^{mn}

where mm is the number of interest periods in the year.

Present value of a single cash flow

PV=FVn(1+k)nPV = \frac{FV_n}{(1 + k)^n}

where PVPV is the present value of the future sum, FVnFV_n the future value at the end of nn years, nn the number of years to receipt, and kk the annual discount or interest rate.

Key Drivers of Market Movements and Asset Values

Quantity theory of money

M×V=P×QM \times V = P \times Q

where MM is the stock of money (currency outside banks plus demand deposits), VV the velocity of money circulation (the number of times per period an average unit of money changes hands), PP the general price level or price index, and QQ the number of transactions in an economy during a year.

Foreign Exchange

Forward foreign exchange contract

Forward Points=S×(Rc−Rb)×n/3601+(Rb×n/360)\text{Forward Points} = \frac{S \times (R_c - R_b) \times n/360}{1 + (R_b \times n/360)}

where SS is the spot rate, RcR_c the annualised interest rate of the counter currency, RbR_b the annualised interest rate of the base currency, and nn the number of days from the spot date.

Interest rate parity

F=S[1+Rc(n360)1+Rb(n360)]F = S \left[ \frac{1 + R_c \left( \frac{n}{360} \right)}{1 + R_b \left( \frac{n}{360} \right)} \right]

where FF is the forward rate, SS the spot rate, RcR_c the annualised counter-currency rate, RbR_b the annualised base-currency rate, and nn the number of days.

Company Analysis and Understanding Financial Statements

Per share ratios

Book Value Per Share=Shareholders’ EquityTotal Number of Shares Outstanding\text{Book Value Per Share} = \frac{\text{Shareholders' Equity}}{\text{Total Number of Shares Outstanding}}

Fully Diluted Earnings Per Share=Net EarningsFully-Diluted Number of Shares\text{Fully Diluted Earnings Per Share} = \frac{\text{Net Earnings}}{\text{Fully-Diluted Number of Shares}}

Dividend Per Share=Dividends PaidTotal Number of Shares Outstanding\text{Dividend Per Share} = \frac{\text{Dividends Paid}}{\text{Total Number of Shares Outstanding}}

Liquidity ratios

Current Ratio=Current AssetsCurrent Liabilities\text{Current Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}

Quick Ratio=Cash+Marketable Securities+Accounts ReceivableCurrent Liabilities\text{Quick Ratio} = \frac{\text{Cash} + \text{Marketable Securities} + \text{Accounts Receivable}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}

Cash Ratio=Cash+Near-CashCurrent Liabilities\text{Cash Ratio} = \frac{\text{Cash} + \text{Near-Cash}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}

Cash Flow Ratio=Cash Flow From Operating ActivitiesCurrent Liabilities\text{Cash Flow Ratio} = \frac{\text{Cash Flow From Operating Activities}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}

Leverage ratios

Debt/Equity Ratio=Total DebtTotal Shareholders’ Equity\text{Debt/Equity Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Debt}}{\text{Total Shareholders' Equity}}

Debt-to-Total Assets Ratio=Total DebtTotal Assets\text{Debt-to-Total Assets Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Debt}}{\text{Total Assets}}

Total Liabilities-to-Total Assets Ratio=Total LiabilitiesTotal Assets\text{Total Liabilities-to-Total Assets Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Liabilities}}{\text{Total Assets}}

Interest Coverage=Earnings Before Interest and TaxesInterest Expense\text{Interest Coverage} = \frac{\text{Earnings Before Interest and Taxes}}{\text{Interest Expense}}

EBITDA Interest Coverage=EBITDAInterest Expense\text{EBITDA Interest Coverage} = \frac{\text{EBITDA}}{\text{Interest Expense}}

Total Fixed Charge Coverage=Earnings Before Interest, Taxes and Lease PaymentsInterest Expense+Lease Payments+Preferred Dividend1−Tax Rate\text{Total Fixed Charge Coverage} = \frac{\text{Earnings Before Interest, Taxes and Lease Payments}}{\text{Interest Expense} + \text{Lease Payments} + \dfrac{\text{Preferred Dividend}}{1 - \text{Tax Rate}}}

Operating efficiency / activity ratios

Total Asset Turnover=SalesAverage Total Assets\text{Total Asset Turnover} = \frac{\text{Sales}}{\text{Average Total Assets}}

Inventory Turnover=SalesAverage Inventory\text{Inventory Turnover} = \frac{\text{Sales}}{\text{Average Inventory}}

Days to Sell Inventory=365 daysInventory Turnover=Average InventorySales/365\text{Days to Sell Inventory} = \frac{365 \text{ days}}{\text{Inventory Turnover}} = \frac{\text{Average Inventory}}{\text{Sales}/365}

Receivables Turnover=SalesAverage Accounts Receivables\text{Receivables Turnover} = \frac{\text{Sales}}{\text{Average Accounts Receivables}}

Collection Period=365Receivables Turnover=Average Accounts ReceivablesSales/365\text{Collection Period} = \frac{365}{\text{Receivables Turnover}} = \frac{\text{Average Accounts Receivables}}{\text{Sales}/365}

Profitability ratios

Gross Profit Margin=Gross ProfitSales\text{Gross Profit Margin} = \frac{\text{Gross Profit}}{\text{Sales}}

Operating Profit Margin=Earnings Before Interest and TaxSales\text{Operating Profit Margin} = \frac{\text{Earnings Before Interest and Tax}}{\text{Sales}}

Net Profit Margin=Net IncomeSales\text{Net Profit Margin} = \frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{Sales}}

Return on Equity=Net IncomeAverage Common Equity\text{Return on Equity} = \frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{Average Common Equity}}

Pre-tax Return on Assets=Pre-Tax Income+Interest ExpenseAverage Total Assets\text{Pre-tax Return on Assets} = \frac{\text{Pre-Tax Income} + \text{Interest Expense}}{\text{Average Total Assets}}

After-tax Return on Assets=Net Income+Interest Expense(1−Tax Rate)Average Total Assets\text{After-tax Return on Assets} = \frac{\text{Net Income} + \text{Interest Expense}(1 - \text{Tax Rate})}{\text{Average Total Assets}}

Earnings Per Share=Net Income Available to Common ShareholdersAverage Number of Common Shares Outstanding\text{Earnings Per Share} = \frac{\text{Net Income Available to Common Shareholders}}{\text{Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding}}

Equity Securities

Revised net asset value per share

RNAVPS=Revised Asset Value−Market Value of LiabilitiesTotal Outstanding Number of SharesRNAVPS = \frac{\text{Revised Asset Value} - \text{Market Value of Liabilities}}{\text{Total Outstanding Number of Shares}}

Valuation ratios

Price-Earnings Ratio (P/E)=Market Price Per ShareEarnings Per Share\text{Price-Earnings Ratio (P/E)} = \frac{\text{Market Price Per Share}}{\text{Earnings Per Share}}

Price-Earnings Growth Ratio (PEG)=P/E% Growth in Earnings\text{Price-Earnings Growth Ratio (PEG)} = \frac{P/E}{\% \text{ Growth in Earnings}}

Price-to-Book Value Ratio (P/BV)=Market Price Per ShareBook Value Per Share\text{Price-to-Book Value Ratio (P/BV)} = \frac{\text{Market Price Per Share}}{\text{Book Value Per Share}}

Price-to-Revised Net Asset Value Ratio (P/RNAV)=Market Price Per Share(Market Value of Assets−Liabilities)/Shares Outstanding\text{Price-to-Revised Net Asset Value Ratio (P/RNAV)} = \frac{\text{Market Price Per Share}}{(\text{Market Value of Assets} - \text{Liabilities})/\text{Shares Outstanding}}

Price-to-Sales Ratio=Current Market Price Per ShareSales Per Share\text{Price-to-Sales Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Market Price Per Share}}{\text{Sales Per Share}}

Enterprise Value-to-Cash Flow Ratio=Market Cap+Debt+Preferred Shares−CashCash Flow from Operations\text{Enterprise Value-to-Cash Flow Ratio} = \frac{\text{Market Cap} + \text{Debt} + \text{Preferred Shares} - \text{Cash}}{\text{Cash Flow from Operations}}

Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA Ratio=Market Cap+Debt+Preferred+Minority Interest+Unfunded Pension−Associates−Cash &Near CashEarnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation\text{Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA Ratio} = \frac{\text{Market Cap} + \text{Debt} + \text{Preferred} + \text{Minority Interest} + \text{Unfunded Pension} - \text{Associates} - \text{Cash \& Near Cash}}{\text{Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation}}

Dividend yield

Dividend Yield=Dividend Per ShareMarket Price Per Share×100\text{Dividend Yield} = \frac{\text{Dividend Per Share}}{\text{Market Price Per Share}} \times 100

Dividend discount model

P0=D1(1+k)+D2(1+k)2+D3(1+k)3+…+D∞(1+k)∞P_0 = \frac{D_1}{(1+k)} + \frac{D_2}{(1+k)^2} + \frac{D_3}{(1+k)^3} + \dots + \frac{D_\infty}{(1+k)^\infty}

where P0P_0 is the intrinsic or theoretical value of the share today, DtD_t the dividends expected at the end of period tt, and kk the required rate of return.

With a subsequent sale of the share:

P0=D1(1+k)+D2(1+k)2+…+Dn(1+k)n+Pn(1+k)nP_0 = \frac{D_1}{(1+k)} + \frac{D_2}{(1+k)^2} + \dots + \frac{D_n}{(1+k)^n} + \frac{P_n}{(1+k)^n}

where nn is the holding period and PnP_n the expected selling price at the end of period nn.

Constant growth dividend discount model

P0=D0(1+g)(1+k)+D0(1+g)2(1+k)2+D0(1+g)3(1+k)3+…+D0(1+g)∞(1+k)∞P_0 = \frac{D_0(1+g)}{(1+k)} + \frac{D_0(1+g)^2}{(1+k)^2} + \frac{D_0(1+g)^3}{(1+k)^3} + \dots + \frac{D_0(1+g)^\infty}{(1+k)^\infty}

where D0D_0 is the current dividend and gg the constant growth rate. This simplifies to:

P0=D1k−gP_0 = \frac{D_1}{k - g}

where D1D_1 is the dividend expected at the end of period 1.

Required Rate of Return (k)=D1P0+g\text{Required Rate of Return } (k) = \frac{D_1}{P_0} + g

g=Retention Rate×Return on Equity=RR×ROEg = \text{Retention Rate} \times \text{Return on Equity} = RR \times ROE

Zero-growth model

P0=DividendDiscount RateP_0 = \frac{\text{Dividend}}{\text{Discount Rate}}

Multi-stage growth dividend discount model

For two-stage dividend growth:

P0=∑t=1nD0(1+g1)t(1+k)t+Dn(1+gc)k−gc(1+k)nP_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{D_0(1+g_1)^t}{(1+k)^t} + \frac{\dfrac{D_n(1+g_c)}{k - g_c}}{(1+k)^n}

where P0P_0 is the intrinsic value today, D0D_0 the current dividend, g1g_1 the growth rate when dividends are more predictable, gcg_c the constant growth rate when dividends are less predictable, kk the required rate of return, nn the number of periods of supernormal or subnormal growth, and DnD_n the dividend at the end of the abnormal growth period.

Deposits and Fixed-Income Securities

T-bill yield

Yd=DF×360tY_d = \frac{D}{F} \times \frac{360}{t}

where YdY_d is the annualised yield on a bank discount basis (as a decimal), DD the dollar discount (face value minus price), FF the face value, and tt the number of days remaining to maturity.

Bond valuation

With annual interest:

P=∑t=1nCt(1+k)t+M(1+k)nP = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1+k)^t} + \frac{M}{(1+k)^n}

where PP is the present value of the bond today, CtC_t the coupon payments for period tt, MM the maturity value, nn the number of years to maturity, and kk the required rate of return.

With semi-annual interest:

P=∑t=12nCt(1+k/2)t+M(1+k/2)2nP = \sum_{t=1}^{2n} \frac{C_t}{(1 + k/2)^t} + \frac{M}{(1 + k/2)^{2n}}

Zero-coupon bond:

P=M(1+k/2)2nP = \frac{M}{(1 + k/2)^{2n}}

Yield measures

Current Yield=Annual Interest PaymentBond Price\text{Current Yield} = \frac{\text{Annual Interest Payment}}{\text{Bond Price}}

Yield-to-maturity kk solves:

P=C11+k/2+C2(1+k/2)2+C3(1+k/2)3+…+C2n(1+k/2)2n+M(1+k/2)2nP = \frac{C_1}{1 + k/2} + \frac{C_2}{(1 + k/2)^2} + \frac{C_3}{(1 + k/2)^3} + \dots + \frac{C_{2n}}{(1 + k/2)^{2n}} + \frac{M}{(1 + k/2)^{2n}}

Effective Annual Yield=(1+Semi-Annual Interest Rate)2−1\text{Effective Annual Yield} = (1 + \text{Semi-Annual Interest Rate})^2 - 1

Approximate Yield-to-Maturity=Annual Interest Payment±Amortised Gain or Loss(Current Market Price+Par Value)/2\text{Approximate Yield-to-Maturity} = \frac{\text{Annual Interest Payment} \pm \text{Amortised Gain or Loss}}{(\text{Current Market Price} + \text{Par Value})/2}

Yield-to-maturity for a zero-coupon bond:

k2=[Maturity ValuePrice]1/2n−1\frac{k}{2} = \left[ \frac{\text{Maturity Value}}{\text{Price}} \right]^{1/2n} - 1

Taxable Equivalent Yield=Tax Exempt Yield1−Marginal Tax Rate\text{Taxable Equivalent Yield} = \frac{\text{Tax Exempt Yield}}{1 - \text{Marginal Tax Rate}}

Analysis of convertible bonds

Conversion Value=Conversion Ratio×Share Price\text{Conversion Value} = \text{Conversion Ratio} \times \text{Share Price}

Conversion Ratio=Par Value of Convertible BondConversion Price\text{Conversion Ratio} = \frac{\text{Par Value of Convertible Bond}}{\text{Conversion Price}}

Conversion Parity Price=Market Price of Convertible BondConversion Ratio\text{Conversion Parity Price} = \frac{\text{Market Price of Convertible Bond}}{\text{Conversion Ratio}}

Conversion Premium ($)=Market Value of Convertible Bond−Conversion Value\text{Conversion Premium (\$)} = \text{Market Value of Convertible Bond} - \text{Conversion Value}

Conversion Premium (%)=Market Value of Convertible Bond−Conversion ValueConversion Value\text{Conversion Premium (\%)} = \frac{\text{Market Value of Convertible Bond} - \text{Conversion Value}}{\text{Conversion Value}}

Breakeven Time/Payback=Conversion PremiumBond Income−Dividend Income\text{Breakeven Time/Payback} = \frac{\text{Conversion Premium}}{\text{Bond Income} - \text{Dividend Income}}

Premium Over Straight Value (%)=Market Price of Convertible BondInvestment Value−1\text{Premium Over Straight Value (\%)} = \frac{\text{Market Price of Convertible Bond}}{\text{Investment Value}} - 1

Portfolio Management

Calculating portfolio return and risk

Expected Return of a Portfolio=Rp=∑i=1nwiri\text{Expected Return of a Portfolio} = R_p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i r_i

where RpR_p is the expected portfolio return, wiw_i the portfolio weight for security ii, rir_i the expected return on security ii, nn the number of securities, and ∑wi=1.0\sum w_i = 1.0.

Portfolio Risk (two assets)=σp=w12σ12+w22σ22+2w1w2ρ1,2σ1σ2\text{Portfolio Risk (two assets)} = \sigma_p = \sqrt{w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \rho_{1,2} \sigma_1 \sigma_2}

where w1w_1 and w2w_2 are the portfolio weights, σ1\sigma_1 and σ2\sigma_2 the standard deviations, and ρ1,2\rho_{1,2} the correlation coefficient.

Capital market line

E(Rp)=Rf+E(Rm)−RfσmσpE(R_p) = R_f + \frac{E(R_m) - R_f}{\sigma_m} \sigma_p

where E(Rp)E(R_p) is the expected return on any efficient portfolio P on the CML, RfR_f the risk-free rate, E(Rm)E(R_m) the expected return on the market portfolio, σm\sigma_m the standard deviation of market returns, and σp\sigma_p the standard deviation of portfolio P's returns.

Capital asset pricing model

E(Ri)=Rf+βi(Rm−Rf)E(R_i) = R_f + \beta_i (R_m - R_f)

where E(Ri)E(R_i) is the expected return on security or portfolio ii, RfR_f the risk-free rate, RmR_m the expected market return, βi\beta_i the systematic risk relative to the market, and Rm−RfR_m - R_f the market risk premium.

Arbitrage pricing theory

Ri=E(Ri)+bi1f1+bi2f2+…+binfn+eiR_i = E(R_i) + b_{i1}f_1 + b_{i2}f_2 + \dots + b_{in}f_n + e_i

where RiR_i is the actual return on security ii in a period, E(Ri)E(R_i) the expected return, ff the deviation of a systematic factor from its expected value, bib_i the sensitivity of security ii's returns to a factor, and eie_i a random error term unique to security ii.

Measuring investment returns

No deposits or withdrawals:

Rp=VE−VBVBR_p = \frac{V_E - V_B}{V_B}

where VEV_E is the end value and VBV_B the beginning value.

Deposits or withdrawals at the end of the measurement period:

Rp=(VE+Withdrawals−Deposits)−VBVBR_p = \frac{(V_E + \text{Withdrawals} - \text{Deposits}) - V_B}{V_B}

Deposits or withdrawals at the beginning of the measurement period:

Rp=VE−(VB+Deposits−Withdrawals)VB+Deposits−WithdrawalsR_p = \frac{V_E - (V_B + \text{Deposits} - \text{Withdrawals})}{V_B + \text{Deposits} - \text{Withdrawals}}

Annualising returns:

Annual Return=[(1+r1)(1+r2)(1+r3)(1+r4)]−1\text{Annual Return} = [(1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3)(1 + r_4)] - 1

where r1,r2,r3,r4r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4 are the quarterly returns.

Modified Dietz method:

Rp=VE−VB−CFVB+WCFR_p = \frac{V_E - V_B - CF}{V_B + WCF}

where CFCF is the net cash flow over the period and WCFWCF the weighted cash flow:

WCF=∑iCFin−tinWCF = \sum_i CF_i \frac{n - t_i}{n}

where CFiCF_i is the cash flow on day tit_i, tit_i the number of days from the beginning of the period until CFiCF_i, and nn the number of days in the period.

Risk-adjusted measures of performance

Sharpe ratio=Rp−Rfσp\text{Sharpe ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}

where RpR_p is the average portfolio return, RfR_f the risk-free rate, and σp\sigma_p the standard deviation of portfolio returns.

Treynor ratio=Rp−Rfβp\text{Treynor ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\beta_p}

where βp\beta_p is the portfolio beta.

Jensen's alpha. The CAPM expected return is:

Re=Rf+βp(Rm−Rf)R_e = R_f + \beta_p (R_m - R_f)

The portfolio's alpha is the difference between the actual return RaR_a and the CAPM-expected return:

αp=Ra−Re=Ra−[Rf+βp(Rm−Rf)]\alpha_p = R_a - R_e = R_a - [R_f + \beta_p(R_m - R_f)]

Information ratio=αpσp\text{Information ratio} = \frac{\alpha_p}{\sigma_p}

where αp\alpha_p is Jensen's alpha and σp\sigma_p the excess risk.

Sortino ratio=Rp−Rfσnegative\text{Sortino ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_{\text{negative}}}

where σnegative\sigma_{\text{negative}} is the average downside volatility.

ETFs, Unit Trusts, REITs and Insurance

Net asset value

NAV=Fund Securities+Other Fund Assets−Liabilities (including management fees)−Debt used for leveragingTotal fund units outstanding\text{NAV} = \frac{\text{Fund Securities} + \text{Other Fund Assets} - \text{Liabilities (including management fees)} - \text{Debt used for leveraging}}{\text{Total fund units outstanding}}

Annuity calculations

Present value, PVannuity=C×[1−(1+i)−ni]\text{Present value, } PV_{\text{annuity}} = C \times \left[ \frac{1 - (1+i)^{-n}}{i} \right]

Future value, FVannuity=C×[(1+i)n−1i]\text{Future value, } FV_{\text{annuity}} = C \times \left[ \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i} \right]

where CC is the cash flow per period, ii the interest rate, and nn the number of payments.

Warrants

Warrant valuation

Intrinsic Value=SP−EPn\text{Intrinsic Value} = \frac{SP - EP}{n}

where SPSP is the share price, EPEP the exercise price, and nn the conversion ratio.

Conversion Price=n×WP+EP\text{Conversion Price} = n \times WP + EP

where WPWP is the warrant price.

Warrant Premium ($)=n×WP+EP−SP\text{Warrant Premium (\$)} = n \times WP + EP - SP

Warrant Premium (%)=n×WP+EP−SPSP×100\text{Warrant Premium (\%)} = \frac{n \times WP + EP - SP}{SP} \times 100

Gearing Ratio=SPn×WP\text{Gearing Ratio} = \frac{SP}{n \times WP}

Minimum Value of Warrant=SP−EP if SP>EP;=0 if SP≤EP\text{Minimum Value of Warrant} = SP - EP \text{ if } SP > EP; \qquad = 0 \text{ if } SP \le EP

Exam cues

  • Six return measures: total, expected, annualised, real, currency-adjusted, IRR. Only total and expected appear on this sheet.
  • Risk measures: variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation. CV is the only one expressed per unit of return.
  • TVM: FVn=PV(1+k)nFV_n = PV(1+k)^n; FVn=PV(1+k/m)mnFV_n = PV(1 + k/m)^{mn}; PV=FVn/(1+k)nPV = FV_n/(1+k)^n; CAGR=(FV/PV)1/n−1CAGR = (FV/PV)^{1/n} - 1. Simple interest uses 36,500 as the denominator.
  • Fisher's equation of exchange: M×V=P×QM \times V = P \times Q.
  • Forward points: S(Rc−Rb)(n/360)/[1+Rb(n/360)]S(R_c - R_b)(n/360) / [1 + R_b(n/360)]. Interest rate parity: F=S[(1+Rcn/360)/(1+Rbn/360)]F = S[(1 + R_c n/360)/(1 + R_b n/360)].
  • Per-share denominators differ: BVPS uses total shares outstanding; diluted EPS uses fully diluted shares; DPS uses total shares outstanding.
  • Liquidity ratios: current, quick (excludes inventory), cash, cash flow.
  • Leverage ratios: debt/equity, debt/total assets, total liabilities/total assets, interest coverage, EBITDA interest coverage, total fixed charge coverage (preferred dividend grossed up by dividing by 1 − tax rate).
  • Efficiency ratios use AVERAGE balances in the denominator.
  • Profitability: gross, operating, net margins; ROE; pre-tax and after-tax ROA; EPS.
  • Valuation ratios: P/E, PEG, P/BV, P/RNAV, P/Sales, EV/CF, EV/EBITDA. EV/EBITDA adds minorities and unfunded pension and subtracts associates and cash.
  • DDM family: general DDM, DDM with a subsequent sale, constant growth (Gordon), zero growth, two-stage. g=RR×ROEg = RR \times ROE.
  • T-bill yield: (D/F)(360/t)(D/F)(360/t).
  • Bond pricing: annual, semi-annual (double the periods, halve the rate), zero-coupon.
  • Yield measures: current yield, YTM, effective annual yield, approximate YTM, zero-coupon YTM, taxable equivalent yield.
  • Convertible measures: conversion value, conversion ratio, conversion parity price, conversion premium in dollars and per cent, breakeven time, premium over straight value.
  • Portfolio risk uses the two-asset formula with the correlation term; portfolio return is a simple weighted average.
  • CML uses total risk (σ); CAPM/SML uses beta.
  • APT is the multifactor model.
  • Return measurement: no cash flow, cash flow at end, cash flow at start, annualising, modified Dietz with weighted cash flow.
  • Risk-adjusted measures: Sharpe (σ), Treynor (β), Jensen's alpha, information ratio, Sortino (downside σ).
  • NAV subtracts liabilities including management fees and any debt used for leveraging.
  • Annuity PV and FV use the same bracket structure with the sign of the exponent reversed.
  • Warrant formulas: intrinsic value, conversion price, premium in dollars and per cent, gearing, minimum value.
  • Trap: the approximate YTM formula uses the average of current price and par in the denominator, not the current price alone.
  • Trap: EV/CF subtracts cash; EV/EBITDA subtracts cash and associates but adds minorities and unfunded pension.
  • Trap: the Sortino denominator is downside volatility, not total standard deviation.

Appendix C — Essential Readings

The source list runs to seven items. Candidates should complete the essential readings before attempting the examination. Use the current edition of each; page references in older editions will not match.

Core investment texts

# Instrument
1 Analysis of Investments and Management of Portfolios — Frank K. Reilly, Keith C. Brown
2 Fundamentals of Investment Management — Geoffrey A. Hirt, Stanley B. Block
3 Essentials of Investments — Zvi Bodie, Alex Kane, Alan J. Marcus
4 Fundamentals of Investments: Valuation and Management — Bradford D. Jordan, Thomas W. Miller, Steven D. Dolvin
5 Investments: Principles of Portfolio and Equity Analysis — Michael G. McMillan et al.

Technical analysis

# Instrument
6 Technical Analysis Plain and Simple: Charting the Markets in Your Language — Michael N. Kahn

Portfolio management

# Instrument
7 Managing Investment Portfolios: A Dynamic Process — John L. Maginn, Donald L. Tuttle, Jerald E. Pinto, Dennis W. McLeavey

How to read the list efficiently

  • Items 1–5 overlap heavily. They are general investments texts covering risk and return, asset classes, valuation and portfolio theory. Read one thoroughly — Bodie, Kane and Marcus (item 3) is the most compact for the risk-return and CAPM material, and Reilly and Brown (item 1) is the most comprehensive on asset classes. Use the others as reference for a topic the first does not explain well.
  • Item 5 is the CFA Institute's portfolio and equity analysis text and maps most closely onto Chapters 6 and 8 of this syllabus — equity valuation, relative valuation ratios and portfolio management.
  • Item 6 is the only technical analysis text and covers Chapter 11. Read it for the chart patterns and indicators; the examination tests recognition and interpretation, not construction.
  • Item 7 is the reference work on the portfolio management process, investment policy statements and performance measurement — Chapters 8 and 9.
  • Nothing on the list covers Chapters 1, 4, 7, 10 or 12 in depth. For those, the official study guide and this teaching guide are the primary sources: Chapter 1 (investor classification and market structure), Chapter 4 (FX quotations and forwards), Chapter 7 (fixed income, duration and convertibles), Chapter 10 (warrants) and Chapter 12 (case studies) are syllabus-specific and not covered by general investment texts at this level of detail.
  • Singapore-specific content — the SFA investor definitions, the Deposit Insurance Scheme, SGS, the CPF Investment Scheme, the Code on CIS, REIT rules and the Business Trusts Act — is not in any of these books. Use the MAS and SGX publications referenced in the chapters.

Exam cues

  • Seven items on the list, across five publishers.
  • Items 1–5 are general investments texts; item 6 is technical analysis; item 7 is portfolio management.
  • Bodie, Kane and Marcus is the most compact for risk-return and CAPM; Reilly and Brown is the most comprehensive on asset classes.
  • McMillan et al. maps most closely to the equity valuation and portfolio chapters.
  • Maginn et al. is the reference for the IPS and performance measurement.
  • Kahn is the only technical analysis text.
  • No listed text covers investor classification, FX mechanics, fixed income duration and convertibles, warrants, or the case studies at syllabus depth — use the official guide and this teaching guide.
  • Singapore regulatory content is not in any listed text. Use MAS and SGX sources.
  • Trap: the list is a reading list, not a syllabus. Reading all seven does not substitute for working the calculations in Chapters 2, 6, 7, 8 and 10.

Appendix D — Glossary

Terms are grouped by the chapter that uses them, so a term can be found from the topic you are revising rather than from its first letter. Each group ends with the chapter reference.

Investor classification and market structure

  • Accredited investor (AI) — an individual or entity meeting the SFA s 4A wealth or income tests, presumed financially savvy and able to bear more risk, with access to more complex products. Chapter 1.
  • Expert investor (EI) — a person whose business involves acquiring, disposing of or holding capital markets products; protected less than a retail investor because of occupational knowledge, not wealth. Chapter 1.
  • Institutional investor (II) — a government, statutory board, bank, insurer, CMS licensee, approved exchange, pension fund or CIS; the widest product access. Chapter 1.
  • Retail investor — anyone outside the AI, EI and II definitions; the highest level of protective regulation. Chapter 1.
  • Primary market — where new securities are issued and the issuer receives the cash. Chapter 1.
  • Secondary market — where already-issued securities trade and the selling investor receives the cash; supplies liquidity. Chapter 1.
  • Marketability — the likelihood of selling a security quickly; necessary but not sufficient for liquidity. Chapter 1.
  • Price continuity — prices do not change much between transactions absent new information. Chapter 1.
  • Internal efficiency — low transaction costs across reaching the market, brokerage and transfer. Chapter 1.
  • Price discovery — the process by which trading establishes a transparent price; the most important function of a market. Chapter 1.
  • Dealer — trades as principal, has a vested interest in the transaction and earns the bid-offer spread. Chapter 1.
  • Broker — acts as agent for a commission and does not take the other side. Chapter 1.

Risk, return and time value

  • Total return — current income plus capital gain or loss, divided by the purchase price. Chapter 2.
  • Expected rate of return — the probability-weighted average of possible returns. Chapter 2.
  • Real rate of return — the nominal return adjusted for inflation: (1+r)/(1+inflation)−1(1 + r)/(1 + \text{inflation}) - 1. Chapter 2.
  • Currency-adjusted return — the return restated in the investor's reference currency; divide when the reference currency is first in the pair, multiply when it is second. Chapter 2.
  • Internal rate of return (IRR) — the rate equating all cash outflows and inflows at one point in time; the money-weighted return. Chapter 2.
  • Compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) — the effective annual rate on the initial cash flow; the time-weighted return. Chapter 2.
  • Variance and standard deviation — measures of the dispersion of returns from the expected return. Chapter 2.
  • Volatility — the standard deviation of the security's returns; historical volatility differs from implied volatility. Chapter 2.
  • Coefficient of variation (CV) — risk per unit of expected return. Chapter 2.
  • Z-score — the number of standard deviations a return deviates from the expected return. Chapter 2.
  • Value at risk (VaR) — the loss at a stated tail probability, for example 2.5% or 0.5%. Chapter 2.
  • Systematic risk — market-wide risk that cannot be diversified away but can be hedged. Chapters 2, 8.
  • Non-systematic (firm-specific) risk — risk peculiar to a firm or industry, reducible to near zero by diversification. Chapters 2, 8.
  • Basis point — 0.01%, or 0.0001. Chapters 2, 7.

Market drivers

  • Fiscal policy — government expenditure and taxation used to influence aggregate demand and supply. Chapter 3.
  • Monetary policy — management of money supply and the cost of funding. Chapter 3.
  • Multiplier effect — fiscal spending rippling through industries, raising incomes and further consumption. Chapter 3.
  • Leading indicator — peaks and troughs precede the economy; a short-term predictor. Chapter 3.
  • Coincident indicator — peaks and troughs align with the economy; reflects the present. Chapter 3.
  • Lagging indicator — peaks and troughs follow the economy; confirms turning points. Chapter 3.
  • Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) — a leading indicator; 50 divides expansion from contraction. Chapter 3.
  • Industry life cycle — early development, rapid expansion, mature growth, stabilisation, decline. Chapter 3.
  • Porter's five forces — rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power. Chapter 3.
  • Herd instinct — following the crowd without independent decision-making; strongest when information is scarce. Chapter 3.
  • Loss aversion — from prospect theory; preferring less uncertainty for gains and more for losses, so investors sell winners and hold losers. Chapter 3.
  • Cognitive bias — concluding from past experience, preferences or predetermined beliefs; confirmation bias is the common form. Chapter 3.

Foreign exchange

  • Base currency — the first currency of a pair; the investor's reference currency. Chapter 4.
  • Counter (term) currency — the second currency of a pair. Chapter 4.
  • Pip — 0.0001, the fourth decimal place; the smallest FX price movement. Chapter 4.
  • Bid — the price at which the dealer buys. Chapter 4.
  • Offer (ask) — the price at which the dealer sells. Chapter 4.
  • Direct quote — foreign currency per unit of domestic currency. Chapter 4.
  • Indirect quote — domestic currency per unit of foreign currency; the reciprocal of the direct quote. Chapter 4.
  • Cross rate — a rate between two non-USD currencies derived from two USD rates. Chapter 4.
  • Forward points (swap points) — the interest differential expressed in FX rate terms; added for a premium, subtracted for a discount. Chapter 4.
  • Interest rate parity — the forward premium or discount equals the interest rate differential for the same maturity. Chapter 4.
  • Covered interest arbitrage — borrowing in one currency, investing in another and covering forward to lock a risk-free profit when parity is violated. Chapter 4.
  • Non-deliverable forward (NDF) — a cash-settled forward with no delivery of the domestic currency and no exchange of notional. Chapter 4.
  • Carry trade — borrowing in a low-yield currency to invest in a higher-yield one, capturing the differential. Chapters 4, 12.
  • Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS) — a settlement mechanism that reduces FX delivery risk. Chapter 4.

Company analysis

  • Balance sheet — a statement of financial position at a point in time: assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity. Chapter 5.
  • Common size statement — every item expressed as a percentage of total assets or of sales. Chapter 5.
  • Goodwill — the premium paid above the book value of an acquired company; written down against equity reserves. Chapter 5.
  • Treasury stock — shares bought back and retired, benefiting remaining shareholders. Chapter 5.
  • Hidden reserves — value not reflected in book value, from rezoned land or provisions not written back. Chapters 5, 6.
  • Current ratio — current assets / current liabilities. Chapter 5.
  • Quick (acid test) ratio — current assets excluding inventory, over current liabilities. Chapter 5.
  • Gearing (debt-to-equity) — total debt / total shareholders' equity. Chapter 5.
  • Interest coverage — EBIT / interest expense. Chapter 5.
  • Total fixed charge coverage — earnings before interest, taxes and lease payments over interest plus lease payments plus the grossed-up preferred dividend. Chapter 5.
  • Cash conversion cycle — the period between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Chapter 5.
  • Window dressing — manipulating reporting-date ratios by collecting receivables early, cutting inventory and delaying purchases. Chapter 5.
  • Quality of earnings — realistic, repeatable earnings supported by conservative accounting and adequate provisioning. Chapter 5.

Equity securities

  • Residual claim — ordinary shareholders are paid last on liquidation. Chapter 6.
  • Limited liability — shareholders can lose only their original investment. Chapter 6.
  • Preference share — a hybrid with a fixed dividend, no vote except in distress, ranked above ordinary and below bonds. Chapter 6.
  • Rights issue — new capital raised from existing shareholders pro rata; prevents dilution. Chapter 6.
  • Bonus issue — additional shares from reserves; raises no capital. Chapter 6.
  • Stock split — divides existing shares to lower the unit price; raises no capital. Chapter 6.
  • Reverse stock split — consolidates shares, often to escape penny-stock restrictions. Chapter 6.
  • Value-weighted index — weights by market capitalisation; adjusts automatically for capital changes. Chapter 6.
  • Price-weighted index — arithmetic average of prices; high-priced shares dominate. Chapter 6.
  • Equal-weighted index — all constituents carry equal weight. Chapter 6.
  • Efficient frontier — the set of portfolios offering the highest return for each level of risk. Chapters 6, 8.
  • Book value — assets net of liabilities as stated on the balance sheet. Chapter 6.
  • Liquidation value — the value realised on a forced sale of assets. Chapter 6.
  • Revised net asset value (RNAV) — book value restated to market value. Chapter 6.
  • Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) — after-tax operating cash flow less capital expenditure, plus non-cash charges. Chapter 6.
  • WACC — the weighted average of the cost of equity and after-tax cost of debt. Chapter 6.
  • Terminal value — the present value at the end of the projection period of all subsequent cash flows. Chapter 6.
  • P/E ratio — price per share / earnings per share; trailing or leading. Chapter 6.
  • PEG ratio — P/E divided by expected EPS growth; below 1 suggests undervaluation. Chapters 6, 12.
  • P/BV ratio — price per share / book value per share; suited to banks, insurers and property companies. Chapter 6.
  • Enterprise value (EV) — market capitalisation plus debt and preferred shares, less cash. Chapter 6.
  • EV/EBITDA — the enterprise multiple; unaffected by capital structure. Chapter 6.
  • Earnings yield — the inverse of P/E; compared with bond yields to give the yield gap. Chapter 6.
  • Depositary receipt (DR) — a security trading in an investor's home market representing a foreign underlying share. Chapter 6.
  • ADR levels — Level 1 OTC, Level 2 exchange-listed, Level 3 exchange-listed with capital raising. Chapter 6.
  • Greenshoe (over-allotment) option — lets underwriters stabilise an IPO price by buying back shares. Chapter 6.
  • Claw-back — reallocation of IPO shares between institutional and retail tranches. Chapter 6.

Fixed income

  • Par (face) value — the redemption value repaid at maturity; usually $1,000. Chapter 7.
  • Coupon rate — the periodic interest rate applied to par value. Chapter 7.
  • Term bond — a single maturity date. Chapter 7.
  • Serial bond — several maturity dates. Chapter 7.
  • Bank discount yield — (D/F)(360/t)(D/F)(360/t); based on face value, so not a true return. Chapter 7.
  • Accrued interest — interest earned since the last coupon, paid by the buyer to the seller. Chapter 7.
  • Eurobond — underwritten internationally, offered simultaneously in several countries, issued outside any single jurisdiction. Chapter 7.
  • Zero-coupon bond — no coupons, sold at a deep discount; no reinvestment risk, highest convexity. Chapter 7.
  • Floating rate bond — coupon reset periodically against a benchmark such as SIBOR. Chapter 7.
  • Covered bond — highly rated paper backed by bank assets; no default since 1769. Chapter 7.
  • High-yield (junk) bond — rated below BBB; trades on creditworthiness rather than rates. Chapter 7.
  • Payment-in-kind (PIK) bond — the issuer may pay cash or issue a similar bond. Chapter 7.
  • Perpetual bond — no maturity; ranks before equities on default. Chapter 7.
  • Call provision — the issuer's right to redeem early; raises the yield. Chapter 7.
  • Put provision — the holder's right to sell back at par; lowers the yield. Chapter 7.
  • Sinking fund — annual retirement of part of the issue; reduces credit risk. Chapter 7.
  • Credit spread — the yield difference between bonds of the same maturity and different credit quality. Chapter 7.
  • Credit default swap (CDS) — a contract transferring default risk for a premium. Chapter 7.
  • Collateralised debt obligation (CDO) — pooled bonds (CBO) or loans (CLO) repackaged and sold in tranches. Chapter 7.
  • Duration — the linear price sensitivity to small yield changes; higher for lower coupons, lower yields and longer maturities. Chapter 7.
  • Convexity — the curvature of the price-yield relationship; higher for lower coupons, highest for zero-coupon bonds. Chapter 7.
  • PVBP (PV01) — the change in portfolio value for a one basis point rate move. Chapter 7.
  • Current yield — annual interest / price; ignores capital gain or loss. Chapter 7.
  • Yield-to-maturity (YTM) — the discount rate equating present value to price. Chapter 7.
  • Bond-equivalent yield — the semi-annual YTM doubled. Chapter 7.
  • Taxable equivalent yield (TEY) — tax-exempt yield / (1 − marginal tax rate). Chapter 7.
  • Reinvestment risk — the risk that coupons cannot be reinvested at the same rate; rises with coupon and maturity. Chapter 7.
  • Term structure (yield curve) — the relationship between YTM and maturity. Chapter 7.
  • Expectations theory — the curve's shape reflects interest rate expectations. Chapter 7.
  • Liquidity preference theory — the curve is always upward sloping because long maturities need a premium. Chapter 7.
  • Market segmentation theory — each maturity's yield is set by supply and demand in that segment. Chapter 7.
  • Conversion parity price — market price of the convertible / conversion ratio. Chapter 7.
  • Conversion premium — the excess of the convertible's market price over its conversion value. Chapter 7.
  • Breakeven time — conversion premium / (bond income − dividend income). Chapter 7.

Portfolio management

  • Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) — prices fully reflect available information; weak, semi-strong and strong forms. Chapter 8.
  • Random walk — price movements are independent over time. Chapters 8, 11.
  • Passive strategy — buy-and-hold or index tracking, minimising cost. Chapter 8.
  • Active strategy — security selection, sector rotation and market timing to beat a benchmark. Chapter 8.
  • Correlation coefficient (ρ) — the extent to which two securities' returns move together; +1 to −1. Chapter 8.
  • Market portfolio (M) — the fully diversified portfolio of all risky assets, containing only systematic risk. Chapter 8.
  • Capital market line (CML) — the risk-return trade-off for efficient portfolios, using total risk. Chapter 8.
  • Security market line (SML) — the risk-return trade-off for all assets, using beta. Chapter 8.
  • Beta — the sensitivity of a security's return to the market; the market's beta is 1. Chapter 8.
  • Alpha — the excess of actual return over the model-predicted return. Chapter 8.
  • Arbitrage pricing theory (APT) — a multifactor equilibrium model; factors must be pervasive, influence expected return and be unpredictable. Chapter 8.
  • Investment policy statement (IPS) — the client's mandate, recording objectives and constraints. Chapter 8.
  • Strategic asset allocation (SAA) — the long-run policy mix, a constant-mix strategy. Chapter 8.
  • Tactical asset allocation (TAA) — short-run overweighting and underweighting within SAA ranges. Chapter 8.
  • Dollar-weighted return (DWR) — the IRR; sensitive to the size and timing of cash flows. Chapter 8.
  • Time-weighted return (TWR) — links sub-period returns; unaffected by client cash flows, so preferred for judging managers. Chapter 8.
  • Modified Dietz method — approximates TWR by weighting each cash flow by the time held. Chapter 8.
  • GIPS — the Global Investment Performance Standards; require total return, TWR, monthly valuation and disclosure. Chapter 8.
  • Sharpe ratio — excess return per unit of total risk. Chapter 8.
  • Treynor ratio — excess return per unit of systematic risk. Chapter 8.
  • Jensen's alpha — actual return less the CAPM-expected return. Chapters 8, 12.
  • Information ratio — alpha per unit of excess risk. Chapter 8.
  • Sortino ratio — excess return per unit of downside volatility. Chapter 8.
  • Bogey — the passive benchmark against which attribution is measured. Chapter 8.
  • Performance attribution — decomposing excess return into asset allocation and selection components. Chapter 8.

Funds, REITs and insurance

  • Collective investment scheme (CIS) — a pooled investment vehicle governed by the Code on CIS. Chapter 9.
  • Variable Capital Company (VCC) — a fund structure allowing free issue and redemption of shares, dividends from capital, and umbrella sub-funds. Chapter 9.
  • Exchange-traded fund (ETF) — a passively managed fund tracking an index, traded during exchange hours. Chapter 9.
  • Net asset value (NAV) — fund assets less liabilities, divided by units outstanding. Chapter 9.
  • Physical (cash) replication — holding the actual index securities, by full replication or representative sampling. Chapter 9.
  • Synthetic replication — using swaps and derivatives to mimic the index; lower tracking error, higher counterparty risk. Chapter 9.
  • Tracking error — the divergence between an ETF's return and its index. Chapter 9.
  • Smart beta — weighting securities on performance criteria rather than market capitalisation. Chapter 9.
  • Securities lending — lending portfolio shares for collateral and interest; creates counterparty risk. Chapter 9.
  • Cash equitisation — converting cash to equities via ETFs to reduce cash drag. Chapter 9.
  • Unit trust — a CIS pooling funds under an independent trustee. Chapter 9.
  • Open-end fund — issues units continuously at NAV. Chapter 9.
  • Closed-end fund — a fixed number of units priced by market demand and supply. Chapter 9.
  • Offer price — the price at which an investor buys units; NAV plus purchase expenses, cash, accrued income and the initial charge. Chapter 9.
  • Bid price — the price at which an investor sells units; NAV less sale expenses, plus cash and accrued income. Chapter 9.
  • Front-end load — a sales charge of 1.5–5% of NAV. Chapter 9.
  • Back-end load — a redemption fee, often waived after a holding period. Chapter 9.
  • High watermark — the profit level a manager must exceed before a performance fee is paid. Chapter 9.
  • Total expense ratio — total expenses including management fees, over NAV. Chapter 9.
  • Retrocession — a distribution fee paid by the fund house to the distributor; a conflict of interest that reduces NAV. Chapter 9.
  • REIT — a CIS investing at least 75% in income-producing real estate and distributing at least 90% of taxable income. Chapter 9.
  • Business trust — a hybrid structure under the Business Trusts Act 2004, not a separate legal entity, with a single trustee-manager. Chapter 9.
  • Stapled security — two or more securities traded as one instrument. Chapter 9.
  • UCITS — the EU directive providing a passport for cross-border fund distribution. Chapter 9.
  • Hedge fund — a fund using short selling, derivatives and leverage with absolute return targets. Chapter 9.
  • Lock-up period — a period during which hedge fund investors cannot redeem. Chapter 9.
  • Gate provision — a limit on withdrawals at a given redemption date. Chapter 9.
  • Private equity J-curve — negative early cash flows during the 5–6 year investment period, with harvest from year 6. Chapter 9.
  • Whole life policy — life cover plus cash value, payable on death whenever it occurs. Chapter 9.
  • Endowment policy — payable on maturity or death, whichever is earlier. Chapter 9.
  • With-profits policy — benefits linked indirectly through annual valuation and a reversionary bonus. Chapter 9.
  • Investment-linked policy — policy values linked directly to underlying unit values. Chapter 9.
  • Immediate annuity — payments begin at purchase, funded by a single premium. Chapter 9.
  • Deferred annuity — payments begin at a future date. Chapter 9.
  • Dollar cost averaging — investing equal amounts over time, accumulating more units when prices are low. Chapter 9.

Warrants

  • Warrant — a right, not an obligation, to buy or sell a specified number of securities at a fixed price within a specified period. Chapter 10.
  • Company warrant — issued by the company on its own shares; call only; new shares issued on exercise. Chapter 10.
  • Structured warrant — issued by a third party such as a bank; call or put; cash-settled; no new shares. Chapter 10.
  • Conversion ratio — the number of warrants needed to convert into one share. Chapter 10.
  • Intrinsic value — (SP − EP)/n when in-the-money; zero otherwise. Chapter 10.
  • Conversion price — the total cost of one share via the warrant: n × WP + EP. Chapter 10.
  • Warrant premium — the extra cost of the warrant route over buying the share outright. Chapter 10.
  • Gearing ratio — SP / (n × WP); the leverage the warrant provides. Chapter 10.

Technical and quantitative analysis

  • Technical analysis — forecasting price movements from historical market data; not concerned with fair value. Chapter 11.
  • Advance-decline (A/D) line — cumulative advances minus declines across all securities; measures market breadth. Chapter 11.
  • Moving average — the average closing price over a period; smooths erratic price changes. Chapter 11.
  • MACD — the difference between a fast and a slow EMA, with a signal line; commonly (12,26,9). Chapter 11.
  • Bollinger Bands — a 20-day SMA plus and minus two standard deviations. Chapter 11.
  • Support level — a price range where a substantial increase in demand is expected. Chapter 11.
  • Resistance level — a price range where buyers refuse to pay more and sellers take profits; the overhang. Chapter 11.
  • Breakout — a move through support or resistance, confirming the trend. Chapter 11.
  • Dow Theory — primary, secondary and daily movements; confirmed when the DJIA and DJTA agree. Chapter 11.
  • Relative Strength Index (RSI) — a momentum indicator from 0 to 100; above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold. Chapter 11.
  • Head and shoulders — a reversal pattern at a peak; the inverse form marks a bottom. Chapter 11.
  • Double top / bottom — a reversal pattern confirmed when the neckline breaks. Chapter 11.
  • Consolidation rectangle — a sideways continuation pattern. Chapter 11.
  • Triangle — symmetrical (either direction), ascending (bullish) or descending (bearish). Chapter 11.
  • Flag and pennant — short continuation patterns after a sharp move; parallel lines versus converging lines. Chapter 11.
  • Wedge — converging lines both moving the same direction; a rising wedge is bearish. Chapter 11.
  • Gap — a price range with no transactions; breakaway, runaway or exhaustion. Chapter 11.
  • Elliott Wave Theory — 5-wave advances and 3-wave retreats exhibiting the Golden Ratio 1.618. Chapter 11.
  • Quantitative analysis — abstracting market reality into models to find price anomalies and arbitrage. Chapter 11.

Exam cues

  • Grouped by chapter, not alphabetically — find a term from the topic you are revising.
  • Four investor categories: II, AI, EI, retail. AI thresholds: S2mnetpersonalassets(residencecappedatS2m net personal assets (residence capped at S1m), S1mfinancialassets,orS1m financial assets, or S300k income; entity S$10m.
  • Primary market: issuer gets the cash. Secondary market: selling investor gets the cash.
  • Dealer = principal earning the spread; broker = agent earning commission.
  • Six return measures; three risk measures (variance, standard deviation, CV).
  • IRR is money-weighted; CAGR is time-weighted.
  • Systematic risk cannot be diversified but can be hedged; non-systematic can be diversified away.
  • Leading precedes, coincident aligns, lagging follows. PMI 50 is the dividing line.
  • Base currency first; pip = 0.0001; bid is where the dealer buys.
  • Forward points: add for a premium, subtract for a discount; the higher-rate currency is at a discount.
  • NDF: cash-settled, no delivery, no notional exchange.
  • Balance sheet is a snapshot; common size uses total assets or sales as 100%.
  • Goodwill write-downs shrink equity and raise ROE.
  • Efficiency ratios use average balances.
  • Residual claim and limited liability define an ordinary share.
  • Rights issue raises capital; bonus issue and stock split do not.
  • Value-weighted adjusts automatically; price-weighted needs a divisor.
  • PEG below 1 suggests undervaluation.
  • EV subtracts cash; EV/EBITDA also subtracts associates and adds minorities and unfunded pension.
  • Bank discount yield uses face value, so it overstates the true return.
  • Zero-coupon bonds have no reinvestment risk and the highest convexity.
  • Duration rises with lower coupon, lower yield and longer maturity.
  • CML uses total risk; SML uses beta.
  • TWR is the correct measure for judging a manager.
  • Sharpe uses σ; Treynor uses β; Sortino uses downside σ.
  • REIT: 75% investment, 90% distribution, 45% gearing. Business trust: no gearing cap, no investment restrictions.
  • Company warrant: call only, new shares issued. Structured warrant: call or put, cash-settled.
  • RSI above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold.
  • Head and shoulders is a reversal; triangles, flags and rectangles are continuations.
  • Trap: a dealer and a broker are not interchangeable.
  • Trap: marketability is necessary but not sufficient for liquidity.
  • Trap: a beta of zero does not make an asset risk-free.
  • Trap: an unrated bond is not automatically a default risk.

Exam method and final revision checklist

The CM-EIP paper is 90 questions in 2 hours 30 minutes — about 100 seconds per question, including the three case studies that carry nine questions between them. The pass mark is 70%, so 63 correct answers. That leaves room for 27 errors and no more, which means the method matters as much as the knowledge.

How to work the paper

  1. Answer every question. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank. If time is short, fill the remaining answers with your best judgement and return only if time allows.
  2. Read the stem for the qualifier first. Words such as least likely, most appropriate, not, except and which of the following is TRUE decide the answer more often than the technical content does.
  3. Classify the question before computing. Most calculation questions name the measure they want. Identify whether it is a return measure, a risk measure, a valuation ratio, a bond measure or a warrant measure, then recall the formula from Appendix B.
  4. Check the convention. 365-day for Singapore Government Securities, 360-day for everything else. Semi-annual coupons double the periods and halve the rate. Currency adjustment divides when the reference currency is first in the pair and multiplies when it is second.
  5. Sanity-check the magnitude. A bond priced at $1,147 against a $1,000 par with an 8% coupon and a 6% yield is plausible; $1,014 is not. A P/E of 12x on a mature industrial and 37x on a high-growth semiconductor are both plausible; 370x is not.
  6. For multiple-response questions, evaluate each option independently. Do not look for a pattern in the letters. A statement is true or false on its own merits.
  7. Do the case studies last if they are grouped at the end, or first if you prefer to bank the applied marks while fresh. Either way, read the scenario once and note the client's objective, horizon, risk tolerance and any constraint — the questions usually turn on one of those.
  8. Leave the hardest calculation for a second pass. Mark it, move on, and return. Two minutes lost on one question costs two easier questions.

The ten distinctions that decide the most marks

Distinction The rule
Primary vs secondary market Primary: the issuer receives the cash. Secondary: the selling investor does
Dealer vs broker Dealer trades as principal and earns the spread; broker acts as agent for a commission
Money market vs capital market Money market: ≤ 1 year. Capital market: > 1 year
Direct vs indirect quote Direct: foreign/domestic. Indirect: domestic/foreign — the reciprocal
Discount vs premium bond Coupon below yield → discount. Coupon above yield → premium. Equal → par
Duration vs convexity Duration is the linear first-order sensitivity; convexity is the curvature, the second derivative
CML vs SML CML: efficient portfolios, total risk. SML: all assets, beta
DWR vs TWR DWR = IRR, driven by client cash flows. TWR = manager skill, unaffected by them
REIT vs business trust REIT: 90% distribution, 45% gearing cap, real estate only. Business trust: no minimum, no cap, any business
Company vs structured warrant Company: call only, new shares issued, years. Structured: call or put, cash-settled, 6–12 months

Before the examination, be able to explain the difference between

  • An institutional, accredited, expert and retail investor, and the statutory thresholds for each.
  • A financial asset and a real asset, and why the distinction matters to an adviser.
  • Money market and capital market instruments, and which are quoted on a discount basis.
  • Total return, expected return, annualised return, real return, currency-adjusted return and IRR — and which question each answers.
  • Variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation and value at risk.
  • Systematic and non-systematic risk, and how each is managed.
  • Fiscal and monetary policy, and how each transmits to asset prices.
  • Leading, coincident and lagging indicators, with one example of each.
  • Direct, indirect and cross FX quotations, and the bid-offer spread.
  • Forward points and interest rate parity, and why the higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount.
  • A non-deliverable forward and why it exists.
  • Qualitative and quantitative company analysis.
  • The balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement, and what each reveals that the others do not.
  • Liquidity, leverage, efficiency and profitability ratios, and which use average balances.
  • Ordinary and preference shares, and the claim order on liquidation.
  • A rights issue, bonus issue, stock split and reverse split.
  • Value-weighted, price-weighted and equal-weighted indices.
  • Net asset, absolute (DCF) and relative valuation.
  • P/E, PEG, P/BV, P/Sales, EV/CF and EV/EBITDA, and when each is appropriate.
  • Deposits, money market instruments and bonds, and the deposit insurance limits.
  • Duration and convexity, and what each implies for price risk.
  • Current yield, YTM, bond-equivalent yield and taxable equivalent yield.
  • The expectations, liquidity preference and market segmentation theories of the yield curve.
  • Conversion value, conversion parity price, conversion premium and breakeven time for a convertible bond.
  • The weak, semi-strong and strong forms of the efficient market hypothesis.
  • Passive and active management, and the three active strategies.
  • Strategic and tactical asset allocation.
  • The Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen, information and Sortino measures, and which risk each uses.
  • Performance attribution and the difference between allocation and selection effects.
  • An ETF, a unit trust, a REIT, a business trust and a stapled security.
  • Whole life, endowment, with-profits and investment-linked insurance.
  • An immediate and a deferred annuity, and why annuities hedge longevity risk.
  • Dollar cost averaging and market timing.
  • A company warrant and a structured warrant, and the four warrant valuation measures.
  • Technical analysis and fundamental analysis, and the assumptions that separate them.
  • Support, resistance, breakout and the main reversal and continuation patterns.

Final week

  • Re-read every chapter's Exam cues block. They are written to be the last thing you read.
  • Work the Appendix A review questions without looking at the answers, then check.
  • Rehearse the formulae sheet in Appendix B until you can locate any formula within seconds. It is provided in the examination, so the skill is retrieval, not memorisation.
  • Practise the case studies in Chapter 12 as full sets of three questions, timed.
  • Take at least two full mock exams on this site at the real length and pass mark.
  • Confirm the logistics: original NRIC or passport, a non-programmable calculator, arrival about 30 minutes early, and no notes or smart devices.

Exam cues

  • 90 questions, 150 minutes, 70% pass — 63 correct. About 100 seconds per question.
  • Never leave a blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer.
  • Read the qualifier first: least likely, most appropriate, not, except, TRUE.
  • Classify before computing — return, risk, valuation, bond or warrant measure.
  • Conventions: 365 for SGS, 360 for everything else; semi-annual doubles periods and halves the rate; currency adjustment divides when the reference currency is first in the pair.
  • Sanity-check magnitudes before committing to an answer.
  • Multiple response: evaluate each option independently; do not look for letter patterns.
  • Case studies: note the client's objective, horizon, risk tolerance and constraints first.
  • Mark and return on the hardest calculation rather than losing two easier marks.
  • The ten highest-value distinctions are listed in the table above — learn them as pairs.
  • The formulae sheet is provided, so practise retrieval, not memorisation.
  • Trap: the pass mark is 70%, not 75% — do not carry over the FMRP or RES 12B figure.
  • Trap: the paper includes 3 case studies of 9 questions, not a separate case-study section worth a fifth of the marks.
